The biggest shift: from 2025 onward the paper dropped the "attempt any 40 of 50" choice and made all 50 questions compulsory, with a longer 60-minute window and 250 total marks instead of 200.

How the kind of questions has changed

2022

Case-study passages (one 5-question case) and graph-based, Data-Interpretation-style questions were common, alongside numericals from National Income and Aggregate Demand/Supply — reported as the toughest, most time-pressured year in this stretch.

2023

A shift toward straightforward questions close to NCERT's own wording — the case study leaned on the Consumer Behaviour/Utility chapter, and questions followed no fixed easy-to-hard sequence.

2024

More theory-based than numerical, with a continued tilt toward Microeconomics and questions taken close to the NCERT text — though some students still found the paper lengthy.

2025

Reports vary — several sources describe a mostly theory/definition-heavy paper, others note 10–12 genuinely calculation-based questions — but Microeconomics clearly dominated, at roughly 70–75% of the paper against 30–35% Macroeconomics.

2026

A more even mix of theoretical, application-based, and numerical questions, with Microeconomics and Macroeconomics given roughly equal weight this time.

Which topics matter more now

Then

2022–2024 leaned on National Income numericals and Aggregate Demand/Supply as the reliable "hard" questions, alongside a growing share of straightforward, NCERT-worded Microeconomics theory.

Now

Microeconomics carries the larger share of the paper overall, but within Macroeconomics specifically, National Income, Money & Banking, and Income Determination are each independently flagged as the most conceptually demanding, highest-weightage topics (~15% each) — the same three chapters this app's own prep checklist below already prioritises.

A short prep checklist

  • Read the NCERT textbook fully at least once before jumping straight into practice questions — CUET stays close to NCERT's own wording.
  • Build one formula sheet covering all three courses and revise it every few days instead of re-deriving formulas each time.
  • Solve real previous-year questions — untimed first to build accuracy, then timed to build speed.
  • Take at least one full 60-minute mock at real exam pace before exam day, not just topic-wise practice.
  • Revisit your wrong answers weekly — a mistake reviewed once is often repeated; review it until it stops happening.
  • Prioritise the numerical-heavy chapters — National Income, Money & Banking, and Income Determination — since these are consistently tested most.
  • Know your skip threshold — decide in advance how confident you need to be before attempting an unsure question, given the −1 negative marking.
  • Spend the final week revising, not learning new topics — consolidate formulas and definitions rather than starting fresh material.

Chapter importance is our own editorial judgement, based on real weightage patterns we found across past papers — not an official CUET ranking.

CUET(UG) 2026 — Economics/Business Economics SyllabusOpen in new tab ↗

The three courses, at a glance

Course I — Introductory Microeconomics
  • Unit I: Introduction & Theory of Consumer Behaviour — meaning of microeconomics, central problems of an economy, consumer's equilibrium (utility approach), demand and price elasticity of demand.
  • Unit II: Production and Costs — production function, TP/MP/AP curves, cost & revenue concepts, producer's equilibrium.
  • Unit III: The Firm under Perfect Competition — features, profit maximisation, price determination, supply and price elasticity of supply.
  • Unit IV: Market Equilibrium and Simple Applications — excess demand/supply, price ceiling and price flooring.
Course II — Introductory Macroeconomics
  • Unit I: Introduction & National Income Accounting — circular flow of income, the three methods of calculating National Income, GDP and welfare.
  • Unit II: Money and Banking — functions of money, money creation & the money multiplier, RBI and policy tools.
  • Unit III: Determination of Income and Employment — aggregate demand, the two-sector model, excess/deficient demand, the multiplier.
  • Unit IV: Government Budget and the Economy — objectives, receipts & expenditure classification, deficit measures.
  • Unit V: Open Economy Macroeconomics — balance of payments, exchange rate regimes, managed floating.
Course III — Indian Economic Development
  • Unit I: Development Policies and Experience (1947–90) — state of the economy at independence, Five Year Plans, agriculture/industry/trade policy.
  • Unit II: Economic Reforms since 1991 — liberalisation, globalisation and privatisation (LPG).
  • Unit III: Current Challenges Facing the Indian Economy — human capital, rural development, employment, environment & sustainable development.
  • Unit IV: Development Experiences of India — comparison with neighbouring countries, development strategies.

    Introductory Macroeconomics · Chapter 3

    Money and Banking

    NCERT's own definitions, worked examples, and diagrams — with memory tricks and CUET pattern-alerts built right in. Pick a topic from the dropdown to jump around.

    01Barter System & Functions of Money

    Before money, exchange needed a coincidence so rare it strangled trade. Money's whole job is to remove that coincidence.

    Conceptual foundation — near-certain 1 question

    Try this first

    A farmer has surplus rice and wants clothing in exchange. Why can't she just walk up to any tailor and trade directly?

    1

    She needs a tailor who happens to want rice and happens to have spare clothing to offer — NCERT calls this a "double coincidence of wants."

    2

    That coincidence is rare. As the number of people in the economy grows, finding it gets prohibitively costly — most potential trades simply never happen.

    3

    Money fixes this by breaking the trade into two halves: she sells rice for money to anyone, then buys clothing with that money from a different anyone.

    4

    That single fix — removing the need for a double coincidence — is money's core job as a medium of exchange. Its other two jobs, unit of account and store of value, both grow out of solving this same original problem.

    NCERT Definition Ch. 3, §3.1

    "Economic exchanges without the mediation of money are referred to as barter exchanges. However, they presume the rather improbable double coincidence of wants."

    The three functions of money

    FunctionWhat it meansNCERT's own illustration
    Medium of exchangeremoves the need for double coincidence of wants — sell for money, then buy with moneythe principal, "first and foremost" role of money
    Unit of accounta common yardstick to express the value of every good, and compare goods to each otherpencil ₹2, pen ₹10 → a pen is worth 10 ÷ 2 = 5 pencils
    Store of valuewealth can be held in money for future use, without it perishing or costing a lot to storerice is perishable and bulky to store; money is not

    Worked example — Unit of Account

    Pencil = ₹2, Pen = ₹10. Relative price of a pen in terms of pencils = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 pencils. Value of ₹1 (a rupee) in terms of a pencil = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 pencil; in terms of a pen = 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1 pen. If all prices rise (general price rise), the value of money in terms of any commodity must fall — this is a deterioration in the purchasing power of money.

    Try it yourself — which function is at work?

    Tap the correct function for each everyday scenario.

    Paying cash to a shopkeeper for groceries

    Money is directly facilitating a transaction — medium of exchange.

    Saying a wristwatch is "worth ₹500"

    Expressing the value of a good in monetary units — unit of account.

    Keeping savings in a bank account for use five years later

    Wealth is being carried forward for future use — store of value.

    Using a debit card to pay for a train ticket

    Settling a transaction directly — medium of exchange.

    Comparing prices of two smartphones before buying

    Using money as the common yardstick to compare value — unit of account.

    Holding cash under a mattress instead of buying perishable rice as an asset

    Money is being used to carry wealth forward — store of value.

    Memory Trick

    MUS — Money is a Medium of exchange (transactions), a Unit of account (measuring value), and a Store of value (carrying wealth forward). All three trace back to solving the same problem: barter's double coincidence of wants.

    Why CUET asks this —It's the conceptual entry point to the whole chapter, so expect a direct definition MCQ or an assertion-reason pairing "double coincidence of wants" with "barter exchange."

    02Demand for Money — Transaction Motive

    People don't hold money for its own sake — they hold it to bridge the gap between when income arrives and when it gets spent.

    Numerical favourite — average cash balance & velocity

    Try this first

    A firm pays a worker ₹100 at the start of every month, and the worker spends it evenly over the month. How much money does the economy actually need people to hold, on average, just to make this happen?

    1

    At the start of the month, the worker holds the full ₹100; the firm holds ₹0.

    2

    By month-end, spending has flowed back to the firm — the firm now holds ₹100, the worker holds ₹0.

    3

    Each side's average holding across the month = (100 + 0) ÷ 2 = ₹50.

    4

    Total average money held in the economy = ₹50 + ₹50 = ₹100 — even though ₹200 worth of transactions happened (₹100 in sales + ₹100 in wages). That gap between money held and value transacted is exactly what the transaction demand formula below captures.

    NCERT Definition Box 3.1

    "The principal motive for holding money is to carry out transactions... Demand for money balance is thus often referred to as liquidity preference."
    SymbolStands forNote
    MdTTransaction demand for moneya stock concept — money people wish to hold at a point in time
    TTotal value of (nominal) transactions in the perioda flow variable
    kA positive fractionthe proportion of transactions value held as money
    vVelocity of circulation = 1/knumber of times a unit of money changes hands in the period

    Transaction demand for money

    MdT = k.T
    v.MdT = T  (where v = 1/k, the velocity of circulation)
    MdT = k.P.Y  (in terms of real GDP Y and price level P)

    In the worker–firm example, k = ½ (average balance is half the transaction value) so v = 2 — each rupee changes hands twice a month.

    1Higher income → higher transaction demand

    More income means more planned transactions, which directly raises MdT (via Y in the kPY formula).

    2Higher price level → higher transaction demand

    The same real basket now costs more money, so nominal transaction value (and money needed) rises with P.

    3It does NOT depend on the interest rate

    Transaction demand is about facilitating spending, not about the opportunity cost of holding money — that's the speculative motive's job (next topic).

    Memory Trick

    Transaction demand tracks PY, not r. It rises with real income and prices — it has nothing to do with the rate of interest. If a question links money demand to the interest rate, it's talking about the speculative motive, not this one.

    CUET Insight —A classic numerical: given monthly income and an even spending pattern, compute average cash balance (= income ÷ 2) or velocity of circulation (= transactions ÷ average balance).

    03Demand for Money — Speculative Motive & Liquidity Trap

    The other reason to hold money: you might expect bond prices to fall, and would rather hold cash than lose value.

    Bond-price numericals are a recurring favourite

    Try this first

    A firm issues a 2-year bond promising ₹10 at the end of year 1, and ₹110 at the end of year 2, for a ₹100 loan today. If the market interest rate is 5%, would you value that bond at exactly ₹100 — or more, or less?

    1

    The bond pays more than a 5% savings account would on the same money, so buyers bid its price up — its present value works out to about ₹109.29, not ₹100.

    2

    Now suppose the market rate rises to 6% instead. Money elsewhere earns more, so this bond looks relatively less attractive — its present value falls to about ₹107.33.

    3

    The general rule: bond price and the market interest rate always move in opposite directions.

    4

    That's exactly why people's appetite for holding bonds vs. cash flips as the interest rate changes — which is the whole idea behind speculative demand for money.

    Bond price and the interest rate

    The price of a bond is always inversely related to the market rate of interest — as r rises, present value (and price) falls; as r falls, price rises.

    Capital gains, capital losses, and what people do

    1Interest rate very high (near rmax)

    Everyone expects it to fall → bond prices expected to rise → people buy bonds now for the future capital gain → speculative demand for money is zero.

    2Interest rate very low (near rmin)

    Everyone expects it to rise → bond prices expected to fall (a capital loss) → people sell bonds and hold money instead → speculative demand for money is infinite.

    3The liquidity trap

    At r = rmin, any extra money injected is simply absorbed into idle balances — nobody wants more bonds. Monetary policy loses its grip on the interest rate here.

    Speculative demand for money

    MdS = (rmax − r) ÷ (r − rmin)

    As r falls from rmax to rmin, MdS rises from 0 to ∞ — an inverse relationship with the rate of interest.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 3.1

    Fig. 3.1 — as r falls toward rmin, speculative demand for money rises and flattens into the liquidity trap, where the curve becomes horizontal (infinitely elastic).

    Total money demand

    Md = MdT + MdS = k.P.Y + (rmax − r) ÷ (r − rmin)

    Memory Trick

    Bond price and interest rate move opposite ways. High interest rate today → you expect it to fall → bond prices will rise → buy bonds now (speculative money demand low). Low interest rate today → you expect it to rise → bond prices will fall → sell bonds, hold money (speculative demand high, or infinite in the liquidity trap).

    CUET Insight —Expect either a direct present-value/bond-price numerical, or a conceptual question testing whether you know speculative demand is inversely related to the interest rate (opposite of transaction demand's relationship with income).

    04Central Bank (RBI) — Functions & High-Powered Money

    Every modern economy has exactly one institution that alone can issue currency — in India, that's the RBI.

    Direct fact-recall favourite

    Try this first

    The RBI is the only institution in India legally allowed to issue currency notes. Starting from just that one fact, can you reason out what its other five jobs might be?

    1

    If you're the one printing the notes, you're also the natural body to decide how much money is in circulation — that's controller of money supply (via bank rate, OMOs, reserve ratios).

    2

    Since you're already managing the nation's money, the government would want its own banking done through you too — banker to the government.

    3

    Someone has to hold the country's foreign exchange reserves so external payments stay stable — custodian of forex reserves.

    4

    Every other bank in the country needs somewhere safe to park its reserves — bank to the banking system.

    5

    And when a bank runs short of funds and no one else will lend, someone has to be willing to — lender of last resort.

    NCERT Fact

    "India got its central bank in 1935. Its name is the 'Reserve Bank of India'."

    Functions of the RBI

    FunctionWhat it means
    Issuer of currencyonly institution that can issue currency notes in India
    Controller of money supplyvia bank rate, open market operations, reserve ratios
    Banker to the governmentmanages government's banking transactions
    Custodian of forex reservesholds and manages the economy's foreign exchange reserves
    Bank to the banking systemcommercial banks keep their reserves with the RBI
    Lender of last resortalways ready to lend to commercial banks when they need funds

    High-Powered Money

    Currency issued by the central bank — held by the public or by commercial banks — is called high-powered money, reserve money, or the monetary base. It acts as the basis for all credit creation in the economy (the next two topics show exactly how).

    Memory Trick

    "I-C-B-C-B-L" — Issuer of currency, Controller of money supply, Banker to government, Custodian of forex, Bank to banks, Lender of last resort. Six functions, one institution.

    Why CUET asks this —Pure fact-recall makes for cheap, high-confidence MCQs — expect "which of the following is NOT a function of the RBI" style questions, or a direct year/name fact-check.

    05Commercial Banks & Money Creation

    A goldsmith's receipts, circulating as money, is exactly how modern banks create money out of deposits.

    Sets up the multiplier topic that follows

    Try this first

    Lala the goldsmith holds 100kg of gold, fully backed by paper receipts. Ramu asks to borrow 25kg. If Lala assumes not everyone will withdraw their gold on the same day, should he actually hand it over — and what happens to the total receipts in circulation if he does?

    1

    Lala reasons that villagers won't all show up demanding gold on the same day — so he lends the 25kg to Ramu.

    2

    Ramu pays Ali with it. Ali doesn't want to hold raw gold, so he deposits it back with Lala and gets a fresh receipt.

    3

    Receipts in circulation are now worth 125kg — even though Lala still only physically holds 100kg of gold.

    4

    Lala created 25kg of new "money" (in receipt form) purely by lending out gold he judged wouldn't be reclaimed immediately — exactly what a modern commercial bank does with deposits.

    Bank balance sheet basics

    Assets = Reserves + Loans
    Liabilities = Deposits
    Net Worth = Assets − Liabilities

    Reserves are deposits commercial banks keep with the RBI (partly cash, partly RBI bonds/T-bills) — similar to how our own bank deposits are our assets.

    The fictional bank example

    Table 3.1 — Balance Sheet of a Bank

    Ms Fernandes deposits ₹100. The bank keeps the entire ₹100 with the RBI as reserves (no lending yet, no currency in circulation).

    Assets₹Liabilities₹
    Reserves100Deposits100
    Net Worth0
    Total100Total100

    Money supply here

    M1 = Currency + Deposits = 0 + 100 = 100

    Memory Trick

    Banks don't print money — they multiply deposits into loans, and loans back into deposits. The chain only works because banks bet correctly that not everyone withdraws on the same day. That bet is exactly what the next topic (money multiplier) puts a legal limit on.

    CUET Insight —Expect a basic balance-sheet-construction question (given deposits and reserves, find loans or net worth) or a definitional MCQ on what counts as a bank's "assets" vs "liabilities."

    06Money Multiplier & Limits to Credit Creation

    Banks can't lend forever — the RBI's reserve requirement puts a hard ceiling on how much money the banking system can create.

    The single most-tested numerical in this chapter

    Try this first

    CRR is 20%. Someone deposits ₹100 in a bank. If every bank keeps only the required reserve and lends out the rest — and every rupee lent eventually comes back as a new deposit somewhere — how much can total deposits across the banking system add up to?

    1

    Round 1: the bank keeps ₹20 (20% of ₹100) as required reserve, lends out ₹80.

    2

    That ₹80 gets spent and re-deposited elsewhere. Round 2 begins with that new deposit — the bank keeps ₹16, lends ₹64.

    3

    Each round is smaller than the last — a shrinking geometric series — but the rounds never fully stop, they just keep getting negligibly small.

    4

    Add every round together and total deposits settle at exactly ₹500 — five times the original ₹100.

    NCERT Definition §3.3.2

    "The RBI decides a certain percentage of deposits which every bank must keep as reserves... This is called the 'Required Reserve Ratio' or the 'Reserve Ratio' or 'Cash Reserve Ratio' (CRR)."
    TermMeaning
    Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)% of deposits a bank must keep as cash reserves with the RBI
    Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)% of deposits banks must additionally keep in liquid form (short-term)

    The multiplier process, worked step by step (CRR = 20%)

    RoundDeposit in BankRequired ReserveLoan made
    1100.0020.0080.00
    2180.0036.0064.00
    …………
    Last500.00100.00400.00

    The process repeats until required reserves reach the original ₹100 — which only happens once total deposits reach ₹500 (since 20% of 500 = 100). Final balance sheet: Reserves ₹100 + Loans ₹400 = Deposits ₹500.

    Money Multiplier

    Money Multiplier = 1 ÷ CRR

    With CRR = 20% = 0.2, multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. Reserves of ₹100 therefore support deposits of 5 × 100 = ₹500. (This is an infinite geometric series with first term a = 1 and common ratio r = 0.8 — NCERT derives it fully in Appendix 3.1.)

    1Higher CRR → smaller multiplier

    Raising CRR to 25% shrinks the multiplier to 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 — the same ₹100 in reserves now supports only ₹400 in deposits, so money supply falls.

    2The reserve requirement is the limit

    Without a CRR, banks would in theory lend without bound — the legally mandated reserve ratio is what caps credit creation.

    Memory Trick

    Multiplier = 1 ÷ CRR, always the reciprocal. A higher reserve ratio always means a smaller multiplier and less money creation — CRR and the multiplier move in opposite directions.

    CUET Insight —Almost every year: "given initial deposits and CRR, find the total deposits/money supply created" or the reverse — "given the multiplier, find CRR." Learn the 1÷CRR formula cold.

    07Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

    The RBI has a toolkit to expand or shrink money supply at will — some tools are precise numbers, others are persuasion.

    Repo vs Reverse Repo is a recurring trap

    Try this first

    RBI wants to fight inflation by making it more expensive for banks to create new loans. If it raises the CRR from 4% to 4.5%, is that a hard numeric lever or a soft persuasion tool — and what happens to money supply as a result?

    1

    Raising CRR is a precise, numeric change — squarely a quantitative tool, not persuasion.

    2

    A higher CRR means banks must hold back a bigger slice of every deposit as reserves.

    3

    Less of each deposit is available to re-lend, which shrinks the money multiplier (recall: Multiplier = 1 ÷ CRR).

    4

    A smaller multiplier means the same base of reserves supports a smaller total money supply — exactly what RBI wants when fighting inflation.

    NCERT Definition §3.4

    "The tools used by the Central bank to control money supply can be quantitative or qualitative."
    ToolTypeHow it works
    Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)Quantitativehigher CRR → smaller multiplier → less money supply
    Bank RateQuantitativethe rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks; higher rate → costlier loans → less money supply
    Open Market Operations (OMO)QuantitativeRBI buying/selling government bonds in the open market
    Moral suasion, margin requirementQualitativepersuasion to encourage/discourage lending, not a hard numeric lever

    Open Market Operations — outright vs repo

    BasisOutright OMORepo / Reverse Repo
    NaturePermanent — no promise to reverse the tradeTemporary — an agreed date & price to reverse it
    RBI buys securitiesInjects money permanentlyRepo: injects money temporarily, at the repo rate
    RBI sells securitiesWithdraws money permanentlyReverse repo: withdraws money temporarily, at the reverse repo rate

    Repo and reverse repo (at overnight, 7-day, 14-day maturities) are now the RBI's main tool of monetary policy.

    Try it yourself — Quantitative or Qualitative?

    Raising the Cash Reserve Ratio from 4% to 4.5%

    A precise numeric lever on reserves — quantitative.

    RBI selling government bonds in the open market

    An Open Market Operation — quantitative.

    RBI persuading banks to discourage speculative lending

    Persuasion, not a hard number — moral suasion, a qualitative tool.

    Increasing the Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points

    A precise rate change — quantitative.

    Memory Trick

    Repo = Receive (RBI receives securities, injects money). Reverse repo = Reduce (RBI reduces money in the system). Both involve a promised buy-back date — that's what makes them different from an outright, permanent OMO trade.

    Warning —Repo vs reverse repo is the single most commonly flipped pair in this chapter — always double-check which direction the money is moving before answering.

    08Measures of Money Supply — Fiat Money, Legal Tender & M1–M4

    Money supply isn't one number — RBI publishes four alternative measures, ordered by how easily each can be spent.

    M1–M4 formulas are near-guaranteed

    Try this first

    You have a ₹500 currency note and a cheque drawn on your savings account, both worth ₹500. Can a shopkeeper legally refuse either one as payment?

    1

    The currency note is fiat money issued by the RBI — by law, nobody can refuse it. It's legal tender.

    2

    The cheque draws on a demand deposit — and anyone is free to decline a cheque as payment (it's just a promise to pay, not money itself).

    3

    So demand deposits are not legal tender, even though they function like money for almost every practical purpose.

    4

    This distinction — legal-tender currency vs. non-legal-tender bank deposits — is exactly what separates the different measures of money supply (M1 through M4), which simply add progressively less liquid items to the base.

    NCERT Definition §3.2.2

    "Currency notes and coins are... called fiat money. They do not have intrinsic value... They are also called legal tenders as they cannot be refused by any citizen... Cheques drawn on savings or current accounts... can be refused by anyone as a mode of payment. Hence, demand deposits are not legal tenders."

    The four measures of money supply

    MeasureFormulaCategory
    M1CU + DDNarrow money (most liquid)
    M2M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office savings banks
    M3M1 + Net time deposits of commercial banksBroad money (less liquid)
    M4M3 + Total deposits with Post Office savings organisations (excl. NSCs)

    CU = currency (notes + coins) held by the public · DD = net demand deposits of commercial banks. M3 is the most commonly used measure, also called aggregate monetary resources.

    Demand deposits vs Time deposits

    Demand deposits (savings/current accounts) are payable on demand — cheques can be drawn on them, but the cheque itself can still be refused as payment. Time deposits (e.g. fixed deposits) have a fixed maturity period.

    Try it yourself — Legal Tender or Not?

    A ₹500 currency note

    Issued by the RBI, backed by its guarantee — cannot be refused. Legal tender.

    A cheque drawn on a savings account

    Can be refused as a mode of payment by anyone. Not legal tender.

    A ₹5 coin issued by the Government of India

    Coins carry the same guarantee as currency notes. Legal tender.

    A demand deposit balance in a current account

    Only accessed via cheques/transfers that can be declined. Not legal tender.

    Memory Trick

    "M grows as liquidity shrinks." M1 → M2 → M3 → M4 adds progressively less-liquid items each time — M1 is cash-like and easiest to spend, M4 is the least liquid of all.

    CUET Insight —Given CU and DD values, expect a direct "calculate M1" numerical, or a classification MCQ on narrow vs broad money.

    09Demonetisation — A CUET Case Study

    A real policy event NCERT boxes as a case study — exactly the kind of reading CUET likes to test with case-based questions.

    High case-study potential

    Try this first

    In November 2016, the Government of India declared that the ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes people were holding were no longer valid money, overnight. If you were holding old notes, what were your options — and why would a government do this to its own currency?

    1

    You could deposit the old notes in a bank by 31 December 2016 — or, with a declaration at the RBI, by 31 March 2017. After that, they were worthless paper.

    2

    The government's stated goals: tackle corruption, black money, terrorism financing, and fake currency circulation.

    3

    Short-run, this caused real pain — cash shortages, long bank queues, disrupted economic activity.

    4

    Longer-run, NCERT frames some genuine gains too — more savings pulled into the formal banking system, better tax compliance, and a push toward electronic payments.

    NCERT Box 3.2 — Demonetisation

    "Demonetisation was a new initiative taken by the Government of India in November 2016 to tackle the problem of corruption, black money, terrorism and circulation of fake currency... Old currency notes of ₹500 and ₹1000 were no longer legal tender. New currency notes in the denomination of ₹500 and ₹2000 were launched."
    AspectDetail
    WhenNovember 2016
    Notes withdrawn₹500 and ₹1,000 (old series)
    Notes introduced₹500 (new) and ₹2,000
    Deposit deadline (no declaration)31 December 2016
    Deposit deadline (with declaration, at RBI)31 March 2017
    Daily exchange limit allowed₹4,000 of old notes per person, per day

    Impact — both sides, as NCERT frames it

    Negative / short-runPositive / longer-run
    Long queues outside banks and ATMsImproved tax compliance — more people brought into the tax net
    Currency shortage disrupted economic activitySavings channelised into the formal financial system
     Banks gained resources to lend at lower interest rates
     Push from cash to electronic payment technologies

    Memory Trick

    Demonetisation = old notes lose legal tender status overnight. Remember the four goals NCERT lists: corruption, black money, terrorism financing, and fake currency.

    Why CUET asks this —Real, dated policy events are a natural fit for case-based passage questions — expect a short passage followed by 2–3 questions on dates, amounts, or which impact (positive/negative) a given statement describes.
    Notes prepared from NCERT Introductory Macroeconomics, Chapter 3 — Money and Banking, for CUET revision. Definitions and diagrams are reproduced in NCERT's own wording and structure; connecting explanation, memory tricks, and layout are adapted for classroom use.

    01Final & Intermediate Goods, and Their Types

    Everything in national income accounting starts with one question: has this good finished its journey, or is it still being transformed into something else?

    High-frequency classification question

    Try this first

    A farmer's cotton becomes yarn, then cloth, then a shirt sold to a customer. At which point in that chain does it become a “final good”?

    1

    Every sale along the chain — cotton to the mill, yarn to the weaver, cloth to the tailor — feeds straight back into someone else's production process. Each of those is an intermediate good.

    2

    The very last sale — to the customer who won't transform it further — is what matters.

    3

    That's the whole definition of “final”: not what the object physically is, but whether it leaves the active economic flow for good.

    4

    Proof it's about use, not the object: the same tea leaves are a final good bought by a household, but an intermediate good bought by a restaurant that brews and resells them.

    Start here — the textbook's own example

    NCERT traces one commodity through a whole chain to show where "final" begins: "a farmer producing cotton sells it to a spinning mill where the raw cotton undergoes transformation to yarn; the yarn is, in turn, sold to a textile mill where... it is transformed into cloth; the cloth is, in turn, transformed... into an article of clothing which is then ready to be sold finally to the consumers for final use."

    Traced directly from the chapter's cotton example
    CottonGrown by farmer
    YarnSpinning mill
    ClothTextile mill
    Article of clothingTailoring/garment unit
    Sold to consumerFinal use — leaves the flow
    Every sale up to the last step = intermediate good Sale to the final consumer = final good

    Now the definitions

    NCERT Definition Ch. 2, §2.1

    "Such an item that is meant for final use and will not pass through any more stages of production or transformations is called a final good."

    NCERT Definition Ch. 2, §2.1

    "Such goods may be used by other producers as material inputs... These are intermediate goods, mostly used as raw material or inputs for production of other commodities. These are not final goods."

    Characteristics, side by side

    BasisFinal GoodIntermediate Good
    Meaning (NCERT)meant for final use; will not pass through any more stages of production/transformationused as material input for producing another good
    Stage in productionleaves the active economic flow once soldstays inside the production process; gets transformed further
    Counted in GDP?YesNo — excluded to avoid double counting
    Decided byeconomic use, not physical natureeconomic use, not physical nature
    Textbook exampletea leaves bought & brewed by a householdtea leaves bought by a restaurant to brew and resell

    The litmus test — how to classify any good

    1Ask the transformation question

    Will it be transformed again by a producer, or has it left the "active economic flow"? If it leaves the flow, it's final.

    2Judge by use, not by nature

    It is not the physical nature of the good that decides this — it is the economic use to which it is put.

    3Ignore what the final buyer does with it

    Transformation by the ultimate purchaser (e.g. cooking at home) does not count — "cooking at home is not an economic activity."

    4Same object, different fate

    The same physical good can switch categories depending on who buys it and why.

    NCERT's own proof — tea leaves

    "The tea leaves purchased by the consumer are not consumed in that form — they are used to make drinkable tea... cooking at home is not an economic activity, even though the product involved undergoes transformation. Home cooked food is not sold to the market. However, if the same cooking or tea brewing was done in a restaurant where the cooked product would be sold to customers, then the same items, such as tea leaves, would cease to be final goods and would be counted as inputs to which economic value addition can take place."

    Memory Trick

    If it leaves the shop for good (into a household's hands, never to be resold or reworked by a producer) — it's a FINAL good. If it walks back into somebody else's factory to get transformed again — it's INTERMEDIATE. Same physical item, different fate.

    Why does this distinction matter?

    Money is our common measuring rod — we can't add metres of cloth to tonnes of rice — so we sum the monetary value of final goods only. The value of intermediate goods is already embedded inside the value of the final good; counting both separately causes double counting and inflates the true value of output.

    Try it yourself — classify each item

    Tap Final Good or Intermediate Good for each item below, then check the reasoning.

    Tea leaves bought by a household to brew at home

    Bought by the household for direct use, never resold or reworked — a final good.

    Tea leaves bought by a restaurant to brew and sell to customers

    The restaurant transforms and resells it — value is added and it's sold on, so it's an intermediate good.

    Raw cotton bought by a spinning mill to make yarn

    Gets transformed into yarn and resold — stays inside the production process. Intermediate good.

    A finished shirt bought by a customer from a shop

    Bought for personal use — leaves the active economic flow. Final good.

    Steel sheets bought by a car manufacturer to build cars

    Transformed into cars and resold — a raw material input. Intermediate good.

    A new car bought by a household for personal use

    Bought by a household for its own use, not for resale. Final good (specifically a consumer durable — see the next topic).

    Sugar bought by a bakery to bake cakes for sale

    Used up in producing cakes that are then sold — an input, not a final good. Intermediate good.

    A packet of biscuits bought by a household from a store

    Bought for direct consumption by the household. Final good.

    Why CUET asks this —It's the cheapest possible MCQ to write: give a real-world item, ask which bucket it falls in. Expect it as classification, assertion-reason, or a "restaurant vs household" case study.

    Types of final goods

    Final goods themselves split further, based on who uses them and how long they last.

    NCERT Definition — Consumption Goods §2.1

    "Goods like food and clothing, and services like recreation that are consumed when purchased by their ultimate consumers are called consumption goods or consumer goods."

    NCERT Definition — Capital Goods §2.1

    Durable goods "used in the production process... they themselves don't get transformed in the production process... they are the crucial backbone of any production process" — these are capital goods.

    NCERT Definition — Consumer Durables §2.1

    "Some commodities like television sets, automobiles or home computers, although they are for ultimate consumption, have one characteristic in common with capital goods — they are also durable... That is why we call these goods consumer durables."
    FactorConsumption GoodsCapital GoodsConsumer Durables
    Who uses itHouseholdsBusiness/producing enterprisesHouseholds
    PurposeSatisfies wants directlyEnables further productionSatisfies wants, over a long life
    DurabilityMostly used up quicklyDurable — needs repair/replacementDurable — needs repair/replacement
    NCERT examplesfood, clothing, recreation servicestools, implements, machinestelevision sets, automobiles, home computers

    All three are final goods. Anything used up as raw material by other producers instead is an intermediate good (e.g. steel sheets for automobiles, copper for utensils).

    Memory Trick

    Ask WHO buys it. A FIRM buying a durable item to help it produce → capital good. A HOUSEHOLD buying the exact same kind of item (say, a computer or vehicle) for personal use → consumer durable. Same object, different buyer, different label.

    Quick classification checklist

    • Bought by a household, used up quickly? → Consumption good.
    • Bought by a household, but lasts for years and needs repair? → Consumer durable.
    • Bought by a firm to help it produce, without being transformed itself? → Capital good.
    • Bought by a firm and gets used up / transformed into another good? → Intermediate good.
    Warning —Students frequently confuse a capital good with a consumer durable when the object itself is identical (e.g. a laptop, a vehicle). The buyer, not the object, decides the label.

    02Stocks and Flows

    "The average salary is ₹10,000" is meaningless without a time frame — per day? per month? per year? That's the stock–flow distinction.

    Common as an assertion / true-false pair

    Try this first

    Water flows into a tank from a tap. Is the amount flowing in per minute the same kind of measurement as the amount of water sitting in the tank right now?

    1

    The amount flowing in per minute only makes sense with a time period attached to it — that's a flow.

    2

    How much water is in the tank at a given moment doesn't need a time period at all — that's a stock.

    3

    A stock can change over a period, and that change is itself a flow — e.g. a change in inventories, or net investment.

    4

    Same logic, different variables: income is a flow, wealth is a stock; new machines added this year is a flow, total capital stock is a stock.

    NCERT Definition §2.1

    "Flows are defined over a period of time."  ·  "Stocks are defined at a particular point of time."
    NCERT's own tap-and-tank illustration
    Flow "The amount of water which is flowing into the tank from the tap per minute is a flow."
    Stock "How much water there is in the tank at a particular point of time is a stock concept."

    Memory Trick

    STOCK = a photograph (frozen at one moment — "as on 31 March"). FLOW = a video (only makes sense over a stretch of time — "during the year"). If the number needs a time period attached to mean anything, it's a flow.

    BasisStockFlow
    DefinedAt a particular point in timeOver a period of time
    NCERT examplescapital, wealth, inventory, water level in the tankincome, output, profit, investment, water entering the tank per minute
    RelationA stock can change over a period — that change itself is a flow (e.g. change in inventories, net investment)

    A machine's double life

    "A particular machine can be part of the capital stock for many years... but that machine can be part of the flow of new machines added to the capital stock only for a single year when it was initially installed."

    CUET Insight —Typical MCQ shape: a short pair of statements ("Statement 1... Statement 2...") testing whether you can tell a stock from a flow without hesitation. Quick trick: ask "does this number need a time period to make sense?" — if yes, it's a flow.

    03Investment & Depreciation

    Gross investment isn't one thing — it's three different kinds of spending on capital, netted against the wear-and-tear that eats into it every year.

    Know the three types of investment, not just the depreciation formula

    Try this first

    A pair of shoes wears out gradually over two years of normal use. A factory burns down overnight in an earthquake. Are both examples of depreciation?

    1

    The shoes' wear-and-tear is planned, expected, and spread evenly over their useful life — that is depreciation.

    2

    The earthquake is sudden and unplanned — that's a capital loss, not depreciation.

    3

    Depreciation = cost of the good ÷ number of years of its useful life — an accounting concept, not necessarily real spending every single year.

    4

    Net Investment = Gross Investment − Depreciation.

    NCERT Definition — Gross Investment §2.1

    "That part of our final output that comprises of capital goods constitutes gross investment of an economy."

    NCERT Definition — Depreciation §2.1

    "This deletion, which is made from the value of gross investment in order to accommodate regular wear and tear of capital, is called depreciation."

    Core Identity

    Net Investment = Gross Investment − Depreciation

    Three types of investment that make up Gross Investment

    TypeWhat it covers
    Fixed Business InvestmentSpending by firms on new machinery, plant, equipment, and tools used in production.
    Residential InvestmentSpending on constructing new housing — by households and firms alike.
    Inventory InvestmentThe change in a firm's stock of unsold finished goods, semi-finished goods, or raw materials — can be positive (accumulation) or negative (decumulation).

    These three add up to an economy's Gross Investment — the capital-goods portion of final output. Inventory investment is covered in more depth in the Product Method topic, since NCERT introduces it alongside the value-added calculation.

    Memory Trick

    Depreciation is only planned, expected wear-and-tear (like shoes wearing out over two years of normal use). An earthquake destroying the factory overnight is NOT depreciation — that's an unplanned capital loss. CUET loves testing this exact distinction.

    Characteristics of depreciation, per NCERT

    • It is an accounting concept — "no real expenditure may have actually been incurred each year yet depreciation is annually accounted for."
    • It assumes a fixed expected life for the capital good (e.g. 20 years), and spreads the cost evenly.
    • It does not account for sudden, unexpected destruction — accidents or natural calamities are excluded.
    • Depreciation = cost of the good ÷ number of years of its useful life.

    Careful — economist's "investment" ≠ everyday "investment"

    "This must not be confused with the commonplace notion of investment which implies using money to buy physical or financial assets... Investment for us is always capital formation, a gross or net addition to capital stock."

    The consumption–investment trade-off

    At a given level of total output, producing more capital goods means producing fewer consumer goods right now. But more capital goods raise future productivity, so future total output — and future consumption — can rise. It is a trade-off across time, not a contradiction.

    Ranker's Tip —Typical MCQ shape: "which of these is NOT depreciation", a one-liner asking you to compute Net Investment, or "identify the type of investment" for a given spending example. Quick trick: if the loss was sudden/unplanned (accident, disaster), it's never depreciation.

    04Circular Flow of Income

    In the simplest possible economy — no government, no savings, no foreign trade — income just goes round and round between two sectors.

    "Which point (A/B/C) matches which method?" is a classic diagram question

    Try this first

    In a simple two-sector economy (just households and firms, no government, no savings), can you measure the whole economy's income by looking at spending — or do you have to look at factor payments instead?

    1

    At Point A, households' spending flows to firms — this is the Expenditure Method.

    2

    At Point B, firms' goods and services flow back to households as the value of what's produced — this is the Product Method.

    3

    At Point C, firms pay wages, interest, profit and rent to households for their factor services — this is the Income Method.

    4

    Since it's the same rupee travelling around the same circle, all three points must give exactly the same number.

    "The households receive their payments from the firms for productive activities they perform for the latter... In this simplified economy, there is only one way in which the households may dispose off their earnings — by spending their entire income on the goods and services produced by the domestic firms."

    Factor of ProductionRemuneration
    LabourWage
    CapitalInterest
    EntrepreneurshipProfit
    Land (fixed natural resources)Rent
    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 2.1 — same boxes, same four flows, same points A/B/C, redrawn as a real loop
    Green arrows — money/services flowing from households to firms Navy arrows — money/goods flowing from firms to households A, B, C — where each flow's annual value is measured

    Fig. 2.1 — Circular Flow of Income in a Simple Economy (NCERT). The dashed track is the loop the same rupee travels around every cycle.

    Because the same value moves in a circle, we can measure the economy's aggregate income at any of the three marked points — and all three must give the same number:

    Point A

    Expenditure Method
    aggregate spending firms receive

    =

    Point B

    Product Method
    aggregate value of final goods produced

    =

    Point C

    Income Method
    sum total of factor payments

    Memory Trick

    A-B-C = Amount spent (Expenditure) → goods flow Back to households (Product) → Cash paid to factors (Income). Same rupee, travelling in a circle, measured three times.

    A useful (if paradoxical-sounding) result

    If households spend more than their current income (by borrowing), firms produce more and pay out more in factor income. "Their income will rise exactly by the amount which is necessary to carry out the extra spending." In a circular flow, a rise at one point must eventually raise every point.

    Why CUET asks this —The A/B/C diagram is the cleanest possible "point identification" question — examiners just point at an arrow and ask which method matches. Quick trick: A = spending, B = goods produced, C = factor payments.

    05The Product (Value Added) Method

    The first of three ways to measure GDP — count what every firm actually adds to the economy, not what it merely produces.

    Numerical MCQs on this method appear almost every year

    Try this first

    Farmers produce ₹100 of wheat (using no inputs), sell ₹50 of it to bakers, who use it to produce ₹200 of bread. Is the economy's total output ₹300 (100 + 200)?

    1

    No — simply adding 100 + 200 counts the ₹50 of wheat twice, once on its own and once again inside the bread. That mistake is double counting.

    2

    Each firm's value added = its output − intermediate goods bought: farmer = 100 − 0 = 100; baker = 200 − 50 = 150.

    3

    Aggregate value added = 100 + 150 = ₹250, not ₹300 — this is the Product Method.

    4

    The other two methods (Expenditure and Income, covered next) would both also land on ₹250 — same rupee, three vantage points on the same circular flow.

    The master identity — hold this in your head throughout

    GDP ≡ Σ GVAi  (Point B)  ≡  C + I + G + X − M  (Point A)  ≡  W + P + In + R  (Point C)

    Memory Trick

    The PEI wheel: Product (what firms MAKE) = Expenditure (what buyers SPEND) = Income (what factors EARN). Three different questions about the exact same rupee.

    Measured at Point B. Suppose farmers produce ₹100 worth of wheat (no inputs needed). They sell ₹50 worth to bakers, who use it to produce ₹200 worth of bread.

    The naive (wrong) approach

    Simply adding ₹200 + ₹100 = ₹300. Wrong — the ₹50 of wheat gets counted twice. This mistake is double counting.

    NCERT Definition — Value Added §2.2.1

    "The term that is used to denote the net contribution made by a firm is called its value added... value added of a firm is, value of production of the firm – value of intermediate goods used by the firm."
    FarmerBaker
    Total production100200
    Intermediate goods used050
    Value added100150

    Aggregate value added = ₹100 + ₹150 = ₹250 — not ₹300. This exact farmer–baker set-up is one of the most recycled numerical questions on this chapter — always subtract intermediate goods once.

    Gross vs Net Value Added

    Net Value Added = Gross Value Added − Depreciation

    Example: Output ₹100, intermediate goods ₹20, depreciation ₹10 → GVA = 100−20 = ₹80 · NVA = 100−20−10 = ₹70

    Inventories — the wrinkle every firm has

    NCERT Definition — Inventory §2.2.1

    "The stock of unsold finished goods, or semi-finished goods, or raw materials which a firm carries from one year to the next is called inventory. Inventory is a stock variable."

    Key identity

    Change in Inventories ≡ Production during the year − Sale during the year

    Change in inventories is a form of investment, alongside fixed business investment and residential investment.

    NCERT's shirt-factory example — planned vs unplanned

    A firm starts the year with 100 shirts in stock, expects to sell 1,000, and produces 1,000.

    • Sales turn out to be only 600 → 400 shirts pile up unexpectedly → unplanned accumulation.
    • Sales turn out to be 1,050 → firm dips into stock too → unplanned decumulation.
    • Firm deliberately raises stock 100→200 by producing 1,100 → planned accumulation.
    • Firm deliberately cuts stock 100→25 by producing only 925 → planned decumulation.

    Memory Trick

    Sales below plan → stock piles up you didn't want → accumulation. Sales above plan → stock drains faster than you wanted → decumulation. If it was the firm's own decision, it's planned; if sales surprised them, it's unplanned.

    Full identity with inventories

    GVAi ≡ Sales (Vi) + Change in Inventories (Ai) − Intermediate Goods Used (Zi)
    GDP ≡ Σ GVAi

    Worked example — Firms A & B

    Firm A grows cotton (no raw materials) and sells it to Firm B for ₹50. Firm B turns it into cloth and sells it to consumers for ₹200.

    Firm AFirm B
    Sales50200
    Intermediate consumption050
    Value added50150

    GDP = 50 + 150 = ₹200

    Why CUET asks this —This is the most numerically-tested of the three methods — expect a farmer-baker-style chain, a GVA calculation, or an inventory accumulation/decumulation identification question.

    06The Expenditure Method

    The second way to measure GDP — from the buyer's side: what does everyone actually spend on final goods and services?

    Don't forget the −M — a classic one-mark trap

    Try this first

    GDP ≡ C + I + G + X − M. If a student writes GDP = C + I + G + X and stops there, what have they gotten wrong?

    1

    C+I+G+X counts all spending by households, firms, government, and foreigners — on both domestic AND foreign goods.

    2

    But GDP should only count spending on goods actually produced within the domestic economy.

    3

    Imports (M) are spending that leaked abroad — on goods produced by someone else's economy — so they must be subtracted back out.

    4

    Forgetting −M is the single most common trap when writing this formula from memory.

    The master identity — hold this in your head throughout

    GDP ≡ Σ GVAi  (Point B)  ≡  C + I + G + X − M  (Point A)  ≡  W + P + In + R  (Point C)

    Memory Trick

    The PEI wheel: Product (what firms MAKE) = Expenditure (what buyers SPEND) = Income (what factors EARN). Three different questions about the exact same rupee.

    Measured at Point A. Same value as the product method, viewed from the demand side.

    SymbolComponentNCERT description
    CConsumptionfinal consumption expenditure on goods & services
    IInvestmentfinal investment expenditure on capital goods
    GGovernmentincludes both consumption and investment
    XExportsexport revenues earned abroad
    MImportsdeducted — not spent on domestic firms

    The Expenditure Method Formula

    GDP ≡ C + I + G + X − M

    Of these five, investment expenditure (I) is the most unstable — NCERT flags this explicitly, and CUET loves to test it.

    Memory Trick

    Don't forget the −M! A very common trap is to write GDP = C+I+G+X and stop there. Imports must always be subtracted — that money left the domestic economy.

    Worked example — Firms A & B

    Firm A sells cotton to Firm B for ₹50; Firm B turns it into cloth and sells it to consumers for ₹200. Final expenditure = spending by consumers on cloth only (the ₹50 cotton sale was intermediate, not final, spending).

    GDP = ₹200 — exactly matching the Product Method's answer for the same economy.

    Warning —Only count expenditure on final goods and services — spending between firms on intermediate goods is already embedded inside the final good's price and must not be counted again.

    07The Income Method

    The third way to measure GDP — add up every rupee actually paid out to the four factors of production.

    Ties the whole "three methods" idea together

    Try this first

    Firm A pays ₹20 in wages and keeps ₹30 profit. Firm B pays ₹60 in wages and keeps ₹90 profit. Does adding up everyone's income also land on ₹200 — the same answer as the Product and Expenditure methods?

    1

    Firm A's total factor payments: ₹20 wages + ₹30 profit = ₹50.

    2

    Firm B's total factor payments: ₹60 wages + ₹90 profit = ₹150.

    3

    Total = 50 + 150 = ₹200 — exactly matching the Product Method's ₹200 and the Expenditure Method's ₹200.

    4

    That's the entire point of "three vantage points on one circular flow" — measure from whichever side you like, GDP comes out the same.

    The master identity — hold this in your head throughout

    GDP ≡ Σ GVAi  (Point B)  ≡  C + I + G + X − M  (Point A)  ≡  W + P + In + R  (Point C)

    Memory Trick

    The PEI wheel: Product (what firms MAKE) = Expenditure (what buyers SPEND) = Income (what factors EARN). Three different questions about the exact same rupee.

    Measured at Point C. Same value again, viewed as payments to the four factors of production.

    The Income Method Formula

    GDP ≡ W + P + In + R

    W = Wages & salaries · P = Profits · In = Interest · R = Rent

    Comparing all three methods, side by side

    MethodWhat is summedPointFormula
    ProductGross value added of every firmBGDP ≡ ΣGVAi
    ExpenditureFinal spending received by firmsAGDP ≡ C+I+G+X−M
    IncomeFactor payments to householdsCGDP ≡ W+P+In+R

    Worked example — Firms A & B

    Firm A pays ₹20 wages, keeps ₹30 profit. Firm B pays ₹60 wages, keeps ₹90 profit.

    Firm AFirm B
    Wages2060
    Profits3090

    GDP = 80 + 120 = ₹200 — all three methods agree.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a direct factor-income calculation, a "which method sums factor payments" definition question, or a comparison question testing whether you can match Product/Expenditure/Income to what each one actually adds up.

    08Factor Cost, Basic Prices & Market Prices

    Three ways of pricing the same output, depending on whether taxes/subsidies are folded in.

    Try this first

    A producer receives ₹1,000 for their output — with no tax included. The government then adds ₹100 in production taxes, then ₹150 in product taxes before it reaches the shop shelf. What does the final consumer actually pay?

    1

    Factor Cost (₹1,000) is what the producer actually pockets — no tax at all.

    2

    Add net production taxes (₹100) → Basic Price = ₹1,100.

    3

    Add net product taxes (₹150) on top of that → Market Price = ₹1,250 — what the consumer actually pays.

    4

    Price only ever grows as you move Factor Cost → Basic Price → Market Price, since each step just adds a tax the previous one didn't include.

    NCERT Definition §2.2.4

    "Factor cost includes only the payment to factors of production, it does not include any tax. In order to arrive at market prices, we have to add to the factor cost the total indirect taxes less total subsidies. The basic prices lie in between: they include the production taxes (less production subsidies) but not product taxes (less product subsidies)."
    A worked example — same output, three different price tags

    Factor Cost

    ₹1,000

    what the producer actually receives — no tax at all

    + ₹100
    Net Production Taxes

    Basic Price

    ₹1,100

    factor cost + production taxes, less production subsidies

    + ₹150
    Net Product Taxes

    Market Price

    ₹1,250

    what the final consumer actually pays

    Same ₹1,000 of factor payments, taxed twice on its way to the shop shelf — each step only ever adds a tax the previous one didn't include. (Numbers are illustrative.)

    BasisFactor CostBasic PricesMarket Prices
    IncludesOnly payments to factorsFactor cost + net production taxesBasic prices + net product taxes
    Example taxesNoneLand revenue, stamp & registration feeExcise, service tax, export/import duties

    Memory Trick

    FC → BP → MP: the price grows as you add taxes, like a restaurant bill growing as GST is added on top. Factor Cost is the "base price" the producer actually pockets.

    Building up from Factor Cost to Market Price

    GVA at Factor Cost + Net Production Taxes = GVA at Basic Prices
    GVA at Basic Prices + Net Product Taxes = GVA at Market Prices

    CUET note

    Since 2015, India's CSO reports GVA at basic prices and GDP at market prices — the older "GDP at factor cost" headline measure was replaced.

    CUET Insight —Typical MCQ shape: "arrange Factor Cost, Basic Price, Market Price in ascending order" or a fill-in-the-blank on which taxes belong where. Quick trick: FC → BP → MP, price only ever grows as you move right.

    09From GDP to Personal Disposable Income

    GDP belongs to whoever produces inside our borders — even a foreign-owned factory. NCERT's Fig. 2.3 traces the same total value down through every sub-category.

    The single most-tested numeric chain in this chapter

    Try this first

    GDP at Market Price = ₹2,000 crore, Net Factor Income from Abroad = −₹40 crore, Depreciation = ₹150 crore, Net Indirect Taxes = ₹210 crore. What is the country's National Income?

    1

    GNPₘₚ = GDPₘₚ + NFIA = 2,000 + (−40) = 1,960.

    2

    NNPₘₚ = GNPₘₚ − Depreciation = 1,960 − 150 = 1,810.

    3

    National Income = NNP_FC = NNPₘₚ − Net Indirect Taxes = 1,810 − 210 = ₹1,600 crore.

    4

    Notice the pattern: only the very first step (GDP→GNP) adds something (NFIA) — every step after that only ever subtracts.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 2.3, redrawn left-to-right
    GDPat Market Price
    + NFIA
    GNPat Market Price
    − Depreciation (D)
    NNPat Market Price
    − (ID − Sub)
    NNP at Factor Cost= National Income (NI)
    − UP − NIH
    − CT + TrH
    Personal Income(PI)
    − PTP − NP
    Personal Disposable Income(PDI)

    Fig. 2.3 — subcategories of aggregate income (NCERT). NFIA: Net Factor Income from Abroad · D: Depreciation · ID: Indirect Taxes · Sub: Subsidies · UP: Undistributed Profits · NIH: Net Interest Payments by Households · CT: Corporate Taxes · TrH: Transfers to Households · PTP: Personal Tax Payments · NP: Non-Tax Payments.

    Memory Trick

    Only the very first step ADDS something (NFIA, to go GDP→GNP). Every step after that subtracts — except transfer payments sneak back in at the PI step (households receive pensions/scholarships they didn't "earn"). If you remember "one add, then a run of subtracts (with one sneaky add-back)", you can rebuild the whole ladder.

    NCERT Definitions — the aggregates, verbatim §2.3

    "GNP ≡ GDP + Net factor income from abroad."

    "NNP ≡ GNP − Depreciation."

    "NNP at factor cost ≡ National Income (NI) ≡ NNP at market prices − Net indirect taxes."

    "Personal Income (PI) ≡ NI − Undistributed profits − Net interest payments made by households − Corporate tax + Transfer payments to the households from the government and firms."

    "Personal Disposable Income (PDI) ≡ PI − Personal tax payments − Non-tax payments."

    Why each adjustment happens

    • NFIA: an Indian working abroad earns wages counted in that country's GDP, not India's — add income Indians earn abroad, subtract income foreigners earn here.
    • Depreciation: wear-and-tear doesn't become anyone's income.
    • Net Indirect Taxes: market price includes taxes that go to government, not to factors — remove them to find factor cost = National Income.
    • Undistributed Profits & Corporate Tax: retained by firms/government, never reaches households.
    • Transfer Payments (pensions, scholarships, prizes): households receive these without producing anything — add them in.
    • Personal & Non-Tax Payments: must be paid away before the money is truly "disposable."

    Try this first

    NNP at Market Price tells us what a country produced. Does that automatically tell us the maximum the country can actually spend and save?

    1

    Not quite — the country may also receive transfers from abroad (foreign aid, remittances given as gifts) that add to what it can spend, without being production at all.

    2

    National Disposable Income = NNP at Market Price + Other current transfers from the rest of the world.

    3

    Private Income takes a different slice again — factor income accruing to the private sector, plus national debt interest, NFIA, and government/foreign transfers.

    4

    Think of NDI as the whole-country version of what Personal Disposable Income is for a single household.

    10National Disposable Income & Private Income

    National Disposable Income

    NDI = NNP at Market Price + Other current transfers from the rest of the world

    Tells us the maximum a country's households, firms and government can spend on final consumption and savings.

    Private Income

    Private Income = Factor income from NDP accruing to the private sector + National debt interest + NFIA + Current transfers from government + Other net transfers from abroad

    Memory Trick

    NDI = what the whole COUNTRY can spend + save. PDI = what ONE HOUSEHOLD can spend + save. Same idea, different scale — don't mix them up on an MCQ.

    Warning —This is one of the lower-yield sub-topics in the chapter — worth knowing the formula shape, but don't over-invest revision time here relative to the ladder above.

    11Nominal vs Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI & WPI

    If GDP doubles, did the economy actually produce twice as much — or did prices just double?

    Deflator numericals are almost guaranteed every year

    Try this first

    In 2000, an economy produced 100 units of bread at ₹10 each. In 2001, it produced 110 units at ₹15 each. Did the economy actually produce more — or did prices just rise?

    1

    Nominal GDP (2001) = 110 × ₹15 = ₹1,650 — measured at current prices.

    2

    Real GDP (2001) = 110 × ₹10 (2000's price) = ₹1,100 — measured at constant, base-year prices.

    3

    GDP Deflator = (Nominal ÷ Real) × 100 = (1,650 ÷ 1,100) × 100 = 150%.

    4

    Since both figures use the exact same physical output (110 units), the entire ₹550 gap between them is a pure price effect.

    NCERT Definition §2.4

    "Real GDP is calculated in a way such that the goods and services are evaluated at some constant set of prices (or constant prices)... Nominal GDP... is simply the value of GDP at the current prevailing prices."

    NCERT's bread economy

    2000 (base year): 100 units of bread @ ₹10 → Nominal GDP = ₹1,000.
    2001: 110 units @ ₹15 → Nominal GDP = 110×15 = ₹1,650.
    Real GDP (2001 output at 2000 prices) = 110×10 = ₹1,100.

    GDP Deflator

    GDP Deflator = Nominal GDP ⁄ Real GDP  (×100 for percentage)

    1,650 ⁄ 1,100 = 1.50 → 150%. Since both use the same physical output, any difference is purely a price effect.

    Memory Trick

    Nominal = today's price tag. Real = yesterday's (base-year) price tag on today's basket. If only the price tag changed and not the actual goods produced, real GDP stays put even while nominal GDP climbs.

    CPI & WPI — other ways to track prices

    Besides the GDP Deflator, two more price indices track how prices move over time.

    NCERT Definition — CPI §2.4

    "The Consumer Price Index (CPI)... is the index of prices of a given basket of commodities which are bought by the representative consumer."

    NCERT's rice & cloth basket

    Basket: 90 kg rice + 5 pieces of cloth.
    2000: rice ₹10/kg, cloth ₹100/piece → 900+500 = ₹1,400
    2005: rice ₹15/kg, cloth ₹120/piece → 1,350+600 = ₹1,950
    CPI = (1,950 ⁄ 1,400) × 100 ≈ 139.29

    NCERT Definition — WPI §2.4

    "Like CPI, the index for wholesale prices is called Wholesale Price Index (WPI)." In the USA it is called the Producer Price Index (PPI).

    Memory Trick

    CPI packs the same suitcase every year (fixed basket — you never change what you're buying). The GDP Deflator's "basket" changes with whatever the economy actually produced that year. That single difference explains almost every CPI-vs-Deflator MCQ.

    FactorCPIGDP Deflator
    CoverageOnly goods bought by the representative consumerAll goods and services produced domestically
    Imported goodsIncludedExcluded
    WeightsFixed — same basket every yearVary with each year's actual production mix

    12Is GDP a Good Measure of Welfare?

    Higher income should mean more goods, more well-being — right? NCERT gives three reasons this may not be correct.

    Case-based / scenario MCQs love this section

    Try this first

    An economy has 100 people each earning ₹10 (GDP = ₹1,000). Next year, 90 people earn ₹9 and 10 people earn ₹20 (GDP = ₹1,010). GDP went up — did welfare go up too?

    1

    GDP did rise, by ₹10.

    2

    But 90% of people actually got poorer (₹10 → ₹9) — only 10% gained, and they gained a lot.

    3

    Aggregate GDP hides this entirely — it says nothing about how the gains were distributed.

    4

    This is one of three reasons GDP can mislead welfare, remembered as D-N-E: Distribution, Non-monetary exchanges (unpaid work, barter — invisible to GDP), and Externalities (uncounted harms or benefits to third parties).

    NCERT Definition — Externalities §2.5

    "Externalities refer to the benefits (or harms) a firm or an individual causes to another for which they are not paid (or penalised)."

    Memory Trick — the DNE test

    Three reasons GDP misleads welfare, remembered as D-N-E: Distribution (who actually got the gains?), Non-monetary exchange (barter/unpaid work — invisible to GDP), Externalities (uncounted harms or benefits to third parties).

    D

    Distribution

    NCERT's example: 100 people earning ₹10 each (GDP=1,000) becomes 90 people earning ₹9 and 10 people earning ₹20 (GDP=1,010) — GDP rose, yet 90% of people got poorer.

    N

    Non-Monetary Exchanges

    Unpaid domestic work and barter exchanges never enter GDP since no money changes hands — GDP underestimates true welfare.

    E

    Externalities

    A refinery polluting a river harms fishermen — a negative externality GDP ignores, so GDP overestimates welfare. Positive externalities cause the reverse.

    ReasonEffect on GDP vs. true welfare
    Unequal distributionMisleading — aggregate GDP can rise while most people are worse off
    Non-monetary/barter exchangesGDP underestimates welfare
    Negative externalitiesGDP overestimates welfare
    Positive externalitiesGDP underestimates welfare

    Key Differences — the pairs CUET loves to confuse

    Every commonly-confused concept pair in this chapter, side by side.

    1. Barter Exchange vs. Money Economy

    EfficiencyHigh search costs, breaks down as economy growsLow-cost, scalable exchange

    2. Transaction Motive vs. Speculative Motive

    3. Narrow Money vs. Broad Money

    4. Repo vs. Reverse Repo

    BasisRepoReverse Repo

    5. Quantitative vs. Qualitative Tools

    BasisQuantitative ToolsQualitative Tools

    6. Legal Tender vs. Not Legal Tender

    BasisLegal TenderNot Legal Tender

    7. Outright OMO vs. Repo/Reverse Repo

    BasisOutright OMORepo / Reverse Repo

    8. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) vs. Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)

    BasisCRRSLR
    Form of reserveCash, kept with the RBILiquid assets (cash, gold, approved securities), kept with the bank itself

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Functions of money

    MUS — Medium of exchange, Unit of account, Store of value. All three solve barter's double coincidence of wants problem.

    Transaction vs Speculative demand

    Transaction demand tracks PY (income and prices) — nothing to do with interest rates. Speculative demand tracks r (interest rate) — inversely.

    Bond price and interest rate

    They always move in opposite directions. High rate today → expect it to fall → bond prices rise → buy bonds (speculative demand low).

    Money multiplier

    Multiplier = 1 ÷ CRR, always the reciprocal. Higher CRR always means a smaller multiplier and less money creation.

    Repo vs Reverse Repo

    Repo = Receive (RBI receives securities, injects money). Reverse repo = Reduce (RBI reduces money in the system).

    M1 → M4

    "M grows as liquidity shrinks." Each step adds a progressively less-liquid item. M1 is most liquid, M4 is least liquid.

    Legal tender

    Currency notes and coins cannot be refused. Cheques/demand deposits can be refused — they are NOT legal tender.

    Liquidity trap

    At r = rmin, injecting more money changes nothing about the interest rate — it's all absorbed into idle balances.

    Bank balance sheet

    Assets = Reserves + Loans; Liabilities = Deposits. The bank's whole business model is choosing how to split its assets between the two.

    Demonetisation

    Remember the four goals: corruption, black money, terrorism, fake currency. November 2016; old ₹500/₹1,000 out, new ₹500/₹2,000 in.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 23 definitions

    1. Barter exchange: "economic exchanges without the mediation of money."

    2. Double coincidence of wants: the requirement that barter presumes — each party must want exactly what the other has to offer, described by NCERT as "the rather improbable double coincidence of wants."

    3. Money: "the commonly accepted medium of exchange."

    4. Medium of exchange: the "first and foremost role of money" — facilitating exchange without a double coincidence of wants.

    5. Unit of account: money as "a convenient unit of account" — the value of all goods and services can be expressed in monetary units.

    6. Store of value: "wealth can be stored in the form of money for future use," provided the value of money stays sufficiently stable.

    7. Liquidity preference: another name for "demand for money balance," reflecting the trade-off between liquidity and foregone interest.

    8. Velocity of circulation: "the number of times a unit of money changes hands during the unit period."

    9. Bonds: "papers bearing the promise of a future stream of monetary returns over a certain period of time," issued by governments or firms to borrow from the public.

    10. Capital loss / capital gain: the loss (or gain) to a bond holder from a fall (or rise) in bond price.

    11. Liquidity trap: the situation where the interest rate is so low that everybody expects it to rise — "everyone in the economy will hold their wealth in money balance," and speculative money demand becomes infinitely elastic.

    12. High-powered money: currency issued by the central bank, held by the public or commercial banks, also called reserve money or the monetary base, since "it acts as a basis for credit creation."

    13. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): "percentage of deposits which a bank must keep as cash reserves" with the RBI.

    14. Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): the additional ratio of deposits banks must keep "in liquid form in the short term."

    15. Money multiplier: the ratio by which total deposits created exceed the initial reserves, equal to 1 ÷ CRR.

    16. Lender of last resort: the RBI's role of "being ready to lend to banks at all times."

    17. Open Market Operations: "buying and selling of bonds issued by the Government in the open market" by the central bank.

    18. Repo Rate: "the interest rate at which the money is lent" by the RBI under a repurchase agreement.

    19. Reverse Repo Rate: "the rate at which the money is withdrawn" by the RBI under a reverse repurchase agreement.

    20. Bank Rate: "the rate at which [the RBI] gives loans to the commercial banks."

    21. Fiat money: currency notes and coins that "do not have intrinsic value" but derive their value from the guarantee of the issuing authority.

    22. Legal tender: money that "cannot be refused by any citizen of the country for settlement of any kind of transaction."

    23. Narrow money / Broad money: M1 and M2 are "known as narrow money," M3 and M4 are "known as broad money" — in decreasing order of liquidity.

    Must Remember Numbers

    Every number worth having ready in your head before you open the paper.

    50 / 60 / +5,−1
    CUET Economics: questions / minutes / marking scheme
    +0.5
    Expected value of a blind 4-option guess — always attempt
    1935
    Year the Reserve Bank of India was established
    1 ÷ CRR
    Money multiplier formula — CRR 20% gives a multiplier of 5
    Nov 2016
    Month and year of India's demonetisation
    ₹4,000/day
    Daily exchange limit for old notes during demonetisation
    4
    Official measures of money supply: M1, M2, M3, M4
    2
    Motives for holding money: Transaction and Speculative

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • Barter's core problem is the double coincidence of wants — money exists to remove it.
    • Transaction demand depends on income and prices (Y, P); speculative demand depends inversely on the interest rate (r) — never mix these up.
    • Bond price and the market interest rate are always inversely related.
    • The money multiplier is the reciprocal of the CRR (1 ÷ CRR), not the CRR itself.
    • Repo injects money (RBI buys); reverse repo withdraws money (RBI sells) — opposite directions.
    • Currency notes and coins are legal tender; cheques and demand deposits are not.
    • Narrow money = M1, M2 (most liquid). Broad money = M3, M4 (least liquid). M3 is the most commonly used measure.
    • In CUET, a blind guess has positive expected value (+0.5 marks) — never leave a question blank.

    One Minute Revision

    Read this, then close the laptop

    1. Barter fails because of the double coincidence of wants. Money's three functions — medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value — all solve this.
    2. Transaction demand = k.P.Y — rises with income and prices, unrelated to the interest rate.
    3. Speculative demand is inversely related to the interest rate; at r = rmin, it becomes infinite (the liquidity trap).
    4. Bond price and interest rate always move in opposite directions.
    5. Bank balance sheet: Assets (Reserves + Loans) = Liabilities (Deposits) + Net Worth.
    6. Money multiplier = 1 ÷ CRR. A higher CRR always shrinks the multiplier and money supply.
    7. Repo = RBI injects money (buys securities). Reverse repo = RBI withdraws money (sells securities).
    8. Currency and coins are legal tender; cheques/demand deposits are not.
    9. M1 = CU+DD, M3 = M1 + net time deposits. M1/M2 = narrow money, M3/M4 = broad money.
    10. Demonetisation (Nov 2016): old ₹500/₹1,000 out, new ₹500/₹2,000 in — aimed at corruption, black money, terrorism, fake currency.
