    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Final vs Intermediate

    If it leaves the shop for good, it's a FINAL good. If it goes back into someone else's factory, it's INTERMEDIATE.

    Capital good vs Consumer durable

    Ask WHO buys it: a FIRM → capital good. A HOUSEHOLD → consumer durable.

    Stock vs Flow

    STOCK = a photograph (one moment). FLOW = a video (needs a time period).

    Depreciation

    Only planned, expected wear-and-tear. An earthquake destroying a factory is NOT depreciation.

    Circular flow points

    A-B-C = Amount spent (Expenditure) → goods flow Back (Product) → Cash to factors (Income).

    Three methods

    The PEI wheel: Product (what firms MAKE) = Expenditure (what buyers SPEND) = Income (what factors EARN).

    Expenditure formula

    Don't forget the −M! GDP = C+I+G+X−M, never stop at +X.

    Inventory accumulation

    Sales below plan → pile-up → accumulation. Sales above plan → drain → decumulation.

    Factor Cost → Market Price

    FC → BP → MP: price grows as taxes are added, like GST added to a restaurant bill.

    GDP → PDI ladder

    Only the first step ADDS (NFIA). Every step after that subtracts — except transfers sneak back in at the PI step.

    NDI vs PDI

    NDI = what the whole COUNTRY can spend+save. PDI = what ONE HOUSEHOLD can spend+save.

    Nominal vs Real GDP

    Nominal = today's price tag. Real = yesterday's (base-year) price tag on today's basket.

    CPI vs GDP Deflator

    CPI packs the same suitcase every year (fixed basket). The Deflator's basket changes with what was actually produced.

    GDP & Welfare — the DNE test

    Distribution, Non-monetary exchange, Externalities — the three reasons GDP can mislead you about welfare.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 21 definitions

    1. Final good: "an item that is meant for final use and will not pass through any more stages of production or transformations."

    2. Intermediate good: "used by other producers as material inputs... mostly used as raw material or inputs for production of other commodities."

    3. Consumption goods: "goods like food and clothing, and services like recreation that are consumed when purchased by their ultimate consumers."

    4. Capital goods: durable goods "used in the production process... they themselves don't get transformed... the crucial backbone of any production process."

    5. Consumer durables: goods for ultimate consumption that "have one characteristic in common with capital goods — they are also durable."

    6. Flow: "defined over a period of time."

    7. Stock: "defined at a particular point of time."

    8. Gross investment: "that part of our final output that comprises of capital goods."

    9. Depreciation: "the deletion... made from the value of gross investment in order to accommodate regular wear and tear of capital."

    10. Value added: "the net contribution made by a firm... value of production of the firm − value of intermediate goods used by the firm."

    11. Inventory: "the stock of unsold finished goods, or semi-finished goods, or raw materials which a firm carries from one year to the next."

    12. GNP: "GDP + Net factor income from abroad."

    13. NNP: "GNP − Depreciation."

    14. National Income (NI): "NNP at factor cost ≡ NNP at market prices − Net indirect taxes."

    15. Personal Income (PI): "NI − Undistributed profits − Net interest payments made by households − Corporate tax + Transfer payments to the households from the government and firms."

    16. Personal Disposable Income (PDI): "PI − Personal tax payments − Non-tax payments."

    17. Real GDP: "goods and services are evaluated at some constant set of prices (or constant prices)."

    18. Nominal GDP: "simply the value of GDP at the current prevailing prices."

    19. CPI: "the index of prices of a given basket of commodities which are bought by the representative consumer."

    20. WPI: "the index for wholesale prices."

    21. Externalities: "the benefits (or harms) a firm or an individual causes to another for which they are not paid (or penalised)."

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • Only final goods are counted in GDP — intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting.
    • The three methods (Product, Expenditure, Income) always yield the same GDP — an identity guaranteed by the circular flow.
    • Investment, to an economist, always means capital formation — never shares/property/insurance.
    • Change in inventories can be negative (decumulation) — it's still counted as investment.
    • NNP at Factor Cost = National Income. Learn this equivalence cold.
    • GDP Deflator = Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP — reflects the whole output basket, unlike CPI's fixed consumer basket.
    • GDP is not a perfect welfare measure: distribution, non-monetary exchange, and externalities all break the link.
    • In CUET, a blind guess has positive expected value (+0.5 marks) — never leave a question blank.

    One Minute Revision

    Read this, then close the laptop

    1. Final good = leaves the flow for good. Intermediate good = goes back into someone's factory. Same object, different fate depending on the buyer.
    2. Capital good = bought by a firm. Consumer durable = bought by a household. Ask WHO buys it.
    3. Stock = a photograph (one moment). Flow = a video (needs a time period).
    4. Value Added = Output − Intermediate Goods. Never add up raw outputs — that double counts.
    5. GDP ≡ ΣGVA ≡ C+I+G+X−M ≡ W+P+In+R. Don't forget the −M.
    6. The ladder: GDP → GNP (+NFIA) → NNP (−Depreciation) → National Income (−Net Indirect Taxes) → Personal Income (−UP−CT−NIH+TrH) → PDI (−PTP−NP).
    7. NNP at Factor Cost = National Income. One identity, not two facts.
    8. GDP Deflator = Nominal ÷ Real GDP × 100. CPI uses a fixed basket; the Deflator's basket changes every year.
    9. GDP is not welfare: Distribution, Non-monetary exchange, Externalities (DNE) can all break the link.
    10. In the exam hall: a blind guess has positive expected value (+0.5 marks). Never leave a question blank.

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Ex Ante vs Ex Post

    "Ante" = before, "Post" = after. Ex ante is a plan drawn up before the year happens; ex post is the record tallied after.

    MPC + MPS = 1

    Always. Given one, subtract from 1 to instantly get the other.

    Investment is autonomous

    Machines aren't "used up" — they yield services over years, which is why they're final (capital) goods, and why I = Ī doesn't depend on income in this model.

    The 45° line

    It's just a ruler for aggregate supply — "whatever is produced, is supplied." The real action is where AD crosses it.

    Shift vs Swing

    A̅ changes → the AD line shifts parallel. c changes → the AD line swings. The multiplier is a shift story; the Paradox of Thrift is a swing story.

    The Multiplier

    k = 1 ÷ MPS. The smaller the savings leakage each round, the bigger the multiplier — same "infinite geometric series ÷ (1−r)" pattern as the money multiplier in the Money and Banking chapter.

    Paradox of Thrift

    Individually rational (saving more) can be collectively self-defeating — aggregate savings can end up unchanged or lower.

    Deficient vs Excess Demand

    Deficient = too little demand = prices fall. Excess = too much demand = prices rise. Both describe a gap against full-employment output, not against supply.

    Effective Demand Principle

    With price fixed and AS perfectly elastic, aggregate demand alone determines output — supply just follows along.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 14 definitions

    1. Aggregate Demand: the ex ante sum of consumption and investment expenditure on final goods, AD = C + I.

    2. Aggregate Supply: shown by the 45° line — whatever output level is produced, that much is supplied, when price is fixed and resources are unused.

    3. Equilibrium: the point where "ex ante aggregate demand is equal to ex ante aggregate supply."

    4. Ex Ante: "the planned values of the variables — consumption, investment or output of final goods."

    5. Ex Post: "depicts what has actually happened."

    6. Ex Ante Consumption: the planned consumption expenditure, as opposed to what households actually end up consuming.

    7. Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC): "the change in consumption per unit change in income."

    8. Ex Ante Investment: "the amount a producer plans to add to her inventory" — which may differ from what she ends up doing.

    9. Unintended Changes in Inventories: "stocks piling up in the warehouses" (or running down) when ex ante demand for final goods differs from planned output.

    10. Autonomous Change: a change in an autonomous component of expenditure (C̄ or Ī), independent of income, that shifts the AD line in parallel.

    11. Parametric Shift: a shift or swing of a line caused by a change in one of its parameters (intercept or slope) — a change in A̅ shifts the line, a change in c swings it.

    12. Effective Demand Principle: "aggregate output is determined solely by the level of aggregate demand," when price and interest rate are fixed and aggregate supply is perfectly elastic.

    13. Paradox of Thrift: "as people become more thrifty they end up saving less or same as before."

    14. Autonomous Expenditure Multiplier: "the ratio of the total increment in equilibrium value of final goods output to the initial increment in autonomous expenditure," equal to 1 ÷ (1 − c).

    Non-negotiables to remember

    One Minute Revision

    Read this, then close the laptop

    1. Ex ante = planned. Ex post = actual. They match only at equilibrium; otherwise the gap shows up as unintended inventory change.
    2. C = C̄ + cY. MPC + MPS = 1, always. APC = C÷Y, APS = S÷Y.
    3. I = Ī — autonomous, independent of income in this model.
    4. Equilibrium: Y = A̅ + cY, so Y = (C̄+Ī) ÷ (1−c).
    5. The 45° line is aggregate supply; equilibrium is where AD crosses it.
    6. A change in A̅ shifts the AD line (parallel); a change in c swings it.
    7. Multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1−c) = 1 ÷ MPS. ΔY = ΔA × k — a small push, a bigger result.
    8. Paradox of Thrift: economy-wide thrift can leave total savings unchanged or lower.
    9. Deficient demand (below full employment) → prices fall. Excess demand (above full employment) → prices rise.
    10. In the exam hall: a blind guess has positive expected value (+0.5 marks). Never leave a question blank.

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Revenue vs Capital

    "Does it create an asset or a liability?" Yes → Capital. No → Revenue. Ask this test for receipts AND expenditure.

    Three Deficits, in Order

    Revenue → Fiscal → Primary. Each one strips away one more layer: Revenue only looks at the current account; Fiscal adds capital borrowing; Primary strips out interest on old debt.

    Balanced Budget Multiplier = 1

    Spend ₹100 crore more, tax ₹100 crore more — income still rises by exactly ₹100 crore. Government spending always "hits harder" than an equal tax.

    Proportional Tax Shrinks the Multiplier

    Effective MPC becomes c(1−t) — always smaller than c alone. A bigger t means a smaller multiplier, which means smaller swings in income — that's the stabiliser at work.

    Automatic vs Discretionary

    Automatic = no new decision needed. Discretionary = someone in government had to decide and act.

    Ricardian Equivalence

    "They know the bill is coming." Consumers save today for the tax hike they expect tomorrow, so the deficit changes nothing real.

    FRBMA — Remember "3 and 2003"

    Enacted in 2003, capped the fiscal deficit at 3% of GDP. Rules kicked in from July 2004.

    GST — "One Nation, One Tax"

    Destination-based, since 1 July 2017, via the 101st Amendment. Input Tax Credit is the mechanism that kills the cascading effect.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 16 definitions

    1. Government Budget: an annual statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the government over a fiscal year, presented to Parliament under Article 112.

    2. Revenue Budget: consists of revenue receipts and revenue expenditure, both relating only to the current financial year.

    3. Capital Budget: consists of capital receipts and capital expenditure — items concerning the assets and liabilities of the government.

    4. Public Good: a good whose consumption by one person does not reduce its availability to others (non-rivalrous) and from which no one can be excluded (non-excludable).

    5. Free-rider: a person who enjoys the benefit of a public good without paying for it.

    6. Revenue Receipts: receipts that neither create a liability nor cause a reduction in the assets of the government — non-redeemable.

    7. Capital Receipts: receipts that either create a liability (e.g. borrowing) or reduce a financial asset (e.g. disinvestment) of the government.

    8. Revenue Expenditure: expenditure that neither creates an asset nor reduces a liability of the government.

    9. Capital Expenditure: expenditure that either creates an asset (e.g. a building) or reduces a liability of the government.

    10. Revenue Deficit: the excess of the government's revenue expenditure over its revenue receipts.

    11. Fiscal Deficit: the difference between the government's total expenditure and its total receipts excluding borrowing — its total borrowing requirement.

    12. Primary Deficit: the fiscal deficit minus interest payments, showing the borrowing requirement net of interest on past debt.

    13. Automatic Stabiliser: a built-in feature of the budget, such as a proportional income tax, which dampens fluctuations in national income without any fresh policy action.

    14. Ricardian Equivalence: the view that a rational, forward-looking consumer raises current saving in anticipation of the higher future taxes needed to repay government debt, leaving national saving broadly unaffected.

    15. FRBMA (2003): the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, which required the government to eliminate the revenue deficit and bring the fiscal deficit down to 3% of GDP.

    16. Goods and Services Tax (GST): a single, destination-based indirect tax on the supply of goods and services, levied across India from 1 July 2017.

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • A revenue receipt/expenditure neither creates nor reduces an asset/liability; a capital one does.
    • Revenue Deficit = Rev. Exp − Rev. Receipts; Fiscal Deficit = Total Exp − (Rev. Receipts + Non-debt Cap. Receipts); Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest.
    • The balanced budget multiplier is always 1, whatever the value of MPC.
    • A proportional tax shrinks the effective MPC to c(1−t), lowering the multiplier and acting as an automatic stabiliser.
    • Ricardian equivalence says deficits don't matter if consumers save today for tomorrow's taxes — but this is a debated, not settled, view.
    • FRBMA (2003) capped the fiscal deficit at 3% of GDP; rules took effect from July 2004.
    • GST is a destination-based tax since 1 July 2017, introduced via the 101st Amendment.

    One Minute Revision

    Read this, then close the laptop

    1. The budget is the government's annual statement of receipts & expenditure (Article 112), split into Revenue and Capital accounts.
    2. Its three objectives: allocation (public goods), redistribution (taxes & transfers), stabilisation (smoothing AD).
    3. Test for receipts/expenditure: does it create/reduce an asset or liability? Yes → Capital, No → Revenue.
    4. Three deficits, in order: Revenue (current account gap) → Fiscal (total borrowing) → Primary (borrowing minus interest).
    5. With government added: Y = C̄ + Ī + G + c(Y−T). Spending multiplier > tax multiplier in size; balanced budget multiplier is always 1.
    6. A proportional tax shrinks the effective MPC to c(1−t) — smaller multiplier, smoother income swings — this is the automatic stabiliser.
    7. The deficit-debt debate: traditional view (deficits can crowd out investment) vs Ricardian equivalence (consumers save for future taxes, so it doesn't matter).
    8. FRBMA (2003) capped the fiscal deficit at 3% of GDP, effective July 2004.
    9. GST: one destination-based indirect tax since 1 July 2017, via the 101st Amendment, using Input Tax Credit to kill cascading taxation.
    10. In the exam hall: a blind guess has positive expected value (+0.5 marks). Never leave a question blank.

    Economic agents/units"Individuals or institutions which take economic decisions."
    Capitalist economy"An economy in which most of the economic activities have (a) private ownership of means of production (b) production for selling in the market (c) sale and purchase of labour at a price called the wage rate."
    Great Depression"The time period of the 1930s (started with the stock market crash in New York in 1929) which saw output in the developed countries fall and unemployment rise by huge amounts."
    Unemployment rate"The number of people who were unable to find a job (though they were looking for jobs), as a ratio of total number of people who were looking for jobs."

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    • Micro = one player, Macro = the whole stadium.
    • 1929 crash → 1936 book → new subject. The Depression supplied the puzzle; Keynes supplied the theory.
    • Three tests for "capitalist": Private ownership + Market sale + Wage labour — all three, or it doesn't count.
    • H-F-G-E: Households, Firms, Government, External sector.

    Key Concepts Glossary

    TermMeaning
    Adam Smith (1723–1790)Regarded as the father of modern economics; author of Wealth of Nations.
    John Maynard Keynes (1883–1946)Founder of macroeconomics as a separate discipline.
    Capitalist firmsFirms with private ownership, market-oriented production, wage labour, and continuous capital accumulation.
    EntrepreneurshipThe task of organising, coordinating, and risk-taking during production.
    Four factors of productionLand, Labour, Capital, Entrepreneurship.
    FirmsEconomic units that carry out production and employ factors of production.
    HouseholdsFamilies or individuals who supply factors of production to firms and buy goods/services.
    GovernmentThe state, which maintains law and order, imposes taxes, and promotes economic wellbeing.
    External sectorThe economic transactions of the domestic country with the rest of the world.
    ExportsSale of goods and services by the domestic country to the rest of the world.
    ImportsPurchase of goods and services from the rest of the world.
    Wage labourLabour that is sold and purchased against wages.
    Investment expenditureExpenses that raise productive capacity, e.g. new machinery or factories.
    Notes prepared from NCERT Introductory Macroeconomics, Chapter 1 — Introduction, for CUET revision.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    TermNCERT's own words
    Balance of Payments"The balance of payments (BoP) record the transactions in goods, services and assets between residents of a country with the rest of the world for a specified time period typically a year."
    Current Account"Current Account is the record of trade in goods and services and transfer payments."
    Capital Account"Capital Account records all international transactions of assets."
    Foreign Exchange Rate"The price of one currency in terms of another. It links the currencies of different countries and enables comparison of international costs and prices."
    Flexible Exchange Rate"This exchange rate is determined by the market forces of demand and supply... also known as Floating Exchange Rate."
    Fixed Exchange Rate"In this exchange rate system, the Government fixes the exchange rate at a particular level."

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    • BOT = goods only. Current Account = goods + services + transfers.
    • A deficit in one account needs a surplus in the other — Current + Capital ≡ 0.
    • Buying from abroad = demand for forex. Selling abroad = supply of forex.
    • Rate UP = currency DOWN (depreciation). Rate DOWN = currency UP (appreciation).
    • Depreciation/Appreciation = the market did it. Devaluation/Revaluation = the government did it.
    • Nominal = the number on the board. Real = what it actually buys.
    • Openness = an extra leak in the bucket — the open economy multiplier is always smaller.

    Key Concepts Glossary

    TermMeaning
    Open economyAn economy that trades with other nations in goods, services, and financial assets.
    Current account deficitPayments on the current account exceed receipts.
    Official reserve transactionsCentral bank buying/selling of foreign exchange to manage BoP gaps.
    Autonomous and accommodating transactionsAutonomous = independent of the BoP gap; accommodating = made to bridge it.
    Nominal and real exchange rateNominal = currency price; real = relative price of foreign vs domestic goods.
    Purchasing power parityTheory that identical goods should cost the same across countries, long run.
    DepreciationA decrease in the price of domestic currency in terms of foreign currency, under floating rates.
    Fixed exchange rateAn exchange rate fixed at some level, adjusted only infrequently.
    Managed floatingCentral bank allows the rate to float but intervenes at times.
    Marginal propensity to importFraction of an extra rupee of income spent on imports.
    Open economy multiplierThe multiplier when imports are included as a leakage: 1÷(1−c+m).
    Net exportsExports minus imports (X − M).
    Notes prepared from NCERT Introductory Macroeconomics, Chapter 6 — Open Economy Macroeconomics, for CUET revision.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    TermNCERT's own words
    Central problems of an economy"The allocation of scarce resources and the distribution of the final goods and services are the central problems of any economy."
    Production Possibility Frontier"The curve gives the maximum amount of corn that can be produced in the economy for any given amount of cotton and vice-versa."
    Opportunity cost"There is always a cost of having a little more of one good in terms of the amount of the other good that has to be forgone."
    Market (economics)"A market is a set of arrangements where economic agents can freely exchange their endowments or products with each other."
    Positive vs Normative"In positive economic analysis, we study how the different mechanisms function, and in normative economics, we try to understand whether these mechanisms are desirable or not."
    Microeconomics"We study the behaviour of individual economic agents in the markets for different goods and services."
    Macroeconomics"We try to get an understanding of the economy as a whole by focusing our attention on aggregate measures such as total output, employment and aggregate price level."

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    • WHAT–HOW–FOR WHOM — the three central problems, in that order.
    • Point on the PPF = efficient. Below = wasted. Above = impossible.
    • Planned = plan (government). Market = price (self-interest + coordination).
    • Positive = "what IS." Normative = "what SHOULD BE."
    • Micro = one market's price and quantity. Macro = the whole economy's aggregates.

    Key Concepts Glossary

    TermMeaning
    ScarcityResources are limited relative to what people collectively want.
    AllocationHow much of which resource is devoted to producing each good/service.
    Production possibility setAll output combinations achievable from given resources and technology.
    Production Possibility Frontier (PPF)The boundary of the production possibility set — maximum attainable combinations.
    Opportunity costAmount of one good sacrificed to produce one more unit of another; also called economic cost.
    Centrally planned economyGovernment/central authority decides all major production, exchange, consumption activities.
    Market economyActivities coordinated through free exchange and price signals.
    Mixed economyCombines government decisions with market-driven activity.
    InstitutionAn organisation with some purpose — NCERT's framing for what a "market" is.
    Positive economicsDescriptive study of how economic mechanisms function.
    Normative economicsEvaluative study of whether outcomes are desirable.
    MicroeconomicsStudy of individual agents' behaviour in specific markets.
    MacroeconomicsStudy of the economy as a whole via aggregate measures.

    #Number/ExampleWhat it refers to
    115 → 12 bananas, ₹5→₹7NCERT's own worked eD example: eD = 0.5 (inelastic)

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    TermNCERT's own words
    Marginal Utility"The change in total utility due to consumption of one additional unit of a commodity."
    Indifference Curve"A curve joining all points representing bundles among which the consumer is indifferent."
    Budget Set"The collection of all bundles that the consumer can buy with her income at the prevailing market prices."
    Consumer's Optimum"Located at the point where the budget line is tangent to one of the indifference curves."
    Normal Good"A consumer's demand for a normal good moves in the same direction as the income of the consumer."
    Price Elasticity of Demand"The percentage change in demand for the good divided by the percentage change in its price."

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    • TU is the running total; MU is today's addition. MU=0 at TU's peak.
    • Convex IC = diminishing MRS. Straight-line IC = perfect substitutes.
    • Income change → parallel budget-line shift. Price change → pivot.
    • Tangency = equilibrium: MRS = price ratio.
    • Its OWN price changing = movement ALONG. Anything else = the curve SHIFTS.
    • Vertical demand curve = perfectly inelastic. Horizontal = perfectly elastic.
    • Elastic = expenditure runs opposite to price. Inelastic = runs with price.

    Key Concepts Glossary

    TermMeaning
    UtilityThe want-satisfying capacity of a commodity.
    BundleA specific combination of quantities of two or more goods.
    Monotonic preferencesMore of at least one good, no less of the other, is always preferred.
    Indifference mapThe complete family of a consumer's indifference curves.
    Budget constraintp1x1 + p2x2 ≤ M — the inequality defining the budget set.
    Demand functionX = f(P) — quantity demanded as a function of the good's own price.
    Substitution effectChange in quantity demanded from substituting the relatively cheaper good.
    Income effectChange in quantity demanded from a change in real purchasing power.
    Giffen goodAn inferior good whose demand moves with (not against) its own price.
    Market demandThe sum of all individual consumers' demand at a given price.
    Price elasticity of demandResponsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.
    Rectangular hyperbolaA curve of the form xy = constant; the unit-elastic demand curve shape.
    Notes prepared from NCERT Introductory Microeconomics, Chapter 2 — Theory of Consumer Behaviour, for CUET revision.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    TermNCERT's own words
    Production function"A relationship between inputs used and output produced by the firm... the maximum quantity of output that can be produced."
    Law of Variable Proportions"The marginal product of a factor input initially rises with its employment level. But after reaching a certain level of employment, it starts falling."
    Total Fixed Cost"The cost that a firm incurs to employ these fixed inputs is called the total fixed cost."
    Constant Returns to Scale"When a proportional increase in all inputs results in an increase in output by the same proportion."
    Long Run Costs"In the long run, all inputs are variable. There are no fixed costs."

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    • Isoquant = "equal quantity" of output. Same shape logic as an indifference curve.
    • AP is the running average of all MPs — above pulls it up, below pulls it down, equal means it's at the peak.
    • Rises first (factor proportions improve), then falls (input gets "crowded").
    • Double the inputs — did output more/exactly/less-than double? IRS / CRS / DRS.
    • Fixed cost never changes; variable cost always rises.
    • Cost curves flip the MP-AP crossing direction: SMC cuts AVC/SAC/LRAC from BELOW, not above.
    • IRS → LRAC falls. CRS → LRAC flat. DRS → LRAC rises.

    Key Concepts Glossary

    TermMeaning
    Factors of productionInputs used by a firm — labour, capital, land, raw materials.
    IsoquantCurve of input combinations yielding the same maximum output.
    Fixed factorAn input that cannot be varied in the short run.
    Factor proportionsThe ratio in which two inputs are combined.
    Returns to ScaleHow output responds to a proportional change in ALL inputs, in the long run.
    Total Fixed CostCost of fixed inputs; constant regardless of output.
    Total Variable CostCost of variable inputs; rises with output.
    Rectangular hyperbolaCurve of the form xy=constant; the shape of the AFC curve.
    Long Run Average Cost (LRAC)Total cost per unit of output when all inputs are variable.
    Notes prepared from NCERT Introductory Microeconomics, Chapter 3 — Production and Costs, for CUET revision.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    TermNCERT's own words
    Perfectly competitive market"Large number of buyers and sellers... homogenous product... free entry and exit... perfect information."
    Shut-down point"The point of minimum AVC where the SMC curve cuts the AVC curve. Below this, there will be no production."
    Normal profit"The minimum level of profit that is needed to keep a firm in the existing business."
    Break-even point"The point on the supply curve at which a firm earns only normal profit."
    Price elasticity of supply"Percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price."

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    • 4 features → 1 consequence: price-taking.
    • AR = MR = Price, always, under perfect competition.
    • P = MC isn't enough — MC must ALSO be rising there.
    • Supply curve = rising part of the MC curve, above min AVC/LRAC.
    • Shut-down = produce nothing. Break-even = normal profit only.
    • Better tech/cheaper inputs → supply shifts RIGHT. Costlier inputs/new tax → LEFT.
    • A straight-line supply curve through the origin is ALWAYS unit-elastic.

    Key Concepts Glossary

    TermMeaning
    Price-takingA firm/buyer believes it cannot influence the market price by its own actions.
    Price lineHorizontal line at the market price — the firm's AR and demand curve.
    Normal profitMinimum profit needed to keep a firm in business; treated as a cost.
    Super-normal profitProfit earned above normal profit.
    Shut-down pointMinimum AVC (short run) or minimum LRAC (long run) — below which output is zero.
    Break-even pointWhere the firm earns exactly normal profit.
    Unit taxA tax levied per unit of output sold; raises AC and MC by the tax amount.
    Market supply curveHorizontal summation of all firms' individual supply curves.
    Price elasticity of supplyResponsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price.

    BasisExcess DemandExcess Supply
    DefinitionDemand > SupplySupply > Demand
    Price tends toRiseFall
    BasisPrice CeilingPrice Floor
    Set relative to equilibriumBelowAbove

    Must Remember Numbers

    #Number/ExampleWhat it refers to
    1qD=200−p, qf=10+p (p≥20)NCERT's own Example 5.2: p0=20, q0=180, n0=6 firms
    24 combinationsNCERT's Table 5.1 — simultaneous demand/supply shift cases

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    TermNCERT's own words
    Equilibrium"A situation where the plans of all consumers and firms in the market match and the market clears."
    Excess demand / supply"Zero excess demand-zero excess supply situation" defines equilibrium.
    Free entry/exit result"The market price will always be equal to the minimum average cost, that is p = min AC."
    Price ceiling"The government-imposed upper limit on the price of a good or service."
    Price floor"The government-imposed lower limit on the price that may be charged for a particular good or service."

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    • Demand > Supply → price rises. Supply > Demand → price falls.
    • Above equilibrium → excess supply. Below equilibrium → excess demand.
    • Same-direction shifts → quantity certain, price ambiguous. Opposite-direction shifts → price certain, quantity ambiguous.
    • Free entry/exit = price glued to min AC forever — demand shifts only change quantity and firm count.
    • Ceiling is a CAP (below equilibrium) → shortage. Floor is a MINIMUM (above equilibrium) → surplus.

    Key Concepts Glossary

    TermMeaning
    Equilibrium price/quantityThe price and quantity at which market demand exactly equals market supply.
    Invisible HandAdam Smith's automatic price-adjustment mechanism responding to market imbalance.
    Supernormal profitProfit earned above normal profit; attracts new firms under free entry.
    RationingDistributing a scarce good via coupons/fair price shops under a price ceiling.
    Black marketIllegal sale above a price ceiling, driven by unmet demand.
    Agricultural price supportA price floor on farm goods; government buys the resulting surplus.
    Minimum wage legislationA price floor on the wage rate, set above the equilibrium wage.
    Notes prepared from NCERT Introductory Microeconomics, Chapter 5 — Market Equilibrium, for CUET revision.

    TermNCERT's own words
    Zamindari system's effect"The profit accruing out of the agriculture sector went to the zamindars instead of the cultivators."

    Barter & Functions of Money ✓ All correct

    5 questions on this topic. Answer, then check.

    Q1The central problem that a barter economy suffers from, which money solves, is:

    Barter requires each party to want exactly what the other offers — a rare coincidence that money removes.

    Q2Expressing the value of a wristwatch as "₹500" illustrates money's function as a:

    Using money as a common yardstick to express value is the unit-of-account function.

    Q3A pencil costs ₹2 and a pen costs ₹10. How many pencils is one pen worth?

    10 ÷ 2 = 5 pencils — exactly NCERT's own relative-price example.

    Q4Keeping wealth in the form of money instead of perishable rice illustrates money's function as a:

    Carrying wealth forward for future use, since money doesn't perish, is the store-of-value function.

    Q5For each scenario, choose the function of money being used — Medium, Account, or Value:

    (a) Paying for groceries with cash

    (b) Comparing two smartphone prices before buying

    (c) Keeping savings in a bank for use five years later

    (a) Medium of exchange (b) Unit of account (c) Store of value.

    Demand for Money — Transaction Motive ✓ All correct

    5 questions on this topic. Answer, then check.

    Q1Meena earns ₹300 on the first day of the month and spends it evenly. Her average cash balance for the month is (₹):

    (300 + 0) ÷ 2 = ₹150 — average of opening and closing balance.

    Q2Transaction demand for money is positively related to:

    MdT = k.P.Y — it rises with both real income (Y) and the price level (P).

    Q3Total monthly transactions = ₹400, average money balance held = ₹100. The velocity of circulation is:

    v = T ÷ MdT = 400 ÷ 100 = 4.

    Q4Transaction demand for money does NOT depend directly on:

    The interest rate drives speculative demand, not transaction demand.

    Q5If k = 0.25 and total transactions T = ₹800, transaction demand for money MdT (₹) is:

    MdT = k.T = 0.25 × 800 = ₹200.

    Demand for Money — Speculative Motive ✓ All correct

    5 questions on this topic. Answer, then check.

    Q1The price of a bond is:

    As the market interest rate rises, a bond's present value (and price) falls, and vice versa.

    Q2A liquidity trap occurs when the market rate of interest is:

    At r = rmin, everyone expects a future rise (and bond-price fall), so all wealth is held as money — the liquidity trap.

    Q3When the interest rate is at its maximum, rmax, speculative demand for money is:

    Everyone expects the rate to fall (bond prices to rise), so all wealth is converted into bonds — speculative money demand is zero.

    Q4A bond promises ₹126 after one year. The market interest rate is 5%. What is its present value (₹)?

    PV = 126 ÷ 1.05 = ₹120.

    Q5A bond holder suffers a capital loss when:

    A rising interest rate pushes bond prices down — a capital loss to whoever holds the bond.

    Central Bank (RBI) ✓ All correct

    5 questions on this topic. Answer, then check.

    Q1In which year was the Reserve Bank of India established?

    1935 — India's central bank, the RBI, was established this year.

    Q2Which of the following is NOT a function of the RBI?

    Collecting income tax is the job of the tax administration, not the RBI.

    Q3Currency issued by the central bank, held by the public or commercial banks, is also known as:

    Also called the monetary base — it is the basis for all credit creation.

    Q4The RBI's readiness to lend to commercial banks at all times is called its role as:

    This is the exact NCERT phrase for this specific RBI function.

    Q5The RBI acts as the custodian of the economy's:

    The RBI holds and manages India's foreign exchange reserves.

    Commercial Banks & Money Creation ✓ All correct

    5 questions on this topic. Answer, then check.

    Q1A bank has deposits of ₹300 crore and reserves of ₹60 crore. Its loans (₹ crore) must be:

    Loans = Deposits − Reserves = 300 − 60 = ₹240 crore.

    Q2For a commercial bank, the main liability is:

    Deposits are what the bank owes to its depositors — its main liability.

    Q3A bank's assets consist of:

    Assets = Reserves + Loans, matched against Liabilities = Deposits.

    Q4A bank has Reserves ₹50 crore, Loans ₹200 crore, and Deposits ₹240 crore. Its Net Worth (₹ crore) is:

    Net Worth = Assets − Liabilities = (50 + 200) − 240 = ₹10 crore.

    Q5In the goldsmith Lala's story, money was effectively created because Lala assumed that:

    This exact assumption — that all depositors won't demand their gold back simultaneously — is what let Lala (and modern banks) safely lend out deposited funds.

    Money Multiplier & Limits to Credit Creation ✓ All correct

    5 questions on this topic. Answer, then check.

    Q1If the CRR is 25%, the money multiplier is:

    Multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.

    Q2CRR = 10%. An initial deposit of ₹50 crore can eventually support total deposits of (₹ crore):

    Multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10. Total deposits = 10 × 50 = ₹500 crore.

    Q3If the RBI raises the CRR, the money multiplier and money supply will:

    A higher CRR shrinks the multiplier (1 ÷ CRR), which in turn shrinks total money supply.

    Q4If the money multiplier is 8, the CRR (as a percentage) must be:

    CRR = 1 ÷ multiplier = 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125 = 12.5%.

    Q5SLR stands for:

    SLR is the additional ratio of deposits banks must keep in liquid form, apart from CRR.

    Policy Tools to Control Money Supply ✓ All correct

    5 questions on this topic. Answer, then check.

    Q1For each tool, choose Quantitative or Qualitative:

    (a) Cash Reserve Ratio

    (b) Moral suasion

    (c) Open Market Operations

    (a) Quantitative (b) Qualitative (c) Quantitative.

    Q2When the RBI sells government bonds in the open market, money supply:

    Selling bonds withdraws reserves from the banking system, reducing the money supply.

    Q3The rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks is called the:

    This is the specific NCERT term for RBI's lending rate to commercial banks.

    Q4The repo rate is the interest rate at which money is:

    Repo = a repurchase agreement where RBI temporarily injects money at the repo rate.

    Q5Money is withdrawn from the system at the reverse repo rate when the RBI:

    This is exactly the reverse repurchase agreement — RBI temporarily withdraws money at the reverse repo rate.

    Measures of Money Supply (M1–M4) ✓ All correct

    5 questions on this topic. Answer, then check.

    Q1Currency with the public (CU) = ₹500 crore, net demand deposits (DD) = ₹700 crore. M1 (₹ crore) is:

    M1 = CU + DD = 500 + 700 = ₹1,200 crore.

    Q2M3 is defined as:

    M3 = M1 + Net time deposits of commercial banks — the most commonly used measure.

    Q3For each item, choose Legal Tender or Not Legal Tender:

    (a) A ₹100 currency note

    (b) A ₹2 coin

    (c) A cheque drawn on a current account

    (a) Legal Tender (b) Legal Tender (c) Not Legal Tender — cheques can always be refused.

    Q4Narrow money consists of:

    M1 and M2 are narrow money (most liquid); M3 and M4 are broad money.

    Q5The measure of money supply also known as "aggregate monetary resources" is:

    M3 is both the most commonly used measure and the one NCERT calls "aggregate monetary resources."

    Demonetisation — A Case Study ✓ All correct

    5 questions on this topic. Answer, then check.

    Q1Demonetisation in India was announced in:

    The Government of India announced demonetisation in November 2016.

    Q2Which currency notes lost their legal tender status in 2016?

    The old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes were withdrawn as legal tender.

    Q3Which new currency denominations were introduced after demonetisation?

    New ₹500 and ₹2,000 notes were launched to replace the withdrawn denominations.

    Q4Which of these was cited as a positive impact of demonetisation?

    More people were brought into the tax net, improving tax compliance.

    01Barter System & Functions of Money

    Before money, exchange needed a coincidence so rare it strangled trade. Money's whole job is to remove that coincidence.

    Conceptual foundation — near-certain 1 question

    Try this first

    A farmer has surplus rice and wants clothing in exchange. Why can't she just walk up to any tailor and trade directly?

    1

    She needs a tailor who happens to want rice and happens to have spare clothing to offer — NCERT calls this a "double coincidence of wants."

    2

    That coincidence is rare. As the number of people in the economy grows, finding it gets prohibitively costly — most potential trades simply never happen.

    3

    Money fixes this by breaking the trade into two halves: she sells rice for money to anyone, then buys clothing with that money from a different anyone.

    4

    That single fix — removing the need for a double coincidence — is money's core job as a medium of exchange. Its other two jobs, unit of account and store of value, both grow out of solving this same original problem.

    NCERT Definition Ch. 3, §3.1

    "Economic exchanges without the mediation of money are referred to as barter exchanges. However, they presume the rather improbable double coincidence of wants."

    The three functions of money

    FunctionWhat it meansNCERT's own illustration
    Medium of exchangeremoves the need for double coincidence of wants — sell for money, then buy with moneythe principal, "first and foremost" role of money
    Unit of accounta common yardstick to express the value of every good, and compare goods to each otherpencil ₹2, pen ₹10 → a pen is worth 10 ÷ 2 = 5 pencils
    Store of valuewealth can be held in money for future use, without it perishing or costing a lot to storerice is perishable and bulky to store; money is not

    Worked example — Unit of Account

    Pencil = ₹2, Pen = ₹10. Relative price of a pen in terms of pencils = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 pencils. Value of ₹1 (a rupee) in terms of a pencil = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 pencil; in terms of a pen = 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1 pen. If all prices rise (general price rise), the value of money in terms of any commodity must fall — this is a deterioration in the purchasing power of money.

    Try it yourself — which function is at work?

    Tap the correct function for each everyday scenario.

    Paying cash to a shopkeeper for groceries

    Money is directly facilitating a transaction — medium of exchange.

    Saying a wristwatch is "worth ₹500"

    Expressing the value of a good in monetary units — unit of account.

    Keeping savings in a bank account for use five years later

    Wealth is being carried forward for future use — store of value.

    Using a debit card to pay for a train ticket

    Settling a transaction directly — medium of exchange.

    Comparing prices of two smartphones before buying

    Using money as the common yardstick to compare value — unit of account.

    Holding cash under a mattress instead of buying perishable rice as an asset

    Money is being used to carry wealth forward — store of value.

    Memory Trick

    MUS — Money is a Medium of exchange (transactions), a Unit of account (measuring value), and a Store of value (carrying wealth forward). All three trace back to solving the same problem: barter's double coincidence of wants.

    Why CUET asks this —It's the conceptual entry point to the whole chapter, so expect a direct definition MCQ or an assertion-reason pairing "double coincidence of wants" with "barter exchange."
    NCERT — Barter System & Functions of Money, p. 36Open in new tab

    02Demand for Money — Transaction Motive

    People don't hold money for its own sake — they hold it to bridge the gap between when income arrives and when it gets spent.

    Numerical favourite — average cash balance & velocity

    Try this first

    A firm pays a worker ₹100 at the start of every month, and the worker spends it evenly over the month. How much money does the economy actually need people to hold, on average, just to make this happen?

    1

    At the start of the month, the worker holds the full ₹100; the firm holds ₹0.

    2

    By month-end, spending has flowed back to the firm — the firm now holds ₹100, the worker holds ₹0.

    3

    Each side's average holding across the month = (100 + 0) ÷ 2 = ₹50.

    4

    Total average money held in the economy = ₹50 + ₹50 = ₹100 — even though ₹200 worth of transactions happened (₹100 in sales + ₹100 in wages). That gap between money held and value transacted is exactly what the transaction demand formula below captures.

    NCERT Definition Box 3.1

    "The principal motive for holding money is to carry out transactions... Demand for money balance is thus often referred to as liquidity preference."
    SymbolStands forNote
    MdTTransaction demand for moneya stock concept — money people wish to hold at a point in time
    TTotal value of (nominal) transactions in the perioda flow variable
    kA positive fractionthe proportion of transactions value held as money
    vVelocity of circulation = 1/knumber of times a unit of money changes hands in the period

    Transaction demand for money

    MdT = k.T
    v.MdT = T  (where v = 1/k, the velocity of circulation)
    MdT = k.P.Y  (in terms of real GDP Y and price level P)

    In the worker–firm example, k = ½ (average balance is half the transaction value) so v = 2 — each rupee changes hands twice a month.

    1Higher income → higher transaction demand

    More income means more planned transactions, which directly raises MdT (via Y in the kPY formula).

    2Higher price level → higher transaction demand

    The same real basket now costs more money, so nominal transaction value (and money needed) rises with P.

    3It does NOT depend on the interest rate

    Transaction demand is about facilitating spending, not about the opportunity cost of holding money — that's the speculative motive's job (next topic).

    Memory Trick

    Transaction demand tracks PY, not r. It rises with real income and prices — it has nothing to do with the rate of interest. If a question links money demand to the interest rate, it's talking about the speculative motive, not this one.

    CUET Insight —A classic numerical: given monthly income and an even spending pattern, compute average cash balance (= income ÷ 2) or velocity of circulation (= transactions ÷ average balance).
    NCERT — Demand for Money — Transaction Motive, p. 43Open in new tab

    03Demand for Money — Speculative Motive & Liquidity Trap

    The other reason to hold money: you might expect bond prices to fall, and would rather hold cash than lose value.

    Bond-price numericals are a recurring favourite

    Try this first

    A firm issues a 2-year bond promising ₹10 at the end of year 1, and ₹110 at the end of year 2, for a ₹100 loan today. If the market interest rate is 5%, would you value that bond at exactly ₹100 — or more, or less?

    1

    The bond pays more than a 5% savings account would on the same money, so buyers bid its price up — its present value works out to about ₹109.29, not ₹100.

    2

    Now suppose the market rate rises to 6% instead. Money elsewhere earns more, so this bond looks relatively less attractive — its present value falls to about ₹107.33.

    3

    The general rule: bond price and the market interest rate always move in opposite directions.

    4

    That's exactly why people's appetite for holding bonds vs. cash flips as the interest rate changes — which is the whole idea behind speculative demand for money.

    Bond price and the interest rate

    The price of a bond is always inversely related to the market rate of interest — as r rises, present value (and price) falls; as r falls, price rises.

    Capital gains, capital losses, and what people do

    1Interest rate very high (near rmax)

    Everyone expects it to fall → bond prices expected to rise → people buy bonds now for the future capital gain → speculative demand for money is zero.

    2Interest rate very low (near rmin)

    Everyone expects it to rise → bond prices expected to fall (a capital loss) → people sell bonds and hold money instead → speculative demand for money is infinite.

    3The liquidity trap

    At r = rmin, any extra money injected is simply absorbed into idle balances — nobody wants more bonds. Monetary policy loses its grip on the interest rate here.

    Speculative demand for money

    MdS = (rmax − r) ÷ (r − rmin)

    As r falls from rmax to rmin, MdS rises from 0 to ∞ — an inverse relationship with the rate of interest.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 3.1

    Fig. 3.1 — as r falls toward rmin, speculative demand for money rises and flattens into the liquidity trap, where the curve becomes horizontal (infinitely elastic).

    Total money demand

    Md = MdT + MdS = k.P.Y + (rmax − r) ÷ (r − rmin)

    Memory Trick

    Bond price and interest rate move opposite ways. High interest rate today → you expect it to fall → bond prices will rise → buy bonds now (speculative money demand low). Low interest rate today → you expect it to rise → bond prices will fall → sell bonds, hold money (speculative demand high, or infinite in the liquidity trap).

    CUET Insight —Expect either a direct present-value/bond-price numerical, or a conceptual question testing whether you know speculative demand is inversely related to the interest rate (opposite of transaction demand's relationship with income).
    NCERT — Demand for Money — Speculative Motive, p. 45Open in new tab

    04Central Bank (RBI) — Functions & High-Powered Money

    Every modern economy has exactly one institution that alone can issue currency — in India, that's the RBI.

    Direct fact-recall favourite

    Try this first

    The RBI is the only institution in India legally allowed to issue currency notes. Starting from just that one fact, can you reason out what its other five jobs might be?

    1

    If you're the one printing the notes, you're also the natural body to decide how much money is in circulation — that's controller of money supply (via bank rate, OMOs, reserve ratios).

    2

    Since you're already managing the nation's money, the government would want its own banking done through you too — banker to the government.

    3

    Someone has to hold the country's foreign exchange reserves so external payments stay stable — custodian of forex reserves.

    4

    Every other bank in the country needs somewhere safe to park its reserves — bank to the banking system.

    5

    And when a bank runs short of funds and no one else will lend, someone has to be willing to — lender of last resort.

    NCERT Fact

    "India got its central bank in 1935. Its name is the 'Reserve Bank of India'."

    Functions of the RBI

    FunctionWhat it means
    Issuer of currencyonly institution that can issue currency notes in India
    Controller of money supplyvia bank rate, open market operations, reserve ratios
    Banker to the governmentmanages government's banking transactions
    Custodian of forex reservesholds and manages the economy's foreign exchange reserves
    Bank to the banking systemcommercial banks keep their reserves with the RBI
    Lender of last resortalways ready to lend to commercial banks when they need funds

    High-Powered Money

    Currency issued by the central bank — held by the public or by commercial banks — is called high-powered money, reserve money, or the monetary base. It acts as the basis for all credit creation in the economy (the next two topics show exactly how).

    Memory Trick

    "I-C-B-C-B-L" — Issuer of currency, Controller of money supply, Banker to government, Custodian of forex, Bank to banks, Lender of last resort. Six functions, one institution.

    Why CUET asks this —Pure fact-recall makes for cheap, high-confidence MCQs — expect "which of the following is NOT a function of the RBI" style questions, or a direct year/name fact-check.
    NCERT — Central Bank (RBI), p. 38Open in new tab

    05Commercial Banks & Money Creation

    A goldsmith's receipts, circulating as money, is exactly how modern banks create money out of deposits.

    Sets up the multiplier topic that follows

    Try this first

    Lala the goldsmith holds 100kg of gold, fully backed by paper receipts. Ramu asks to borrow 25kg. If Lala assumes not everyone will withdraw their gold on the same day, should he actually hand it over — and what happens to the total receipts in circulation if he does?

    1

    Lala reasons that villagers won't all show up demanding gold on the same day — so he lends the 25kg to Ramu.

    2

    Ramu pays Ali with it. Ali doesn't want to hold raw gold, so he deposits it back with Lala and gets a fresh receipt.

    3

    Receipts in circulation are now worth 125kg — even though Lala still only physically holds 100kg of gold.

    4

    Lala created 25kg of new "money" (in receipt form) purely by lending out gold he judged wouldn't be reclaimed immediately — exactly what a modern commercial bank does with deposits.

    Bank balance sheet basics

    Assets = Reserves + Loans
    Liabilities = Deposits
    Net Worth = Assets − Liabilities

    Reserves are deposits commercial banks keep with the RBI (partly cash, partly RBI bonds/T-bills) — similar to how our own bank deposits are our assets.

    The fictional bank example

    Table 3.1 — Balance Sheet of a Bank

    Ms Fernandes deposits ₹100. The bank keeps the entire ₹100 with the RBI as reserves (no lending yet, no currency in circulation).

    Assets₹Liabilities₹
    Reserves100Deposits100
    Net Worth0
    Total100Total100

    Money supply here

    M1 = Currency + Deposits = 0 + 100 = 100

    Memory Trick

    Banks don't print money — they multiply deposits into loans, and loans back into deposits. The chain only works because banks bet correctly that not everyone withdraws on the same day. That bet is exactly what the next topic (money multiplier) puts a legal limit on.

    CUET Insight —Expect a basic balance-sheet-construction question (given deposits and reserves, find loans or net worth) or a definitional MCQ on what counts as a bank's "assets" vs "liabilities."
    NCERT — Commercial Banks & Money Creation, p. 38Open in new tab

    06Money Multiplier & Limits to Credit Creation

    Banks can't lend forever — the RBI's reserve requirement puts a hard ceiling on how much money the banking system can create.

    The single most-tested numerical in this chapter

    Try this first

    CRR is 20%. Someone deposits ₹100 in a bank. If every bank keeps only the required reserve and lends out the rest — and every rupee lent eventually comes back as a new deposit somewhere — how much can total deposits across the banking system add up to?

    1

    Round 1: the bank keeps ₹20 (20% of ₹100) as required reserve, lends out ₹80.

    2

    That ₹80 gets spent and re-deposited elsewhere. Round 2 begins with that new deposit — the bank keeps ₹16, lends ₹64.

    3

    Each round is smaller than the last — a shrinking geometric series — but the rounds never fully stop, they just keep getting negligibly small.

    4

    Add every round together and total deposits settle at exactly ₹500 — five times the original ₹100.

    NCERT Definition §3.3.2

    "The RBI decides a certain percentage of deposits which every bank must keep as reserves... This is called the 'Required Reserve Ratio' or the 'Reserve Ratio' or 'Cash Reserve Ratio' (CRR)."
    TermMeaning
    Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)% of deposits a bank must keep as cash reserves with the RBI
    Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)% of deposits banks must additionally keep in liquid form (short-term)

    The multiplier process, worked step by step (CRR = 20%)

    RoundDeposit in BankRequired ReserveLoan made
    1100.0020.0080.00
    2180.0036.0064.00
    …………
    Last500.00100.00400.00

    The process repeats until required reserves reach the original ₹100 — which only happens once total deposits reach ₹500 (since 20% of 500 = 100). Final balance sheet: Reserves ₹100 + Loans ₹400 = Deposits ₹500.

    Money Multiplier

    Money Multiplier = 1 ÷ CRR

    With CRR = 20% = 0.2, multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. Reserves of ₹100 therefore support deposits of 5 × 100 = ₹500. (This is an infinite geometric series with first term a = 1 and common ratio r = 0.8 — NCERT derives it fully in Appendix 3.1.)

    1Higher CRR → smaller multiplier

    Raising CRR to 25% shrinks the multiplier to 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 — the same ₹100 in reserves now supports only ₹400 in deposits, so money supply falls.

    2The reserve requirement is the limit

    Without a CRR, banks would in theory lend without bound — the legally mandated reserve ratio is what caps credit creation.

    Memory Trick

    Multiplier = 1 ÷ CRR, always the reciprocal. A higher reserve ratio always means a smaller multiplier and less money creation — CRR and the multiplier move in opposite directions.

    CUET Insight —Almost every year: "given initial deposits and CRR, find the total deposits/money supply created" or the reverse — "given the multiplier, find CRR." Learn the 1÷CRR formula cold.
    NCERT — Money Multiplier & Credit Creation, p. 40Open in new tab

    07Policy Tools to Control Money Supply

    The RBI has a toolkit to expand or shrink money supply at will — some tools are precise numbers, others are persuasion.

    Repo vs Reverse Repo is a recurring trap

    Try this first

    RBI wants to fight inflation by making it more expensive for banks to create new loans. If it raises the CRR from 4% to 4.5%, is that a hard numeric lever or a soft persuasion tool — and what happens to money supply as a result?

    1

    Raising CRR is a precise, numeric change — squarely a quantitative tool, not persuasion.

    2

    A higher CRR means banks must hold back a bigger slice of every deposit as reserves.

    3

    Less of each deposit is available to re-lend, which shrinks the money multiplier (recall: Multiplier = 1 ÷ CRR).

    4

    A smaller multiplier means the same base of reserves supports a smaller total money supply — exactly what RBI wants when fighting inflation.

    NCERT Definition §3.4

    "The tools used by the Central bank to control money supply can be quantitative or qualitative."
    ToolTypeHow it works
    Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)Quantitativehigher CRR → smaller multiplier → less money supply
    Bank RateQuantitativethe rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks; higher rate → costlier loans → less money supply
    Open Market Operations (OMO)QuantitativeRBI buying/selling government bonds in the open market
    Moral suasion, margin requirementQualitativepersuasion to encourage/discourage lending, not a hard numeric lever

    Open Market Operations — outright vs repo

    BasisOutright OMORepo / Reverse Repo
    NaturePermanent — no promise to reverse the tradeTemporary — an agreed date & price to reverse it
    RBI buys securitiesInjects money permanentlyRepo: injects money temporarily, at the repo rate
    RBI sells securitiesWithdraws money permanentlyReverse repo: withdraws money temporarily, at the reverse repo rate

    Repo and reverse repo (at overnight, 7-day, 14-day maturities) are now the RBI's main tool of monetary policy.

    Try it yourself — Quantitative or Qualitative?

    Raising the Cash Reserve Ratio from 4% to 4.5%

    A precise numeric lever on reserves — quantitative.

    RBI selling government bonds in the open market

    An Open Market Operation — quantitative.

    RBI persuading banks to discourage speculative lending

    Persuasion, not a hard number — moral suasion, a qualitative tool.

    Increasing the Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points

    A precise rate change — quantitative.

    Memory Trick

    Repo = Receive (RBI receives securities, injects money). Reverse repo = Reduce (RBI reduces money in the system). Both involve a promised buy-back date — that's what makes them different from an outright, permanent OMO trade.

    Warning —Repo vs reverse repo is the single most commonly flipped pair in this chapter — always double-check which direction the money is moving before answering.
    NCERT — Policy Tools — Repo, CRR, OMO, p. 42Open in new tab

    08Measures of Money Supply — Fiat Money, Legal Tender & M1–M4

    Money supply isn't one number — RBI publishes four alternative measures, ordered by how easily each can be spent.

    M1–M4 formulas are near-guaranteed

    Try this first

    You have a ₹500 currency note and a cheque drawn on your savings account, both worth ₹500. Can a shopkeeper legally refuse either one as payment?

    1

    The currency note is fiat money issued by the RBI — by law, nobody can refuse it. It's legal tender.

    2

    The cheque draws on a demand deposit — and anyone is free to decline a cheque as payment (it's just a promise to pay, not money itself).

    3

    So demand deposits are not legal tender, even though they function like money for almost every practical purpose.

    4

    This distinction — legal-tender currency vs. non-legal-tender bank deposits — is exactly what separates the different measures of money supply (M1 through M4), which simply add progressively less liquid items to the base.

    NCERT Definition §3.2.2

    "Currency notes and coins are... called fiat money. They do not have intrinsic value... They are also called legal tenders as they cannot be refused by any citizen... Cheques drawn on savings or current accounts... can be refused by anyone as a mode of payment. Hence, demand deposits are not legal tenders."

    The four measures of money supply

    MeasureFormulaCategory
    M1CU + DDNarrow money (most liquid)
    M2M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office savings banks
    M3M1 + Net time deposits of commercial banksBroad money (less liquid)
    M4M3 + Total deposits with Post Office savings organisations (excl. NSCs)

    CU = currency (notes + coins) held by the public · DD = net demand deposits of commercial banks. M3 is the most commonly used measure, also called aggregate monetary resources.

    Demand deposits vs Time deposits

    Demand deposits (savings/current accounts) are payable on demand — cheques can be drawn on them, but the cheque itself can still be refused as payment. Time deposits (e.g. fixed deposits) have a fixed maturity period.

    Try it yourself — Legal Tender or Not?

    A ₹500 currency note

    Issued by the RBI, backed by its guarantee — cannot be refused. Legal tender.

    A cheque drawn on a savings account

    Can be refused as a mode of payment by anyone. Not legal tender.

    A ₹5 coin issued by the Government of India

    Coins carry the same guarantee as currency notes. Legal tender.

    A demand deposit balance in a current account

    Only accessed via cheques/transfers that can be declined. Not legal tender.

    Memory Trick

    "M grows as liquidity shrinks." M1 → M2 → M3 → M4 adds progressively less-liquid items each time — M1 is cash-like and easiest to spend, M4 is the least liquid of all.

    CUET Insight —Given CU and DD values, expect a direct "calculate M1" numerical, or a classification MCQ on narrow vs broad money.
    NCERT — Measures of Money Supply (M1–M4), p. 48Open in new tab

    09Demonetisation — A CUET Case Study

    A real policy event NCERT boxes as a case study — exactly the kind of reading CUET likes to test with case-based questions.

    High case-study potential

    Try this first

    In November 2016, the Government of India declared that the ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes people were holding were no longer valid money, overnight. If you were holding old notes, what were your options — and why would a government do this to its own currency?

    1

    You could deposit the old notes in a bank by 31 December 2016 — or, with a declaration at the RBI, by 31 March 2017. After that, they were worthless paper.

    2

    The government's stated goals: tackle corruption, black money, terrorism financing, and fake currency circulation.

    3

    Short-run, this caused real pain — cash shortages, long bank queues, disrupted economic activity.

    4

    Longer-run, NCERT frames some genuine gains too — more savings pulled into the formal banking system, better tax compliance, and a push toward electronic payments.

    NCERT Box 3.2 — Demonetisation

    "Demonetisation was a new initiative taken by the Government of India in November 2016 to tackle the problem of corruption, black money, terrorism and circulation of fake currency... Old currency notes of ₹500 and ₹1000 were no longer legal tender. New currency notes in the denomination of ₹500 and ₹2000 were launched."
    AspectDetail
    WhenNovember 2016
    Notes withdrawn₹500 and ₹1,000 (old series)
    Notes introduced₹500 (new) and ₹2,000
    Deposit deadline (no declaration)31 December 2016
    Deposit deadline (with declaration, at RBI)31 March 2017
    Daily exchange limit allowed₹4,000 of old notes per person, per day

    Impact — both sides, as NCERT frames it

    Negative / short-runPositive / longer-run
    Long queues outside banks and ATMsImproved tax compliance — more people brought into the tax net
    Currency shortage disrupted economic activitySavings channelised into the formal financial system
     Banks gained resources to lend at lower interest rates
     Push from cash to electronic payment technologies

    Memory Trick

    Demonetisation = old notes lose legal tender status overnight. Remember the four goals NCERT lists: corruption, black money, terrorism financing, and fake currency.

    Why CUET asks this —Real, dated policy events are a natural fit for case-based passage questions — expect a short passage followed by 2–3 questions on dates, amounts, or which impact (positive/negative) a given statement describes.

    01Final & Intermediate Goods, and Their Types

    Everything in national income accounting starts with one question: has this good finished its journey, or is it still being transformed into something else?

    High-frequency classification question

    Try this first

    A farmer's cotton becomes yarn, then cloth, then a shirt sold to a customer. At which point in that chain does it become a “final good”?

    1

    Every sale along the chain — cotton to the mill, yarn to the weaver, cloth to the tailor — feeds straight back into someone else's production process. Each of those is an intermediate good.

    2

    The very last sale — to the customer who won't transform it further — is what matters.

    3

    That's the whole definition of “final”: not what the object physically is, but whether it leaves the active economic flow for good.

    4

    Proof it's about use, not the object: the same tea leaves are a final good bought by a household, but an intermediate good bought by a restaurant that brews and resells them.

    Start here — the textbook's own example

    NCERT traces one commodity through a whole chain to show where "final" begins: "a farmer producing cotton sells it to a spinning mill where the raw cotton undergoes transformation to yarn; the yarn is, in turn, sold to a textile mill where... it is transformed into cloth; the cloth is, in turn, transformed... into an article of clothing which is then ready to be sold finally to the consumers for final use."

    Traced directly from the chapter's cotton example
    CottonGrown by farmer
    YarnSpinning mill
    ClothTextile mill
    Article of clothingTailoring/garment unit
    Sold to consumerFinal use — leaves the flow
    Every sale up to the last step = intermediate good Sale to the final consumer = final good

    Now the definitions

    NCERT Definition Ch. 2, §2.1

    "Such an item that is meant for final use and will not pass through any more stages of production or transformations is called a final good."

    NCERT Definition Ch. 2, §2.1

    "Such goods may be used by other producers as material inputs... These are intermediate goods, mostly used as raw material or inputs for production of other commodities. These are not final goods."

    Characteristics, side by side

    BasisFinal GoodIntermediate Good
    Meaning (NCERT)meant for final use; will not pass through any more stages of production/transformationused as material input for producing another good
    Stage in productionleaves the active economic flow once soldstays inside the production process; gets transformed further
    Counted in GDP?YesNo — excluded to avoid double counting
    Decided byeconomic use, not physical natureeconomic use, not physical nature
    Textbook exampletea leaves bought & brewed by a householdtea leaves bought by a restaurant to brew and resell

    The litmus test — how to classify any good

    1Ask the transformation question

    Will it be transformed again by a producer, or has it left the "active economic flow"? If it leaves the flow, it's final.

    2Judge by use, not by nature

    It is not the physical nature of the good that decides this — it is the economic use to which it is put.

    3Ignore what the final buyer does with it

    Transformation by the ultimate purchaser (e.g. cooking at home) does not count — "cooking at home is not an economic activity."

    4Same object, different fate

    The same physical good can switch categories depending on who buys it and why.

    NCERT's own proof — tea leaves

    "The tea leaves purchased by the consumer are not consumed in that form — they are used to make drinkable tea... cooking at home is not an economic activity, even though the product involved undergoes transformation. Home cooked food is not sold to the market. However, if the same cooking or tea brewing was done in a restaurant where the cooked product would be sold to customers, then the same items, such as tea leaves, would cease to be final goods and would be counted as inputs to which economic value addition can take place."

    Memory Trick

    If it leaves the shop for good (into a household's hands, never to be resold or reworked by a producer) — it's a FINAL good. If it walks back into somebody else's factory to get transformed again — it's INTERMEDIATE. Same physical item, different fate.

    Why does this distinction matter?

    Money is our common measuring rod — we can't add metres of cloth to tonnes of rice — so we sum the monetary value of final goods only. The value of intermediate goods is already embedded inside the value of the final good; counting both separately causes double counting and inflates the true value of output.

    Try it yourself — classify each item

    Tap Final Good or Intermediate Good for each item below, then check the reasoning.

    Tea leaves bought by a household to brew at home

    Bought by the household for direct use, never resold or reworked — a final good.

    Tea leaves bought by a restaurant to brew and sell to customers

    The restaurant transforms and resells it — value is added and it's sold on, so it's an intermediate good.

    Raw cotton bought by a spinning mill to make yarn

    Gets transformed into yarn and resold — stays inside the production process. Intermediate good.

    A finished shirt bought by a customer from a shop

    Bought for personal use — leaves the active economic flow. Final good.

    Steel sheets bought by a car manufacturer to build cars

    Transformed into cars and resold — a raw material input. Intermediate good.

    A new car bought by a household for personal use

    Bought by a household for its own use, not for resale. Final good (specifically a consumer durable — see the next topic).

    Sugar bought by a bakery to bake cakes for sale

    Used up in producing cakes that are then sold — an input, not a final good. Intermediate good.

    A packet of biscuits bought by a household from a store

    Bought for direct consumption by the household. Final good.

    Why CUET asks this —It's the cheapest possible MCQ to write: give a real-world item, ask which bucket it falls in. Expect it as classification, assertion-reason, or a "restaurant vs household" case study.

    Types of final goods

    Final goods themselves split further, based on who uses them and how long they last.

    NCERT Definition — Consumption Goods §2.1

    "Goods like food and clothing, and services like recreation that are consumed when purchased by their ultimate consumers are called consumption goods or consumer goods."

    NCERT Definition — Capital Goods §2.1

    Durable goods "used in the production process... they themselves don't get transformed in the production process... they are the crucial backbone of any production process" — these are capital goods.

    NCERT Definition — Consumer Durables §2.1

    "Some commodities like television sets, automobiles or home computers, although they are for ultimate consumption, have one characteristic in common with capital goods — they are also durable... That is why we call these goods consumer durables."
    FactorConsumption GoodsCapital GoodsConsumer Durables
    Who uses itHouseholdsBusiness/producing enterprisesHouseholds
    PurposeSatisfies wants directlyEnables further productionSatisfies wants, over a long life
    DurabilityMostly used up quicklyDurable — needs repair/replacementDurable — needs repair/replacement
    NCERT examplesfood, clothing, recreation servicestools, implements, machinestelevision sets, automobiles, home computers

    All three are final goods. Anything used up as raw material by other producers instead is an intermediate good (e.g. steel sheets for automobiles, copper for utensils).

    Memory Trick

    Ask WHO buys it. A FIRM buying a durable item to help it produce → capital good. A HOUSEHOLD buying the exact same kind of item (say, a computer or vehicle) for personal use → consumer durable. Same object, different buyer, different label.

    Quick classification checklist

    • Bought by a household, used up quickly? → Consumption good.
    • Bought by a household, but lasts for years and needs repair? → Consumer durable.
    • Bought by a firm to help it produce, without being transformed itself? → Capital good.
    • Bought by a firm and gets used up / transformed into another good? → Intermediate good.
    Warning —Students frequently confuse a capital good with a consumer durable when the object itself is identical (e.g. a laptop, a vehicle). The buyer, not the object, decides the label.
    NCERT — Final Goods vs Intermediate Goods, p. 10Open in new tab

    02Stocks and Flows

    "The average salary is ₹10,000" is meaningless without a time frame — per day? per month? per year? That's the stock–flow distinction.

    Common as an assertion / true-false pair

    Try this first

    Water flows into a tank from a tap. Is the amount flowing in per minute the same kind of measurement as the amount of water sitting in the tank right now?

    1

    The amount flowing in per minute only makes sense with a time period attached to it — that's a flow.

    2

    How much water is in the tank at a given moment doesn't need a time period at all — that's a stock.

    3

    A stock can change over a period, and that change is itself a flow — e.g. a change in inventories, or net investment.

    4

    Same logic, different variables: income is a flow, wealth is a stock; new machines added this year is a flow, total capital stock is a stock.

    NCERT Definition §2.1

    "Flows are defined over a period of time."  ·  "Stocks are defined at a particular point of time."
    NCERT's own tap-and-tank illustration
    Flow "The amount of water which is flowing into the tank from the tap per minute is a flow."
    Stock "How much water there is in the tank at a particular point of time is a stock concept."

    Memory Trick

    STOCK = a photograph (frozen at one moment — "as on 31 March"). FLOW = a video (only makes sense over a stretch of time — "during the year"). If the number needs a time period attached to mean anything, it's a flow.

    BasisStockFlow
    DefinedAt a particular point in timeOver a period of time
    NCERT examplescapital, wealth, inventory, water level in the tankincome, output, profit, investment, water entering the tank per minute
    RelationA stock can change over a period — that change itself is a flow (e.g. change in inventories, net investment)

    A machine's double life

    "A particular machine can be part of the capital stock for many years... but that machine can be part of the flow of new machines added to the capital stock only for a single year when it was initially installed."

    CUET Insight —Typical MCQ shape: a short pair of statements ("Statement 1... Statement 2...") testing whether you can tell a stock from a flow without hesitation. Quick trick: ask "does this number need a time period to make sense?" — if yes, it's a flow.
    NCERT — Stocks and Flows, p. 12Open in new tab

    03Investment & Depreciation

    Gross investment isn't one thing — it's three different kinds of spending on capital, netted against the wear-and-tear that eats into it every year.

    Know the three types of investment, not just the depreciation formula

    Try this first

    A pair of shoes wears out gradually over two years of normal use. A factory burns down overnight in an earthquake. Are both examples of depreciation?

    1

    The shoes' wear-and-tear is planned, expected, and spread evenly over their useful life — that is depreciation.

    2

    The earthquake is sudden and unplanned — that's a capital loss, not depreciation.

    3
