    Depreciation = cost of the good ÷ number of years of its useful life — an accounting concept, not necessarily real spending every single year.

    4

    Net Investment = Gross Investment − Depreciation.

    NCERT Definition — Gross Investment §2.1

    "That part of our final output that comprises of capital goods constitutes gross investment of an economy."

    NCERT Definition — Depreciation §2.1

    "This deletion, which is made from the value of gross investment in order to accommodate regular wear and tear of capital, is called depreciation."

    Core Identity

    Net Investment = Gross Investment − Depreciation

    Three types of investment that make up Gross Investment

    TypeWhat it covers
    Fixed Business InvestmentSpending by firms on new machinery, plant, equipment, and tools used in production.
    Residential InvestmentSpending on constructing new housing — by households and firms alike.
    Inventory InvestmentThe change in a firm's stock of unsold finished goods, semi-finished goods, or raw materials — can be positive (accumulation) or negative (decumulation).

    These three add up to an economy's Gross Investment — the capital-goods portion of final output. Inventory investment is covered in more depth in the Product Method topic, since NCERT introduces it alongside the value-added calculation.

    Memory Trick

    Depreciation is only planned, expected wear-and-tear (like shoes wearing out over two years of normal use). An earthquake destroying the factory overnight is NOT depreciation — that's an unplanned capital loss. CUET loves testing this exact distinction.

    Characteristics of depreciation, per NCERT

    • It is an accounting concept — "no real expenditure may have actually been incurred each year yet depreciation is annually accounted for."
    • It assumes a fixed expected life for the capital good (e.g. 20 years), and spreads the cost evenly.
    • It does not account for sudden, unexpected destruction — accidents or natural calamities are excluded.
    • Depreciation = cost of the good ÷ number of years of its useful life.

    Careful — economist's "investment" ≠ everyday "investment"

    "This must not be confused with the commonplace notion of investment which implies using money to buy physical or financial assets... Investment for us is always capital formation, a gross or net addition to capital stock."

    The consumption–investment trade-off

    At a given level of total output, producing more capital goods means producing fewer consumer goods right now. But more capital goods raise future productivity, so future total output — and future consumption — can rise. It is a trade-off across time, not a contradiction.

    Ranker's Tip —Typical MCQ shape: "which of these is NOT depreciation", a one-liner asking you to compute Net Investment, or "identify the type of investment" for a given spending example. Quick trick: if the loss was sudden/unplanned (accident, disaster), it's never depreciation.
    NCERT — Investment & Depreciation, p. 13Open in new tab

    04Circular Flow of Income

    In the simplest possible economy — no government, no savings, no foreign trade — income just goes round and round between two sectors.

    "Which point (A/B/C) matches which method?" is a classic diagram question

    Try this first

    In a simple two-sector economy (just households and firms, no government, no savings), can you measure the whole economy's income by looking at spending — or do you have to look at factor payments instead?

    1

    At Point A, households' spending flows to firms — this is the Expenditure Method.

    2

    At Point B, firms' goods and services flow back to households as the value of what's produced — this is the Product Method.

    3

    At Point C, firms pay wages, interest, profit and rent to households for their factor services — this is the Income Method.

    4

    Since it's the same rupee travelling around the same circle, all three points must give exactly the same number.

    "The households receive their payments from the firms for productive activities they perform for the latter... In this simplified economy, there is only one way in which the households may dispose off their earnings — by spending their entire income on the goods and services produced by the domestic firms."

    Factor of ProductionRemuneration
    LabourWage
    CapitalInterest
    EntrepreneurshipProfit
    Land (fixed natural resources)Rent
    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 2.1 — same boxes, same four flows, same points A/B/C, redrawn as a real loop
    Green arrows — money/services flowing from households to firms Navy arrows — money/goods flowing from firms to households A, B, C — where each flow's annual value is measured

    Fig. 2.1 — Circular Flow of Income in a Simple Economy (NCERT). The dashed track is the loop the same rupee travels around every cycle.

    Because the same value moves in a circle, we can measure the economy's aggregate income at any of the three marked points — and all three must give the same number:

    Point A

    Expenditure Method
    aggregate spending firms receive

    =

    Point B

    Product Method
    aggregate value of final goods produced

    =

    Point C

    Income Method
    sum total of factor payments

    Memory Trick

    A-B-C = Amount spent (Expenditure) → goods flow Back to households (Product) → Cash paid to factors (Income). Same rupee, travelling in a circle, measured three times.

    A useful (if paradoxical-sounding) result

    If households spend more than their current income (by borrowing), firms produce more and pay out more in factor income. "Their income will rise exactly by the amount which is necessary to carry out the extra spending." In a circular flow, a rise at one point must eventually raise every point.

    Why CUET asks this —The A/B/C diagram is the cleanest possible "point identification" question — examiners just point at an arrow and ask which method matches. Quick trick: A = spending, B = goods produced, C = factor payments.
    NCERT — Circular Flow of Income, p. 14Open in new tab

    05The Product (Value Added) Method

    The first of three ways to measure GDP — count what every firm actually adds to the economy, not what it merely produces.

    Numerical MCQs on this method appear almost every year

    Try this first

    Farmers produce ₹100 of wheat (using no inputs), sell ₹50 of it to bakers, who use it to produce ₹200 of bread. Is the economy's total output ₹300 (100 + 200)?

    1

    No — simply adding 100 + 200 counts the ₹50 of wheat twice, once on its own and once again inside the bread. That mistake is double counting.

    2

    Each firm's value added = its output − intermediate goods bought: farmer = 100 − 0 = 100; baker = 200 − 50 = 150.

    3

    Aggregate value added = 100 + 150 = ₹250, not ₹300 — this is the Product Method.

    4

    The other two methods (Expenditure and Income, covered next) would both also land on ₹250 — same rupee, three vantage points on the same circular flow.

    The master identity — hold this in your head throughout

    GDP ≡ Σ GVAi  (Point B)  ≡  C + I + G + X − M  (Point A)  ≡  W + P + In + R  (Point C)

    Memory Trick

    The PEI wheel: Product (what firms MAKE) = Expenditure (what buyers SPEND) = Income (what factors EARN). Three different questions about the exact same rupee.

    Measured at Point B. Suppose farmers produce ₹100 worth of wheat (no inputs needed). They sell ₹50 worth to bakers, who use it to produce ₹200 worth of bread.

    The naive (wrong) approach

    Simply adding ₹200 + ₹100 = ₹300. Wrong — the ₹50 of wheat gets counted twice. This mistake is double counting.

    NCERT Definition — Value Added §2.2.1

    "The term that is used to denote the net contribution made by a firm is called its value added... value added of a firm is, value of production of the firm – value of intermediate goods used by the firm."
    FarmerBaker
    Total production100200
    Intermediate goods used050
    Value added100150

    Aggregate value added = ₹100 + ₹150 = ₹250 — not ₹300. This exact farmer–baker set-up is one of the most recycled numerical questions on this chapter — always subtract intermediate goods once.

    Gross vs Net Value Added

    Net Value Added = Gross Value Added − Depreciation

    Example: Output ₹100, intermediate goods ₹20, depreciation ₹10 → GVA = 100−20 = ₹80 · NVA = 100−20−10 = ₹70

    Inventories — the wrinkle every firm has

    NCERT Definition — Inventory §2.2.1

    "The stock of unsold finished goods, or semi-finished goods, or raw materials which a firm carries from one year to the next is called inventory. Inventory is a stock variable."

    Key identity

    Change in Inventories ≡ Production during the year − Sale during the year

    Change in inventories is a form of investment, alongside fixed business investment and residential investment.

    NCERT's shirt-factory example — planned vs unplanned

    A firm starts the year with 100 shirts in stock, expects to sell 1,000, and produces 1,000.

    • Sales turn out to be only 600 → 400 shirts pile up unexpectedly → unplanned accumulation.
    • Sales turn out to be 1,050 → firm dips into stock too → unplanned decumulation.
    • Firm deliberately raises stock 100→200 by producing 1,100 → planned accumulation.
    • Firm deliberately cuts stock 100→25 by producing only 925 → planned decumulation.

    Memory Trick

    Sales below plan → stock piles up you didn't want → accumulation. Sales above plan → stock drains faster than you wanted → decumulation. If it was the firm's own decision, it's planned; if sales surprised them, it's unplanned.

    Full identity with inventories

    GVAi ≡ Sales (Vi) + Change in Inventories (Ai) − Intermediate Goods Used (Zi)
    GDP ≡ Σ GVAi

    Worked example — Firms A & B

    Firm A grows cotton (no raw materials) and sells it to Firm B for ₹50. Firm B turns it into cloth and sells it to consumers for ₹200.

    Firm AFirm B
    Sales50200
    Intermediate consumption050
    Value added50150

    GDP = 50 + 150 = ₹200

    Why CUET asks this —This is the most numerically-tested of the three methods — expect a farmer-baker-style chain, a GVA calculation, or an inventory accumulation/decumulation identification question.
    NCERT — The Product (Value Added) Method, p. 17Open in new tab

    06The Expenditure Method

    The second way to measure GDP — from the buyer's side: what does everyone actually spend on final goods and services?

    Don't forget the −M — a classic one-mark trap

    Try this first

    GDP ≡ C + I + G + X − M. If a student writes GDP = C + I + G + X and stops there, what have they gotten wrong?

    1

    C+I+G+X counts all spending by households, firms, government, and foreigners — on both domestic AND foreign goods.

    2

    But GDP should only count spending on goods actually produced within the domestic economy.

    3

    Imports (M) are spending that leaked abroad — on goods produced by someone else's economy — so they must be subtracted back out.

    4

    Forgetting −M is the single most common trap when writing this formula from memory.

    The master identity — hold this in your head throughout

    GDP ≡ Σ GVAi  (Point B)  ≡  C + I + G + X − M  (Point A)  ≡  W + P + In + R  (Point C)

    Memory Trick

    The PEI wheel: Product (what firms MAKE) = Expenditure (what buyers SPEND) = Income (what factors EARN). Three different questions about the exact same rupee.

    Measured at Point A. Same value as the product method, viewed from the demand side.

    SymbolComponentNCERT description
    CConsumptionfinal consumption expenditure on goods & services
    IInvestmentfinal investment expenditure on capital goods
    GGovernmentincludes both consumption and investment
    XExportsexport revenues earned abroad
    MImportsdeducted — not spent on domestic firms

    The Expenditure Method Formula

    GDP ≡ C + I + G + X − M

    Of these five, investment expenditure (I) is the most unstable — NCERT flags this explicitly, and CUET loves to test it.

    Memory Trick

    Don't forget the −M! A very common trap is to write GDP = C+I+G+X and stop there. Imports must always be subtracted — that money left the domestic economy.

    Worked example — Firms A & B

    Firm A sells cotton to Firm B for ₹50; Firm B turns it into cloth and sells it to consumers for ₹200. Final expenditure = spending by consumers on cloth only (the ₹50 cotton sale was intermediate, not final, spending).

    GDP = ₹200 — exactly matching the Product Method's answer for the same economy.

    Warning —Only count expenditure on final goods and services — spending between firms on intermediate goods is already embedded inside the final good's price and must not be counted again.
    NCERT — The Expenditure Method, p. 21Open in new tab

    07The Income Method

    The third way to measure GDP — add up every rupee actually paid out to the four factors of production.

    Ties the whole "three methods" idea together

    Try this first

    Firm A pays ₹20 in wages and keeps ₹30 profit. Firm B pays ₹60 in wages and keeps ₹90 profit. Does adding up everyone's income also land on ₹200 — the same answer as the Product and Expenditure methods?

    1

    Firm A's total factor payments: ₹20 wages + ₹30 profit = ₹50.

    2

    Firm B's total factor payments: ₹60 wages + ₹90 profit = ₹150.

    3

    Total = 50 + 150 = ₹200 — exactly matching the Product Method's ₹200 and the Expenditure Method's ₹200.

    4

    That's the entire point of "three vantage points on one circular flow" — measure from whichever side you like, GDP comes out the same.

    The master identity — hold this in your head throughout

    GDP ≡ Σ GVAi  (Point B)  ≡  C + I + G + X − M  (Point A)  ≡  W + P + In + R  (Point C)

    Memory Trick

    The PEI wheel: Product (what firms MAKE) = Expenditure (what buyers SPEND) = Income (what factors EARN). Three different questions about the exact same rupee.

    Measured at Point C. Same value again, viewed as payments to the four factors of production.

    The Income Method Formula

    GDP ≡ W + P + In + R

    W = Wages & salaries · P = Profits · In = Interest · R = Rent

    Comparing all three methods, side by side

    MethodWhat is summedPointFormula
    ProductGross value added of every firmBGDP ≡ ΣGVAi
    ExpenditureFinal spending received by firmsAGDP ≡ C+I+G+X−M
    IncomeFactor payments to householdsCGDP ≡ W+P+In+R

    Worked example — Firms A & B

    Firm A pays ₹20 wages, keeps ₹30 profit. Firm B pays ₹60 wages, keeps ₹90 profit.

    Firm AFirm B
    Wages2060
    Profits3090

    GDP = 80 + 120 = ₹200 — all three methods agree.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a direct factor-income calculation, a "which method sums factor payments" definition question, or a comparison question testing whether you can match Product/Expenditure/Income to what each one actually adds up.
    NCERT — The Income Method, p. 24Open in new tab

    08Factor Cost, Basic Prices & Market Prices

    Three ways of pricing the same output, depending on whether taxes/subsidies are folded in.

    Try this first

    A producer receives ₹1,000 for their output — with no tax included. The government then adds ₹100 in production taxes, then ₹150 in product taxes before it reaches the shop shelf. What does the final consumer actually pay?

    1

    Factor Cost (₹1,000) is what the producer actually pockets — no tax at all.

    2

    Add net production taxes (₹100) → Basic Price = ₹1,100.

    3

    Add net product taxes (₹150) on top of that → Market Price = ₹1,250 — what the consumer actually pays.

    4

    Price only ever grows as you move Factor Cost → Basic Price → Market Price, since each step just adds a tax the previous one didn't include.

    NCERT Definition §2.2.4

    "Factor cost includes only the payment to factors of production, it does not include any tax. In order to arrive at market prices, we have to add to the factor cost the total indirect taxes less total subsidies. The basic prices lie in between: they include the production taxes (less production subsidies) but not product taxes (less product subsidies)."
    A worked example — same output, three different price tags

    Factor Cost

    ₹1,000

    what the producer actually receives — no tax at all

    + ₹100
    Net Production Taxes

    Basic Price

    ₹1,100

    factor cost + production taxes, less production subsidies

    + ₹150
    Net Product Taxes

    Market Price

    ₹1,250

    what the final consumer actually pays

    Same ₹1,000 of factor payments, taxed twice on its way to the shop shelf — each step only ever adds a tax the previous one didn't include. (Numbers are illustrative.)

    BasisFactor CostBasic PricesMarket Prices
    IncludesOnly payments to factorsFactor cost + net production taxesBasic prices + net product taxes
    Example taxesNoneLand revenue, stamp & registration feeExcise, service tax, export/import duties

    Memory Trick

    FC → BP → MP: the price grows as you add taxes, like a restaurant bill growing as GST is added on top. Factor Cost is the "base price" the producer actually pockets.

    Building up from Factor Cost to Market Price

    GVA at Factor Cost + Net Production Taxes = GVA at Basic Prices
    GVA at Basic Prices + Net Product Taxes = GVA at Market Prices

    CUET note

    Since 2015, India's CSO reports GVA at basic prices and GDP at market prices — the older "GDP at factor cost" headline measure was replaced.

    CUET Insight —Typical MCQ shape: "arrange Factor Cost, Basic Price, Market Price in ascending order" or a fill-in-the-blank on which taxes belong where. Quick trick: FC → BP → MP, price only ever grows as you move right.
    NCERT — Factor Cost, Basic Prices & Market Prices, p. 24Open in new tab

    09From GDP to Personal Disposable Income

    GDP belongs to whoever produces inside our borders — even a foreign-owned factory. NCERT's Fig. 2.3 traces the same total value down through every sub-category.

    The single most-tested numeric chain in this chapter

    Try this first

    GDP at Market Price = ₹2,000 crore, Net Factor Income from Abroad = −₹40 crore, Depreciation = ₹150 crore, Net Indirect Taxes = ₹210 crore. What is the country's National Income?

    1

    GNPₘₚ = GDPₘₚ + NFIA = 2,000 + (−40) = 1,960.

    2

    NNPₘₚ = GNPₘₚ − Depreciation = 1,960 − 150 = 1,810.

    3

    National Income = NNP_FC = NNPₘₚ − Net Indirect Taxes = 1,810 − 210 = ₹1,600 crore.

    4

    Notice the pattern: only the very first step (GDP→GNP) adds something (NFIA) — every step after that only ever subtracts.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 2.3, redrawn left-to-right
    GDPat Market Price
    + NFIA
    GNPat Market Price
    − Depreciation (D)
    NNPat Market Price
    − (ID − Sub)
    NNP at Factor Cost= National Income (NI)
    − UP − NIH
    − CT + TrH
    Personal Income(PI)
    − PTP − NP
    Personal Disposable Income(PDI)

    Fig. 2.3 — subcategories of aggregate income (NCERT). NFIA: Net Factor Income from Abroad · D: Depreciation · ID: Indirect Taxes · Sub: Subsidies · UP: Undistributed Profits · NIH: Net Interest Payments by Households · CT: Corporate Taxes · TrH: Transfers to Households · PTP: Personal Tax Payments · NP: Non-Tax Payments.

    Memory Trick

    Only the very first step ADDS something (NFIA, to go GDP→GNP). Every step after that subtracts — except transfer payments sneak back in at the PI step (households receive pensions/scholarships they didn't "earn"). If you remember "one add, then a run of subtracts (with one sneaky add-back)", you can rebuild the whole ladder.

    NCERT Definitions — the aggregates, verbatim §2.3

    "GNP ≡ GDP + Net factor income from abroad."

    "NNP ≡ GNP − Depreciation."

    "NNP at factor cost ≡ National Income (NI) ≡ NNP at market prices − Net indirect taxes."

    "Personal Income (PI) ≡ NI − Undistributed profits − Net interest payments made by households − Corporate tax + Transfer payments to the households from the government and firms."

    "Personal Disposable Income (PDI) ≡ PI − Personal tax payments − Non-tax payments."

    Why each adjustment happens

    • NFIA: an Indian working abroad earns wages counted in that country's GDP, not India's — add income Indians earn abroad, subtract income foreigners earn here.
    • Depreciation: wear-and-tear doesn't become anyone's income.
    • Net Indirect Taxes: market price includes taxes that go to government, not to factors — remove them to find factor cost = National Income.
    • Undistributed Profits & Corporate Tax: retained by firms/government, never reaches households.
    • Transfer Payments (pensions, scholarships, prizes): households receive these without producing anything — add them in.
    • Personal & Non-Tax Payments: must be paid away before the money is truly "disposable."
    NCERT — From GDP to Personal Disposable Income, p. 25Open in new tab

    Try this first

    NNP at Market Price tells us what a country produced. Does that automatically tell us the maximum the country can actually spend and save?

    1

    Not quite — the country may also receive transfers from abroad (foreign aid, remittances given as gifts) that add to what it can spend, without being production at all.

    2

    National Disposable Income = NNP at Market Price + Other current transfers from the rest of the world.

    3

    Private Income takes a different slice again — factor income accruing to the private sector, plus national debt interest, NFIA, and government/foreign transfers.

    4

    Think of NDI as the whole-country version of what Personal Disposable Income is for a single household.

    10National Disposable Income & Private Income

    National Disposable Income

    NDI = NNP at Market Price + Other current transfers from the rest of the world

    Tells us the maximum a country's households, firms and government can spend on final consumption and savings.

    Private Income

    Private Income = Factor income from NDP accruing to the private sector + National debt interest + NFIA + Current transfers from government + Other net transfers from abroad

    Memory Trick

    NDI = what the whole COUNTRY can spend + save. PDI = what ONE HOUSEHOLD can spend + save. Same idea, different scale — don't mix them up on an MCQ.

    Warning —This is one of the lower-yield sub-topics in the chapter — worth knowing the formula shape, but don't over-invest revision time here relative to the ladder above.
    NCERT — National Disposable Income & Private Income, p. 26Open in new tab

    11Nominal vs Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI & WPI

    If GDP doubles, did the economy actually produce twice as much — or did prices just double?

    Deflator numericals are almost guaranteed every year

    Try this first

    In 2000, an economy produced 100 units of bread at ₹10 each. In 2001, it produced 110 units at ₹15 each. Did the economy actually produce more — or did prices just rise?

    1

    Nominal GDP (2001) = 110 × ₹15 = ₹1,650 — measured at current prices.

    2

    Real GDP (2001) = 110 × ₹10 (2000's price) = ₹1,100 — measured at constant, base-year prices.

    3

    GDP Deflator = (Nominal ÷ Real) × 100 = (1,650 ÷ 1,100) × 100 = 150%.

    4

    Since both figures use the exact same physical output (110 units), the entire ₹550 gap between them is a pure price effect.

    NCERT Definition §2.4

    "Real GDP is calculated in a way such that the goods and services are evaluated at some constant set of prices (or constant prices)... Nominal GDP... is simply the value of GDP at the current prevailing prices."

    NCERT's bread economy

    2000 (base year): 100 units of bread @ ₹10 → Nominal GDP = ₹1,000.
    2001: 110 units @ ₹15 → Nominal GDP = 110×15 = ₹1,650.
    Real GDP (2001 output at 2000 prices) = 110×10 = ₹1,100.

    GDP Deflator

    GDP Deflator = Nominal GDP ⁄ Real GDP  (×100 for percentage)

    1,650 ⁄ 1,100 = 1.50 → 150%. Since both use the same physical output, any difference is purely a price effect.

    Memory Trick

    Nominal = today's price tag. Real = yesterday's (base-year) price tag on today's basket. If only the price tag changed and not the actual goods produced, real GDP stays put even while nominal GDP climbs.

    CPI & WPI — other ways to track prices

    Besides the GDP Deflator, two more price indices track how prices move over time.

    NCERT Definition — CPI §2.4

    "The Consumer Price Index (CPI)... is the index of prices of a given basket of commodities which are bought by the representative consumer."

    NCERT's rice & cloth basket

    Basket: 90 kg rice + 5 pieces of cloth.
    2000: rice ₹10/kg, cloth ₹100/piece → 900+500 = ₹1,400
    2005: rice ₹15/kg, cloth ₹120/piece → 1,350+600 = ₹1,950
    CPI = (1,950 ⁄ 1,400) × 100 ≈ 139.29

    NCERT Definition — WPI §2.4

    "Like CPI, the index for wholesale prices is called Wholesale Price Index (WPI)." In the USA it is called the Producer Price Index (PPI).

    Memory Trick

    CPI packs the same suitcase every year (fixed basket — you never change what you're buying). The GDP Deflator's "basket" changes with whatever the economy actually produced that year. That single difference explains almost every CPI-vs-Deflator MCQ.

    FactorCPIGDP Deflator
    CoverageOnly goods bought by the representative consumerAll goods and services produced domestically
    Imported goodsIncludedExcluded
    WeightsFixed — same basket every yearVary with each year's actual production mix
    NCERT — Nominal vs Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI & WPI, p. 29Open in new tab

    12Is GDP a Good Measure of Welfare?

    Higher income should mean more goods, more well-being — right? NCERT gives three reasons this may not be correct.

    Case-based / scenario MCQs love this section

    Try this first

    An economy has 100 people each earning ₹10 (GDP = ₹1,000). Next year, 90 people earn ₹9 and 10 people earn ₹20 (GDP = ₹1,010). GDP went up — did welfare go up too?

    1

    GDP did rise, by ₹10.

    2

    But 90% of people actually got poorer (₹10 → ₹9) — only 10% gained, and they gained a lot.

    3

    Aggregate GDP hides this entirely — it says nothing about how the gains were distributed.

    4

    This is one of three reasons GDP can mislead welfare, remembered as D-N-E: Distribution, Non-monetary exchanges (unpaid work, barter — invisible to GDP), and Externalities (uncounted harms or benefits to third parties).

    NCERT Definition — Externalities §2.5

    "Externalities refer to the benefits (or harms) a firm or an individual causes to another for which they are not paid (or penalised)."

    Memory Trick — the DNE test

    Three reasons GDP misleads welfare, remembered as D-N-E: Distribution (who actually got the gains?), Non-monetary exchange (barter/unpaid work — invisible to GDP), Externalities (uncounted harms or benefits to third parties).

    D

    Distribution

    NCERT's example: 100 people earning ₹10 each (GDP=1,000) becomes 90 people earning ₹9 and 10 people earning ₹20 (GDP=1,010) — GDP rose, yet 90% of people got poorer.

    N

    Non-Monetary Exchanges

    Unpaid domestic work and barter exchanges never enter GDP since no money changes hands — GDP underestimates true welfare.

    E

    Externalities

    A refinery polluting a river harms fishermen — a negative externality GDP ignores, so GDP overestimates welfare. Positive externalities cause the reverse.

    ReasonEffect on GDP vs. true welfare
    Unequal distributionMisleading — aggregate GDP can rise while most people are worse off
    Non-monetary/barter exchangesGDP underestimates welfare
    Negative externalitiesGDP overestimates welfare
    Positive externalitiesGDP underestimates welfare
    NCERT — Is GDP a Good Measure of Welfare?, p. 31Open in new tab

    01Ex Ante vs Ex Post — Planned vs Actual Values

    Before we can determine income, we need to separate what people planned to do from what actually happened once the year played out.

    The foundational distinction this whole chapter is built on

    Try this first

    A producer plans to add ₹100 worth of goods to her inventory this year. An unexpected demand surge forces her to sell an extra ₹30 from stock. What was her actual investment?

    1

    ₹100 was the planned figure — decided before the year played out. That planned value is called ex ante.

    2

    The unexpected ₹30 sale from stock was never part of the plan — it happened because reality didn't match expectations.

    3

    Actual investment = 100 − 30 = ₹70. This realised figure is called ex post.

    4

    Ex ante and ex post only turn out equal when the economy is exactly in equilibrium — any gap between them shows up as an unintended change in inventories.

    NCERT Definition §4.1

    "We call the planned values of the variables — consumption, investment or output of final goods — their ex ante measures... ex-post depicts what has actually happened."

    The key distinction, in one example

    A producer plans to add ₹100 worth of goods to her inventory (ex ante investment). An unforeseen demand surge forces her to sell an extra ₹30 from stock, so her inventory only rises by ₹70 — her actual (ex post) investment.

    BasisEx AnteEx Post
    MeaningPlanned / intended valueActual / realised value
    Equal to each other?Only when the economy is in equilibrium — otherwise the gap shows up as an unintended change in inventories

    Try it yourself — Ex Ante or Ex Post?

    A firm budgets to spend ₹50 lakh on a new machine next year

    A planned figure, before the year plays out — ex ante.

    The government's final report shows GDP grew 6.5% last year

    An actual, recorded outcome — ex post.

    A household intends to save ₹2,000 this month

    An intention, not yet realised — ex ante.

    Unsold stock actually piled up in a firm's warehouse by year-end

    What actually happened, recorded after the fact — ex post.

    Memory Trick

    "Ante" = before, "Post" = after. Ex ante is drawn up before the year happens (a plan); ex post is tallied after it happens (the record).

    NCERT — Ex Ante vs Ex Post — Planned vs Actual Values, p. 53Open in new tab

    02Consumption Function & MPC/MPS/APC/APS

    The single most important driver of consumption is household income — and NCERT gives us a straight-line equation to describe exactly how.

    Numerical favourite — MPC/MPS calculations every year

    Try this first

    Imagenia's consumption function is C = 100 + 0.8Y. If national income (Y) is ₹500, how much do people consume, and how much do they save?

    1

    Substitute directly: C = 100 + 0.8(500) = 100 + 400 = ₹500.

    2

    Since Y = C + S, savings S = Y − C = 500 − 500 = ₹0 at this exact income level.

    3

    The 100 is autonomous consumption (C̄) — spent even at zero income. The 0.8 is the MPC — 80% of every extra rupee of income gets spent.

    4

    MPC + MPS = 1 always, so MPS here = 1 − 0.8 = 0.2 — the other 20 paise of every extra rupee is saved.

    NCERT Definition §4.1.1

    "A consumption function describes the relation between consumption and income... C = C̄ + cY."

    Breaking the equation down, piece by piece

    C = C̄ + cY has exactly two components, and understanding each one separately is what makes every numerical in this topic straightforward.

    ComponentSymbolWhat it means
    Autonomous consumptionC̄the part of consumption that is independent of income — what households consume even at zero income, by running down savings or borrowing
    Induced consumptioncYthe part of consumption that depends on, and rises with, income — the product of MPC and income
    Marginal Propensity to Consumec (MPC)the fraction of every extra rupee of income that gets spent, not saved

    NCERT's own worked example — Imagenia

    C = 100 + 0.8Y

    Here, C̄ = 100: even with zero income, Imagenia's citizens still consume ₹100 worth of goods. MPC (c) = 0.8: for every extra ₹100 of income earned, ₹80 of it (the induced part, 0.8Y) gets spent, and the remaining ₹20 is saved.

    How C moves as Y moves

    Since C = C̄ + cY, plotting C against Y gives a straight line: C̄ is where the line starts (at Y=0), and c is how steeply it rises — for every 1-rupee rise in Y, C rises by exactly c rupees, no more and no less, since C̄ never changes.

    TermFormulaMeaning
    MPC (c)ΔC ÷ ΔYfraction of an extra rupee of income spent on consumption
    MPS (s)ΔS ÷ ΔY = 1 − cfraction of an extra rupee of income saved
    APCC ÷ Yaverage fraction of total income spent on consumption
    APSS ÷ Yaverage fraction of total income saved

    The MPC–MPS identity

    MPC + MPS = 1,  since S = Y − C

    MPC always lies between 0 and 1 (inclusive) — consumers either spend nothing extra (MPC=0), everything extra (MPC=1), or some fraction in between.

    Try it yourself — complete the consumption schedule

    Using C = 100 + 0.8Y, calculate consumption at each income level below. Enter your answer, then check.

    Y = ₹0 → C = ?

    C = 100 + 0.8(0) = ₹100 — pure autonomous consumption, since income is zero.

    Y = ₹200 → C = ?

    C = 100 + 0.8(200) = 100 + 160 = ₹260.

    Y = ₹500 → C = ?

    C = 100 + 0.8(500) = 100 + 400 = ₹500 — this is exactly where C = Y, i.e. savings is zero.

    Y = ₹1,000 → C = ?

    C = 100 + 0.8(1000) = 100 + 800 = ₹900. Savings here = 1000 − 900 = ₹100.

    Memory Trick

    MPC + MPS = 1, always. If a question gives you one, subtract from 1 to instantly get the other — don't recompute from scratch.

    CUET Insight —A very common numerical: given the consumption function C = C̄ + cY and a value of Y, calculate C, S, APC, or APS directly by substitution.
    NCERT — Consumption Function & MPC/MPS/APC/APS, p. 54Open in new tab

    03Investment Function

    Unlike consumption, this chapter's investment is deliberately kept simple: the same amount, year after year, regardless of income.

    A short but often-tested definition

    Try this first

    This model sets I = Ī = 10, regardless of the level of income Y. If Y rises from 200 to 500, does planned investment change?

    1

    No — I stays at 10 either way. Unlike consumption, investment in this simplified model has no income-dependent (induced) part at all.

    2

    That is exactly what "autonomous" means here: Ī is a fixed constant, not a function of Y.

    3

    NCERT is explicit that this is a simplification — real investment actually depends on the market rate of interest and credit availability, both held constant for this model.

    4

    Graphically, I = Ī is a flat horizontal line — the same height at every point on the Y-axis.

    NCERT Definition §4.1.2

    "Investment is defined as addition to the stock of physical capital... and changes in the inventory... 'investment goods' (such as machines) are also part of the final goods — they are not intermediate goods."

    The (simplified) investment function

    I = Ī

    Ī is a positive constant — autonomous investment — assumed the same regardless of the level of income, for simplicity in this model.

    In reality, investment does vary

    NCERT notes that real-world investment decisions depend on the market rate of interest (higher rates discourage investment) and the availability of credit (easier credit encourages it) — this model just holds those factors constant for simplicity.

    Memory Trick

    Machines aren't "used up" — they yield services over years, which is exactly why they count as final goods (capital goods), not intermediate goods, even though a firm buys them.

    Warning —Don't confuse "autonomous" with "unimportant" — Ī is autonomous only in the sense that it doesn't depend on income in this model; NCERT explicitly says it fluctuates for other reasons (interest rate, credit).
    NCERT — Investment Function, p. 56Open in new tab

    04Aggregate Demand & Equilibrium in a Two-Sector Economy

    Put consumption and investment together, and the condition for the whole economy to be at rest falls out almost immediately.

    The core equilibrium condition of the chapter

    Try this first

    With C = C̄ + cY and I = Ī, what condition must hold for the economy to be at rest (in equilibrium)?

    1

    Aggregate Demand is AD = C + I = C̄ + Ī + cY.

    2

    At equilibrium, output (Y) must exactly equal demand (AD) — nothing is unexpectedly piling up or running down in inventory.

    3

    So Y = C̄ + Ī + cY. Grouping the constants as A̅ = C̄ + Ī, this becomes Y = A̅ + cY — the master equilibrium condition of the chapter.

    4

    If AD falls short of planned output, unsold goods pile up (unintended accumulation); if AD exceeds output, stock is unexpectedly run down (unintended decumulation).

    Building the equilibrium condition

    AD = C + I = C̄ + Ī + cY
    At equilibrium: Y = AD  ⟹  Y = C̄ + Ī + cY = A̅ + cY

    where A̅ = C̄ + Ī is the total autonomous expenditure in the economy.

    A word of caution — don't confuse this with the Chapter 2 identity

    Y = A̅ + cY is an equilibrium condition for ex ante (planned) values — it holds only when the economy is at rest. The Chapter 2 accounting identity (output ≡ consumption + investment) always holds for ex post (actual) values, equilibrium or not.

    Adding the government (briefly)

    If a government is introduced, with autonomous Tax (T) and Government Expenditure (G), disposable income becomes Yd = Y − T, and the equilibrium condition becomes:

    Y = C̄ + Ī + G + c(Y − T)

    G − c.T simply adds to the autonomous term, just like C̄ or Ī — it doesn't change the model qualitatively. NCERT drops the government sector for the rest of the chapter for simplicity, and this portal follows the same convention.

    What happens when plans don't match?

    SituationWhat happens
    Ex ante AD < planned output YGoods pile up unsold — unintended accumulation of inventories
    Ex ante AD > planned output YStock runs down to meet demand — unintended decumulation of inventories
    Ex ante AD = planned output YThe final goods market is in equilibrium — no unintended inventory change

    Even so, ex post (actual) Y will always equal ex post (actual) C + I — the "extra" output shows up as unintended inventory change on the right-hand side of the accounting identity.

    Memory Trick

    Y = A̅ + cY — remember it as "output equals autonomous spending plus induced spending." Solve it by isolating Y: Y(1 − c) = A̅, so Y = A̅ ÷ (1 − c).

    CUET Insight —Expect a direct question asking you to write the equilibrium condition, or to identify whether a scenario describes accumulation or decumulation of inventories.
    NCERT — Aggregate Demand & Equilibrium in a Two-Sector Economy, p. 58Open in new tab

    05Graphical Determination of Equilibrium

    The same equilibrium condition, drawn as a picture — built up one curve at a time, exactly as NCERT presents it.

    The 45° line diagram is a CUET staple

    Try this first

    Given C = 40 + 0.8Y and I = 10, at what level of income Y is the economy in equilibrium?

    1

    Equilibrium condition: Y = A̅ + cY, where A̅ = C̄ + Ī = 40 + 10 = 50 and c = 0.8.

    2

    Rearranged: Y(1 − c) = A̅, so Y = A̅ ÷ (1 − c) = 50 ÷ 0.2 = 250.

    3

    Graphically, this is the single point where the upward-sloping AD line (slope c, intercept A̅) crosses the 45° aggregate-supply line — the line where every point has equal height and base.

    4

    The algebra and the diagram must always agree — Y* = 250 is exactly where the two lines meet.

    Aggregate Demand (AD) Graphs

    Aggregate Demand is built up in three steps: the consumption line on its own, the investment line on its own, and then the two added together.

    Step 1 — The Consumption function alone

    C = C̄ + cY is an upward-sloping straight line: it starts at C̄ on the vertical axis (consumption at zero income) and rises with slope c = MPC (shown as the angle α).

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 4.2

    Fig. 4.2 — the intercept C̄ is consumption at zero income; the slope, tan α, equals the MPC (c).

    Step 2 — The Investment function alone

    Since I = Ī is autonomous (constant), it is shown as a flat, horizontal line — the same height above the axis no matter what Y is.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 4.3

    Fig. 4.3 — a flat line at height Ī, since autonomous investment doesn't depend on the level of income.

    Step 3 — Combined: Aggregate Demand = C + I

    Adding the constant I to C at every level of Y produces a new line, parallel to the C line (same slope c) but shifted vertically upward by exactly Ī.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 4.4 — vertical summation of C and I

    Fig. 4.4 — OM = C̄, OJ = Ī, OL = C̄+Ī. The AD line is parallel to the C line, exactly Ī above it at every level of Y.

    Aggregate Supply (AS) Graph

    With price fixed and unused resources available, whatever firms produce, that much is supplied — shown by a 45° line from the origin, where every point has equal horizontal and vertical coordinates.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 4.5 — GDP of ₹1,000 mapped through the 45° line

    Fig. 4.5 — GDP of ₹1,000 at point A, read up to the 45° line at point B, then across: aggregate supply also equals ₹1,000.

    Equilibrium — Where AD Meets AS

    Putting the AD line and the 45° line on the same diagram, equilibrium is the single point where ex ante aggregate demand equals ex ante aggregate supply.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 4.6

    Fig. 4.6 — E is the only point where the AD line meets the 45° line; dropping straight down gives the equilibrium level of income, Y1. (With C = 40+0.8Y and I = 10, this Y1 works out to 250 — see the algebraic method below.)

    Algebraic confirmation

    Y = (C̄ + Ī) ÷ (1 − c) = (40 + 10) ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 50 ÷ 0.2 = 250

    Try it yourself — find the equilibrium

    Given C = 40 + 0.8Y and I = 10, here is the AD schedule (AD = 50 + 0.8Y) at a few income levels:

    Y200225250275300
    AD210230250270290

    At which level of income (Y) is the economy in equilibrium?

    Y = 250 — the only row where AD exactly equals Y. Below 250, AD > Y (unintended decumulation); above 250, AD < Y (unintended accumulation).

    Memory Trick

    The 45° line is just a ruler for aggregate supply — it does no economic work by itself, it just marks off "whatever is produced, is supplied." The real action is where the AD line crosses it.

    CUET Insight —You may be asked to identify the equilibrium point on a given diagram, or to explain in words why the intersection with the 45° line — not any other point on the AD line — represents equilibrium.
    NCERT — Graphical Determination of Equilibrium, p. 59Open in new tab

    06Effect of an Autonomous Change in Aggregate Demand

    Bump up autonomous spending even slightly, and equilibrium income rises by a lot more than the bump itself.

    Sets up the multiplier topic that follows

    Try this first

    Starting from C = 40 + 0.8Y and I = 10 (equilibrium Y* = 250), investment rises to 20. By how much does equilibrium income rise?

    1

    New A̅ = 40 + 20 = 60. New Y* = 60 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 60 ÷ 0.2 = 300.

    2

    Income rose by 300 − 250 = 50 — far more than the ₹10 rise in investment that caused it.

    3

    Graphically, a change in autonomous spending (C̄ or Ī) shifts the whole AD line parallel — same slope, new intercept.

    4

    Why the amplification? That's the multiplier effect — covered in full in the next topic.

    NCERT's own numeric example, continued

    Investment rises from 10 to 20

    With C = 40 + 0.8Y and I = 10, equilibrium income Y* = 250. If investment rises to 20 (a change of just ΔI = 10), the new equilibrium becomes:

    Y* = (40 + 20) ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 60 ÷ 0.2 = 300

    Income rose by 50, even though autonomous spending only rose by 10.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 4.7 — an autonomous change shifts AD in parallel

    A small parallel upward shift in the AD line (from a ₹10 rise in Ī) moves the equilibrium from E₁ to E₂ — income rises by ₹50, far more than the initial ₹10 injection.

    The algebraic method, in general

    Ex ante AD = C̄ + Ī + cY,  Ex ante AS = Y
    Equilibrium: Y = (C̄ + Ī) ÷ (1 − c)

    Memory Trick

    A change in autonomous spending (C̄ or Ī) shifts the AD line parallel — up or down, same slope. (Contrast this with a change in c, which swings the line — see Paradox of Thrift.)

    CUET Insight —Given C and I equations plus a change in one autonomous term, expect a "find the new equilibrium income" numerical almost every year.
    NCERT — Effect of an Autonomous Change in Aggregate Demand, p. 60Open in new tab

    07The Multiplier Mechanism

    Why did a ₹10 injection turn into a ₹50 rise in income? Because that ₹10 becomes someone's income, part of which gets spent again — round after round.

    The single most-tested numerical in this chapter

    Try this first

    Autonomous investment rises by ₹10 crore, and MPC = 0.8. Why does equilibrium income eventually rise by ₹50 crore, not just ₹10 crore?

    1

    Round 1: the ₹10 crore injection becomes ₹10 crore of extra income for whoever sold that output.

    2

    Round 2: that person spends 80% of it (MPC = 0.8) = ₹8 crore, which becomes someone else's income in turn.

    3

    This repeats endlessly, each round 0.8× the last (₹6.4cr, ₹5.12cr, ...) — an infinite geometric series summing to 10 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 50.

    4

    The multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − c) = 1 ÷ MPS packages this whole round-by-round process into one formula: k = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5, so ΔY = ΔI × k = 10 × 5 = 50.

    The mechanism, round by round

    Take NCERT's own example: autonomous investment rises by ₹10 crore, and MPC = 0.8.

    1Round 1 — the initial injection

    ₹10 crore of extra spending becomes ₹10 crore of extra income for whoever produced and sold that output. Income so far: +₹10 crore.

    2Round 2 — the first re-spend

    Whoever earned that ₹10 crore spends 80% of it (MPC = 0.8), i.e. ₹8 crore, on further consumption. That ₹8 crore becomes someone else's income in turn. Income so far: 10 + 8 = ₹18 crore.

    3Round 3 — the second re-spend

    That new recipient spends 80% of their ₹8 crore, i.e. ₹6.4 crore, which becomes further income downstream. Income so far: 10 + 8 + 6.4 = ₹24.4 crore.

    4Round 4 onward — the process continues, shrinking each time

    Each round is 0.8 times the previous one (₹5.12 crore, ₹4.10 crore, ...), so the additions get smaller and smaller, but never quite reach zero — the total is an infinite geometric series.

    RoundConsumptionAggregate DemandOutput / Income
    1010 (autonomous increment)10
    2(0.8)10(0.8)10(0.8)10 = 8
    3(0.8)²10(0.8)²10(0.8)²10 = 6.4
    …………

    Summing this infinite geometric series: 10 + (0.8)10 + (0.8)²10 + ... = 10 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 50 — exactly the total rise in income seen earlier.

    The Investment (Autonomous Expenditure) Multiplier

    k = ΔY ÷ ΔA = 1 ÷ (1 − c) = 1 ÷ MPS

    With MPC = 0.8, k = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. A ₹10 crore rise in autonomous spending produces a ₹50 crore rise in equilibrium income (10 × 5 = 50).

    Try it yourself — calculate the multiplier and the income change

    If MPC = 0.75, the investment multiplier (k) is:

    k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.75) = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.

    MPC = 0.6 and investment rises by ₹30 crore (ΔI = 30). The resulting change in equilibrium income (ΔY, ₹ crore) is:

    k = 1 ÷ (1−0.6) = 2.5. ΔY = ΔI × k = 30 × 2.5 = ₹75 crore.

    1Higher MPC → bigger multiplier

    As c gets larger (closer to 1), 1 − c gets smaller, so the multiplier k = 1/(1−c) gets larger — more of each round's income gets re-spent.

    2The multiplier applies to ANY autonomous change

    Whether the ₹10 increment comes from C̄ or Ī, the same multiplier formula applies — it multiplies the total change in autonomous expenditure, A̅.

    Memory Trick

    k = 1 ÷ MPS — the smaller the savings leakage each round, the bigger the multiplier. MPC=0.8 → MPS=0.2 → k=5. This is the same "infinite geometric series ÷ (1−r)" pattern as the money multiplier in the Money and Banking chapter.

    CUET Insight —Given MPC (or MPS) and a change in autonomous spending, compute the multiplier and the resulting change in equilibrium income — this pairing appears almost every year.
    NCERT — The Multiplier Mechanism, p. 62Open in new tab

    08Paradox of Thrift

    Saving is good advice for one person, but disastrous advice for an entire economy to follow all at once — this is the Paradox of Thrift.

    A favourite "explain why" conceptual question

    Try this first

    A̅ = 50 stays fixed, but people grow more cautious and MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.5. Does total savings in the economy rise, since everyone is trying to save more?

    1

    Old equilibrium: Y* = 50 ÷ (1−0.8) = 250. New equilibrium: Y* = 50 ÷ (1−0.5) = 100 — income falls sharply.

    2

    Checking savings in both cases (S = Y − C) works out to exactly ₹10 either way — unchanged, despite everyone saving a bigger share of income.

    3

    Why? Your spending is someone else's income. If everyone spends less, everyone's income falls too — and lower income drags total savings back down even as the savings rate rises.

    4

    What's sound advice for one household (save more) becomes self-defeating for the whole economy — a classic fallacy of composition.

    NCERT's Result

    "If all the people of the economy increase the proportion of income they save... the total value of savings in the economy will not increase — it will either decline or remain unchanged."

    Why individual thrift is virtuous, but collective thrift backfires

    At the level of one household

    If you save a larger share of your income, your own wealth grows — you spend less, but your income is unaffected, since it depends on everyone else's spending, not your own. Saving more is simply good, prudent advice.

    At the level of the whole economy

    Your spending is someone else's income. If everyone tries to save a larger share of income at the same time, everyone also spends less — which means everyone's income (which comes from everyone else's spending) falls too. Lower income then drags down the total amount saved, even though each person is saving a bigger fraction of a now-smaller income. What is rational for one person becomes self-defeating when the whole economy does it together — a classic fallacy of composition.

    NCERT's own worked example

    MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.5

    Starting equilibrium: A̅ = 50, c = 0.8 → Y* = 50 ÷ 0.2 = 250. People suddenly become more thrifty (perhaps fearing a downturn) and MPC falls to 0.5. New equilibrium: Y* = 50 ÷ 0.5 = 100. Income falls by 150.

    Yet savings in both cases work out to exactly ₹10: S* = Y* − C* = 250 − (40+0.8×250) = 10, and again 100 − (40+0.5×100) = 10. Trying to save a bigger share of income left total savings exactly where it started.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 4.8 — a change in MPC swings the AD line, it doesn't shift it

    Both AD lines start from the same intercept (A̅ = 50, unchanged) but AD₂ is flatter (lower c) — the line swings down around its intercept rather than shifting parallel, and equilibrium income falls sharply.

    Try it yourself — see the paradox with fresh numbers

    A̅ = 60 (C̄ = 30, Ī = 30) stays unchanged. MPC falls from 0.75 to 0.5.

    What is the new equilibrium income, Y*?

    Y* = 60 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 60 ÷ 0.5 = 120 (down from 240 when MPC was 0.75).

    Using C = 30 + 0.5Y at this new equilibrium, what is total savings, S = Y − C?

    C = 30 + 0.5(120) = 90. S = 120 − 90 = ₹30 — exactly the same as savings before the change (at c=0.75: C=30+0.75(240)=210, S=240−210=30). The paradox holds again with entirely different numbers.

    BasisChange in Autonomous Spending (A̅)Change in MPC (c)
    Effect on AD lineParallel shift (up or down)Swings/rotates around the intercept
    Slope of AD lineUnchangedChanges
    Used inThe multiplier effectThe Paradox of Thrift

    Memory Trick

    Shift vs Swing. A̅ changes → the AD line shifts parallel. c changes → the AD line swings. The Paradox of Thrift is a swing story, not a shift story.

    Why CUET asks this —It's a counter-intuitive result that tests genuine understanding, not just formula-plugging — expect an "explain why" short-answer style question or an assertion-reason MCQ.
    NCERT — Paradox of Thrift, p. 63Open in new tab

    09Full Employment, Deficient & Excess Demand

    Equilibrium income and full-employment income are two different things — and the gap between them has a name and a consequence.

    Ties the whole chapter to real-world policy

    Try this first

    An economy reaches its equilibrium level of income. Does that automatically mean everyone who wants a job has one?

    1

    No — equilibrium (Y = AD) just means the economy has stopped changing on its own. It says nothing about whether that resting point uses all available labour and capital.

    2

    If equilibrium output falls short of full-employment output, aggregate demand is too low — this is deficient demand, and prices tend to fall.

    3

    If equilibrium output exceeds full-employment output, aggregate demand is too high — this is excess demand, and prices tend to rise.

    4

    Either way, the gap is between equilibrium output and full-employment output — not between demand and supply, which are always equal at equilibrium by definition.

    NCERT Definition §4.4

    "Full employment level of income is that level of income where all the factors of production are fully employed."

    Equilibrium ≠ Full Employment

    The equilibrium level of output (where Y = AD) does not automatically mean every factor of production is employed. Equilibrium just means the economy won't change on its own — even if that equilibrium has unemployment.

    SituationCauseLong-run consequence
    Deficient DemandEquilibrium output < full-employment output (AD too low)Prices tend to fall
    Excess DemandEquilibrium output > full-employment output (AD too high)Prices tend to rise

    The Effective Demand Principle

    With price and the interest rate fixed, and aggregate supply perfectly elastic, aggregate output is determined solely by the level of aggregate demand. An increase (decrease) in autonomous spending raises (lowers) output by a larger amount, through the multiplier.

    Memory Trick

    Deficient = too little demand = prices fall. Excess = too much demand = prices rise. Both describe a gap between equilibrium output and full-employment output, not between demand and supply (which are always equal at equilibrium by definition).

    CUET Insight —Expect a scenario-based question describing rising/falling prices or unemployment, asking you to identify whether it's deficient or excess demand.
    NCERT — Full Employment, Deficient & Excess Demand, p. 65Open in new tab

    01Government Budget — Meaning & Components

    Every rupee the government plans to collect and spend in a year has to be laid before Parliament first — that document is the budget.

    Constitutional-fact favourite

    Try this first

    The government builds a new highway (funded by a loan) and also pays salaries to its employees this year. Do both belong in the same account of the budget?

    1

    Salaries are a routine, recurring cost for the current year only — they belong in the Revenue Account.

    2

    The highway creates a physical asset AND is financed by a loan (a liability) — both push it into the Capital Account.

    3

    So no — the same budget splits into two separate accounts precisely because these two kinds of items behave differently over time.

    4

    This entire statement of receipts and expenditure is constitutionally required under Article 112, covering the financial year 1 April to 31 March.

    NCERT Definition §5.1

    "There is a constitutional requirement in India (Article 112) to present before the Parliament a statement of estimated receipts and expenditures of the government in respect of every financial year which runs from 1 April to 31 March. This 'Annual Financial Statement' constitutes the main budget document of the government."

    Why two accounts?

    The budget's impact lasts beyond one year, so NCERT splits it into two accounts: one for the current year's routine running costs, and one for items that affect the government's assets and liabilities over time.

    BasisRevenue Account (Budget)Capital Account (Budget)
    CoversItems relating to the current financial year onlyItems concerning the government's assets and liabilities
    NatureRecurring, routineLong-term, affects future years
    Reproduces NCERT Chart 1 — The Components of the Government Budget

    Chart 1 — Revenue Receipts split into Tax/Non-Tax; Revenue and Capital Expenditure both split into Plan/Non-Plan. Capital Receipts isn't split further in NCERT's own chart (it's discussed separately as debt-creating vs non-debt-creating in the next topic).

    Memory Trick

    Revenue = routine, this year only. Capital = changes what the government owns/owes. If it affects an asset or a liability, it's capital; otherwise, it's revenue.

    Why CUET asks this —Article 112 and the "1 April to 31 March" financial year are exact, checkable facts — expect a direct one-liner MCQ on either.
    NCERT — Government Budget — Meaning & Components, p. 66Open in new tab

    02Objectives of the Government Budget

    Three jobs the budget does at once: provide what markets won't, share income more fairly, and keep the economy on an even keel.

    Public goods classification is a CUET staple

    Try this first

    A city builds a public park that anyone can enter for free, versus a private cinema hall that only ticket-holders can enter. Which one can the market provide efficiently on its own?

    1

    The cinema is excludable (no ticket, no entry) and rivalrous (limited seats) — a private firm can profitably sell tickets for it.

    2

    The park is non-excludable (can't stop anyone entering) and non-rivalrous (one person's enjoyment doesn't reduce another's) — nobody can be charged, so a private firm has no way to profit from providing it.

    3

    That's exactly why the government steps in to provide (finance) public goods like the park — this is the budget's Allocation Function.

    4

    The budget does two more jobs at the same time: Redistribution (taxes and transfers reshape how income is shared) and Stabilisation (managing aggregate demand).

    1. Allocation Function — providing public goods

    NCERT Definition §5.1.1

    Public goods have two key features: their benefits are available to all and "the consumption of many people is not rivalrous"; and there is "no feasible way of excluding anyone from enjoying the benefits" — they are non-excludable. Non-paying users are called free-riders.
    BasisPrivate GoodPublic Good
    Rivalrous?Yes — one person's use reduces what's left for othersNo — non-rivalrous
    Excludable?Yes — non-payers can be excludedNo — non-excludable
    Example (NCERT)Clothes, cars, a movie ticketNational defence, roads, a public park

    Public Provision ≠ Public Production

    Public provision means financed through the budget, usable without direct payment. Public production means the government itself produces the good. A public good can be publicly provided but privately produced.

    Try it yourself — Public Good or Private Good?

    A chocolate bar bought at a shop

    Rivalrous (once eaten, gone) and excludable (must pay) — private good.

    National defence

    Everyone is protected regardless of individual payment — non-rivalrous, non-excludable — public good.

    A street light on a public road

    Anyone walking by benefits, no one can be excluded — public good.

    A movie ticket at a cinema hall

    NCERT's own example — no ticket, no entry — excludable and rivalrous (limited seats) — private good.

    2. Redistribution Function

    National income splits into private income (households & firms) and public income (government). The government reshapes how fairly income is shared by collecting taxes and making transfers, changing households' personal disposable income.

    3. Stabilisation Function

    Aggregate demand doesn't always match the economy's capacity. When demand is too low, the government raises it (deficient demand); when demand is too high and inflationary, the government reduces it (excess demand) — exactly the concepts from the Income & Employment chapter, now with government tools attached.

    Memory Trick

    A-R-S: Allocate (public goods), Redistribute (taxes & transfers), Stabilise (demand management). Three functions, three different tools of the same budget.

    CUET Insight —Expect a scenario naming a good, asking you to identify it as public/private via the rivalrous/excludable test, or a "which function is this?" classification.
    NCERT — Objectives of the Government Budget, p. 67Open in new tab

    03Classification of Receipts

    Every rupee the government receives either creates a future obligation, or it doesn't — that single test sorts all receipts into two buckets.

    Classification MCQs every year

    Try this first

    The government collects income tax from citizens, and separately takes a loan from the World Bank. Are both the same kind of receipt?

    1

    Income tax creates no future obligation for the government to repay anyone — it's non-redeemable.

    2

    The World Bank loan must eventually be repaid — it creates a liability.

    3

    So no — income tax is a Revenue Receipt, while the loan is a Capital Receipt (specifically, debt-creating).

    4

    The one-line test: does this receipt create a claim on the government? Yes → capital. No → revenue.

    NCERT Definition §5.1.2

    "Revenue receipts are those receipts that do not lead to a claim on the government. They are therefore termed non-redeemable." Capital receipts are receipts which "create liability or reduce financial assets."
    BasisRevenue ReceiptsCapital Receipts
    Claim on government?No — non-redeemableYes — creates liability, or reduces assets
    Sub-typesTax revenue, Non-tax revenueDebt-creating (loans/borrowing), Non-debt creating (disinvestment, loan recovery)
    ExamplesIncome tax, GST, dividends from PSUs, feesMarket borrowings, sale of PSU shares

    Tax Revenue — Direct vs Indirect

    BasisDirect TaxIndirect Tax
    ExamplesPersonal income tax, corporation taxExcise duty, customs duty, GST
    StructureProgressive (higher income → higher rate)Necessities exempt/low; luxuries & tobacco taxed heavily

    Non-tax revenue includes

    Interest receipts on loans given by the government, dividends and profits on government investments, fees for services rendered, and grants-in-aid from foreign countries/international organisations.

    Try it yourself — Revenue Receipt or Capital Receipt?

    Corporation tax collected from companies

    A tax — creates no future claim — revenue receipt.

    A loan raised by the government from the World Bank

    Creates a liability — must be repaid — capital receipt (debt-creating).

    Disinvestment — sale of shares in a PSU

    Reduces the government's financial assets — capital receipt (non-debt creating).

    Dividend received from a public sector undertaking

    Non-tax revenue, no future claim created — revenue receipt.

    Memory Trick

    Ask "does this create a future claim on the government?" Yes → capital receipt. No → revenue receipt. Loans and asset-sales are capital; taxes and fees are revenue.

    CUET Insight —A very common classification MCQ: given a receipt item, decide revenue vs capital, or debt-creating vs non-debt-creating within capital receipts.
    NCERT — Classification of Receipts, p. 69Open in new tab

    04Classification of Expenditure

    The mirror image of receipts: does this spending create an asset (or wipe out a liability), or is it just for keeping the lights on?

    Pairs naturally with the receipts topic

    Try this first

    The government pays interest on old loans, and separately builds a new government hospital. Do both count the same way?

    1

    Interest payment creates no asset — it's just an ongoing obligation from past borrowing — a Revenue Expenditure.

    2

    The hospital building is a new physical asset the government now owns — a Capital Expenditure.

    3

    Same test as receipts, mirrored: does this spending build/buy an asset or cancel a liability? Yes → capital. No → revenue.

    4

    Interest payments, defence spending, and subsidies together make up the bulk of India's Non-Plan Revenue Expenditure.

    NCERT Definition §5.1.3

    "Revenue Expenditure is expenditure incurred for purposes other than the creation of physical or financial assets of the central government." Capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities.
    BasisRevenue ExpenditureCapital Expenditure
    Effect on assetsNo asset createdCreates assets, or reduces liabilities
    ExamplesSalaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, grantsLand, buildings, machinery, investment in shares, loans given to states/PSUs
    Sub-classificationPlan / Non-Plan Revenue ExpenditurePlan / Non-Plan Capital Expenditure

    Main items of Non-Plan Revenue Expenditure

    Interest payments (the single largest component), defence services (committed expenditure — little scope for reduction), and subsidies (an explicit welfare instrument on food, fertilisers, exports, interest on loans).

    Try it yourself — Revenue Expenditure or Capital Expenditure?

    Salaries paid to government employees

    No asset created — normal running cost — revenue expenditure.

    Construction of a new government hospital building

    Creates a physical asset — capital expenditure.

    Interest paid on past government borrowings

    No asset created, a recurring obligation — revenue expenditure.

    A loan given by the centre to a state government

    Creates a financial asset (a claim on the state) — capital expenditure.

    Memory Trick

    Same test as receipts, mirrored: does this spending build/buy an asset or cancel a liability? Yes → capital. No (routine running cost) → revenue.

    CUET Insight —Subsidies, interest payments, and defence spending are the three most commonly tested "which type of revenue expenditure" fact-recall items.
    NCERT — Classification of Expenditure, p. 70Open in new tab

    05Balanced, Surplus & Deficit Budget — and Measures of Deficit

    Three formulas, three different lenses on the same gap between what the government spends and what it collects.

    The single most-tested numerical in this chapter

    Try this first

    Revenue Receipts = ₹800 crore, Revenue Expenditure = ₹950 crore. What is the Revenue Deficit, and what does it tell us?

    1

    Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts = 950 − 800 = ₹150 crore.

    2

    A revenue deficit means the government is dissaving — it's borrowing not for investment, but just to fund its own routine consumption.

    3

    Fiscal Deficit goes further: Total Expenditure − (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts) — the economy's total borrowing requirement.

    4

    Primary Deficit strips out interest payments from the fiscal deficit, isolating the current fiscal imbalance from the burden of past borrowing.

    Budget TypeCondition
    Balanced BudgetExpenditure = Revenue collected
    Surplus BudgetTax collection > required expenditure
    Deficit BudgetExpenditure > Revenue (the most common case)

    Revenue Deficit

    Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts

    A revenue deficit means the government is dissaving — borrowing not just for investment, but to fund its own consumption.

    Fiscal Deficit

    Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Creating Capital Receipts)
    Fiscal Deficit = Net Borrowing at Home + Borrowing from RBI + Borrowing from Abroad
    Fiscal Deficit = Revenue Deficit + Capital Expenditure − Non-debt Creating Capital Receipts

    Fiscal deficit shows the total borrowing requirement of the government from all sources.

    Primary Deficit

    Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Net Interest Liabilities

    This isolates current fiscal imbalance by stripping out interest obligations built up from past borrowing.

    NCERT's own worked example (Table 5.1, as % of GDP)

    Item% of GDP
    Revenue Receipts9.0
    Revenue Expenditure11.7
    Revenue Deficit2.7
    Total Expenditure13.5
    Non-debt Receipts10.0
    Fiscal Deficit3.5
    Interest Payments3.1
    Primary Deficit0.4

    Check: Revenue Deficit (2.7) = Revenue Expenditure (11.7) − Revenue Receipts (9.0) ✓. Fiscal Deficit (3.5) = Total Expenditure (13.5) − Non-debt Receipts (10.0) ✓. Primary Deficit (0.4) = Fiscal Deficit (3.5) − Interest Payments (3.1) ✓.

    Try it yourself — calculate the three deficits

    Revenue Receipts = ₹800 crore, Revenue Expenditure = ₹950 crore, Capital Expenditure = ₹300 crore, Non-debt Creating Capital Receipts = ₹100 crore, Interest Payments = ₹120 crore.

    Revenue Deficit (₹ crore) = ?

    950 − 800 = ₹150 crore.

    Fiscal Deficit (₹ crore) = ? (Total Expenditure = Revenue + Capital Expenditure = 950+300 = 1250)

    Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts) = 1250 − (800+100) = ₹350 crore.

    Primary Deficit (₹ crore) = ?

    350 − 120 = ₹230 crore.

    Memory Trick

    Revenue Deficit ⊂ Fiscal Deficit ⊂ (Fiscal Deficit + Interest = ) the full borrowing picture, minus interest = Primary Deficit. Each deficit measure strips away one more layer to isolate a specific imbalance.

    CUET Insight —Given a set of budget figures, expect a direct "calculate the deficit" numerical for at least one of the three measures — write the formula first, then plug in numbers.
    NCERT — Balanced, Surplus & Deficit Budget — and Measures of Deficit, p. 71Open in new tab

    06Box 5.1 — Fiscal Policy in the AD Model

    NCERT's own boxed section: bringing government spending and taxes into the income-determination model from the previous chapter.

    Government-spending & tax multiplier numericals

    Try this first

    MPC = 0.8. If the government raises spending (G) by ₹100 crore, by how much does equilibrium income rise?

    1

    The government spending multiplier is 1 ÷ (1−c) = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5 — the same formula as the investment multiplier.

    2

    ΔY = ΔG × multiplier = 100 × 5 = ₹500 crore.

    3

    A tax cut works differently — it only raises spending indirectly (via consumption), so the tax multiplier is smaller: −c ÷ (1−c) = −0.8÷0.2 = −4.

    4

    That's why the Balanced Budget Multiplier (raising G and T by the same amount) is exactly 1, not zero — G's direct effect always outweighs T's indirect one.

    NCERT Definition Box 5.1

    "One of Keynes's main ideas... was that government fiscal policy should be used to stabilise the level of output and employment. Through changes in its expenditure and taxes, the government attempts to increase output and income and seeks to stabilise the ups and downs in the economy."

    Two channels: G directly, T and TR via disposable income

    Consumption function with lump-sum taxes and transfers

    C = C̄ + cYD = C̄ + c(Y − T + TR̄)

    YD = disposable income. Taxes lower it, transfers raise it — both flow through into consumption via c, the MPC.

    Aggregate Demand & Equilibrium

    AD = C̄ + c(Y − T + TR̄) + I + G
    Y* = [1 ÷ (1 − c)] × (C̄ − cT + cTR̄ + I + G)
    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 5.1 & Fig. 5.2 — a rise in G, or a cut in T, shifts AD up in parallel

    A rise in G (Fig. 5.1) or a cut in T (Fig. 5.2) both shift the AD line up in parallel — same mechanism, same multiplier, different lever.

    The Government Spending & Tax Multipliers

    Government spending multiplier: ΔY ÷ ΔG = 1 ÷ (1 − c)
    Tax multiplier: ΔY ÷ ΔT = −c ÷ (1 − c)  (negative — a tax cut raises income)

    NCERT Example 5.1 (c = 0.8)

    Government spending multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. ΔG = 100 → ΔY = 500. Tax multiplier = −0.8 ÷ 0.2 = −4. A tax cut of 100 (ΔT = −100) → ΔY = 400 — smaller than the spending effect, since tax changes only reach spending indirectly, through consumption.

    The Balanced Budget Multiplier

    Balanced Budget Multiplier = [1 ÷ (1−c)] + [−c ÷ (1−c)] = 1

    If G rises by 100 and T rises by 100 (budget stays balanced), income rises by exactly 100 — not zero. The direct effect of ΔG always outweighs the indirect, consumption-driven effect of ΔT.

    Try it yourself — apply the multipliers

    MPC = 0.75. The government spending multiplier is:

    1 ÷ (1−0.75) = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.

    MPC = 0.75. A tax cut of ₹80 crore (ΔT = −80) changes equilibrium income by how much (₹ crore)?

    Tax multiplier = −0.75÷0.25 = −3. ΔY = −3 × (−80) = +₹240 crore.

    Memory Trick

    The tax multiplier is always exactly 1 less (in absolute size) than the spending multiplier — that gap is precisely why the balanced budget multiplier is 1, not 0.

    CUET Insight —Given MPC, expect a "find both multipliers" numerical, or a "show the balanced budget multiplier equals 1" derivation question.
    NCERT — Box 5.1 — Fiscal Policy in the AD Model, p. 73Open in new tab

    07Box 5.1 — Proportional Taxes & Automatic Stabilisers

    Real-world taxes aren't a fixed lump sum — they're a percentage of income. That one change makes the whole system self-correcting.

    "Automatic stabiliser" is a favourite conceptual term

    Try this first

    c = 0.8 and t = 0.25 (tax is 25% of income, not a fixed lump sum). What is the effective MPC out of income now?

    1

    Effective MPC = c(1−t) = 0.8 × 0.75 = 0.6 — down from 0.8, since 25% of any extra income is siphoned off as tax before it can be spent.

    2

    The multiplier shrinks too: 1 ÷ [1 − c(1−t)] = 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5, much smaller than the lump-sum-tax multiplier of 5.

    3

    This is exactly why proportional taxes are called an automatic stabiliser — in a boom, more income is siphoned off automatically; in a slump, less is — dampening swings without anyone deciding anything.

    4

    Contrast this with discretionary fiscal policy — a deliberate government decision, like raising G to offset a fall in investment.

    Consumption & AD with a proportional tax, T = tY

    C = C̄ + c(1 − t)Y + cTR̄
    AD = A̅ + c(1 − t)Y,  where A̅ = C̄ + cTR̄ + I + G

    The effective MPC out of income falls to c(1 − t) — proportional taxes don't just lower consumption, they lower the slope of the AD line.

    Reproduces NCERT Fig. 5.3 — a proportional tax makes the AD line flatter

    With a proportional tax, the AD line is flatter (lower effective MPC) — for the same autonomous spending, equilibrium income is lower, and swings in the economy get automatically dampened.

    The Multiplier with a Proportional Tax

    Y* = A̅ ÷ [1 − c(1 − t)]
    ΔY ÷ ΔA̅ = 1 ÷ [1 − c(1 − t)]

    NCERT Example 5.2 (c = 0.8, t = 0.25)

    Effective MPC = c(1−t) = 0.8 × 0.75 = 0.6 (down from 0.8). Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1−0.6) = 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5 — smaller than the lump-sum-tax multiplier of 5. ΔG = 100 → ΔY = 2.5 × 100 = 250 only.

    Why this is called an "Automatic Stabiliser"

    When GDP rises, disposable income rises by less (some is siphoned off as tax) — this limits the upward swing in consumption. When GDP falls in a recession, disposable income (and hence consumption) falls by less than it otherwise would — cushioning the downturn. No one has to decide anything; it happens automatically, purely from the tax structure.

    Discretionary Fiscal Policy

    In contrast, a deliberate government decision — e.g. raising G to offset a fall in investment — is called discretionary fiscal policy, distinct from the automatic, built-in stabilising effect of proportional taxes and welfare transfers.

    Transfers have their own (smaller) multiplier

    Transfer Payments Multiplier

    ΔY ÷ ΔTR̄ = c ÷ (1 − c)

    NCERT Example 5.3 (c = 0.75)

    ΔG = 20 → ΔY = [1÷(1−0.75)] × 20 = 4 × 20 = 80. ΔTR̄ = 20 → ΔY = [0.75÷0.25] × 20 = 3 × 20 = 60 — smaller, since part of any transfer is saved, not spent.

    Try it yourself

    c = 0.8, t = 0.25 (as in Example 5.2). The multiplier, 1 ÷ [1 − c(1−t)], equals:

    c(1−t) = 0.8×0.75 = 0.6. Multiplier = 1÷(1−0.6) = 1÷0.4 = 2.5.

    Memory Trick

    Proportional tax = automatic shock absorber. It doesn't eliminate fluctuations, just dampens them — the "rest must be taken care of by deliberate policy," per NCERT.

    CUET Insight —Expect either a numerical using 1÷[1−c(1−t)], or a conceptual question distinguishing "automatic stabiliser" from "discretionary fiscal policy."
    NCERT — Box 5.1 — Proportional Taxes & Automatic Stabilisers, p. 76Open in new tab

    08Government Debt & the Deficit Debate

    Deficits are a flow; debt is the stock they pile up into — and economists genuinely disagree about how much this should worry us.

    "Explain why" conceptual favourite

    Try this first

    The government cuts taxes today, planning to borrow to cover the gap. Will households necessarily spend the extra take-home income?

    1

    The traditional view says yes — households are short-sighted and simply spend the windfall, ignoring that future taxes will have to rise to repay the debt.

    2

    Ricardian Equivalence argues the opposite — forward-looking households anticipate the future tax hike and save the extra income instead, to cover it.

    3

    Under Ricardian Equivalence, taxation and borrowing become equivalent ways to finance spending — national savings doesn't change either way.

    4

    One more nuance: debt owed to fellow citizens is just an internal transfer, but debt owed to foreigners is a genuine burden — real goods must eventually flow abroad to service it.

    Deficit (flow) vs Debt (stock)

    Every year's deficit adds to the accumulated stock of government debt — and a larger debt means larger future interest payments, which themselves add to future deficits.

    Is debt a burden? Two views

    BasisTraditional ViewRicardian Equivalence
    Consumer behaviourShort-sighted — spend more today from a tax cut, ignoring future tax hikesForward-looking — anticipate future taxes, save more today
    Effect on national savingsFalls — future generations bear a reduced-consumption burdenUnchanged — private saving rises to exactly offset government dissaving
    Named after—David Ricardo

    Why "equivalence"?

    It argues that taxation and borrowing are equivalent ways to finance spending — borrowing today, repaid by taxes tomorrow, has the same impact as taxing today, because forward-looking families save enough now to cover their children's future tax bill.

    "We owe it to ourselves" — but only domestically

    Debt owed to fellow citizens doesn't drain the nation's total purchasing power — it's a transfer within the country. But debt owed to foreigners is a genuine burden: real goods must eventually flow abroad to service the interest.

    Other perspectives

    1Are deficits always inflationary?

    Not necessarily — if there are unutilised resources (unemployment), a deficit-driven rise in demand raises output, not just prices. It becomes inflationary mainly when the economy is already at full capacity.

    2"Crowding out" of private investment

    Government borrowing competes with private borrowers for the same pool of savings — but if the deficit itself raises income (and hence total savings), both government and industry can end up borrowing more, not less.

    Deficit Reduction — the main levers
