    Raise taxes (India has leaned on direct taxes, since indirect taxes are regressive), or cut expenditure (more efficient administration, PSU disinvestment, replacing subsidies with targeted cash transfers). Note: a larger deficit doesn't always mean more expansionary policy — in a recession, tax revenue falls on its own, inflating the deficit even with no policy change at all.

    Memory Trick

    Debt to ourselves = a transfer, not a loss. Debt to foreigners = a real burden. And remember: deficits can rise purely because of a recession — that's not the same as a policy choice to spend more.

    Why CUET asks this —A rich "explain why" and assertion-reason source — expect questions on Ricardian equivalence, crowding out, or whether fiscal deficits are always inflationary.
    NCERT — Government Debt & the Deficit Debate, p. 79Open in new tab

    09Box 5.2 — Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003

    NCERT's own boxed case study: India's legal attempt to keep fiscal deficits from spiralling, written into law rather than left to political discretion.

    High case-study / fact-recall potential

    Try this first

    Why would a government pass a law restricting its own future ability to run large deficits?

    1

    Left purely to political discretion, fiscal deficits can spiral — so India enacted the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBMA) in August 2003 to bind the government to a prudent path.

    2

    Its core targets: keep the fiscal deficit at or below 3% of GDP, and eliminate the revenue deficit entirely.

    3

    It also locks the central government out of directly borrowing from the RBI, except for short-term cash-flow advances.

    4

    Deviation from these targets is allowed only for exceptional reasons — national security, a natural calamity, or similar circumstances.

    NCERT Box 5.2

    "The enactment of the FRBMA, in August 2003, marked a turning point in fiscal reforms, binding the government through an institutional framework to pursue a prudent fiscal policy." Rules took effect from July 2004.

    Main features

    #Feature
    1Reduce fiscal deficit to not more than 3% of GDP; eliminate revenue deficit, then build a revenue surplus
    2Annual reduction targets: fiscal deficit by 0.3% of GDP, revenue deficit by 0.5%
    3Deviation allowed only on grounds of national security, natural calamity, or other exceptional circumstances
    4Central government cannot borrow from the RBI, except temporary advances for cash mismatches
    5RBI must not subscribe to primary issues of central government securities (from 2006-07)
    6Greater transparency in fiscal operations
    7Three statements tabled in Parliament: Medium-term Fiscal Policy, Fiscal Policy Strategy, Macroeconomic Framework
    8Quarterly review of receipts/expenditure trends before Parliament

    FRBM Review Committee

    Years after enactment, with India now a middle-income economy and advanced countries moving away from rigid fiscal rules, a Review Committee was tasked with revamping the FRBM framework for a changing India — while still retaining its basic operational structure.

    Memory Trick

    FRBMA = a legal leash on the deficit. 3% fiscal deficit ceiling, zero revenue deficit target, and RBI locked out of directly financing the government — the three numbers worth memorising.

    CUET Insight —Expect a direct fact-recall MCQ on the year (2003), the 3% target, or which body (RBI) is restricted from financing government deficits under the Act.
    NCERT — Box 5.2 — Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003, p. 82Open in new tab

    10Box 5.3 — GST: One Nation, One Tax, One Market

    NCERT's own boxed case study on India's biggest indirect-tax reform — one tax replacing a maze of central and state levies.

    High case-study potential

    Try this first

    Before GST, a good was taxed at every stage of production on its FULL value — including tax already paid earlier. What problem did this create?

    1

    Taxing the full value at each stage means later-stage tax is charged partly on tax already paid — a "tax on tax," known as the cascading effect.

    2

    GST fixes this by taxing only the value added at each stage, giving credit for tax already paid earlier — the Input Tax Credit.

    3

    GST rolled out on 1 July 2017, replacing a maze of separate central and state taxes (Excise, Service Tax, VAT, Octroi) with one comprehensive tax.

    4

    It's a destination-based tax — collected where a good is consumed, not where it's produced — summed up as "One Nation, One Tax, One Market."

    NCERT Box 5.3

    "Goods and Service Tax (GST) is the single comprehensive indirect tax... a destination based consumption tax with facility of Input Tax Credit in the supply chain." Rolled out 1 July 2017.
    AspectDetail
    Rollout date1 July 2017 (midnight session of Parliament)
    Constitutional basis101st Constitution Amendment Act; introduced Article 246A
    Standard rates0%, 3%, 5%, 12%, 18%, 28%
    Kept outside GST (for now)Five petroleum products; alcohol (still state VAT)
    Special caseTobacco & tobacco products attract both GST and Central Excise Duty

    The problem GST solves — cascading tax

    Before GST, tax was charged on the total value of a good at each stage, including tax already paid earlier — a "tax on tax," or cascading effect. Under GST, tax is charged only on value added at each stage, with credit for tax already paid at the previous stage (Input Tax Credit).

    BasisPre-GST RegimeGST Regime
    StructureMultiple central & state taxes (Excise, Service Tax, VAT, Entry Tax, Octroi, etc.)One comprehensive tax, one rate per good/service nationwide
    Effect on intermediate goodsCascading — tax charged on tax already paidInput Tax Credit removes cascading
    ComplianceFragmented across statesSingle common online portal

    Memory Trick

    GST = "One Nation, One Tax, One Market." Destination-based (taxed where consumed, not produced), value-added at every stage, Input Tax Credit kills the cascading effect.

    CUET Insight —Expect a fact-recall MCQ on the rollout date, the constitutional amendment number, or a conceptual question on why GST removes the cascading effect.
    NCERT — Box 5.3 — GST: One Nation, One Tax, One Market, p. 83Open in new tab

    01Microeconomics vs Macroeconomics

    Macroeconomics doesn't study individual buyers and sellers — it studies a whole economy by imagining one representative good standing in for all of them.

    The very first distinction CUET tests in this chapter

    Try this first

    A single company decides to cut its own workers' wages to raise its profit. Is that a microeconomic decision or a macroeconomic one?

    1

    The company is acting in the interest of its own shareholders — a "micro" (small) decision-maker, even if the company itself is large.

    2

    Microeconomics studies exactly this: individual buyers and sellers trying to maximise their own profit or personal satisfaction.

    3

    Macroeconomics only enters if we ask how this decision affects the economy as a whole — total employment, aggregate wages, overall demand.

    4

    So the wage cut itself is microeconomic; its ripple effect on the whole economy's employment level would be a macroeconomic question.

    NCERT Definition — Economic Agents §1

    "By economic units or economic agents, we mean those individuals or institutions which take economic decisions. They can be consumers... producers... entities like the government, corporation, banks which also take different economic decisions."

    The representative good — why macro can simplify

    If output, price, and employment levels across an economy's many goods tend to move together (food grain output rising alongside industrial output, prices rising or falling together), we can study a single imaginary representative good instead of every real commodity — its output, price, and employment level standing in for the whole economy's average.

    BasisMicroeconomicsMacroeconomics
    ScaleIndividual ("micro" = small) markets and agentsThe economy as a whole ("macro" = large)
    Decision-makersIndividual consumers, producers, firmsThe State, RBI, SEBI — pursuing public goals, not private profit
    Typical questionsHow does one consumer choose between two goods?Is the economy's price level rising? Is unemployment worsening?
    Closest overlapGeneral Equilibrium — supply/demand across every marketStudies the aggregate effects of those same market forces

    NCERT on Adam Smith §1

    Adam Smith suggested that if buyers and sellers in each market follow only their own self-interest, economists "will not need to think of the wealth and welfare of the country as a whole separately." But economists found markets sometimes don't exist, sometimes fail to reach equilibrium, and society often pursues goals (employment, defence, education, health) that need modifying the aggregate effects of individual decisions.

    Memory Trick

    Micro = one player, Macro = the whole stadium. If the question is about a single buyer/seller/firm's own choice, it's micro. If it's about a country's total output, price level, or employment, it's macro.

    CUET Insight —Expect a direct "which is a macroeconomic variable" MCQ (inflation, unemployment rate, GDP — not one firm's profit), or a fact-recall question naming Adam Smith and his book.
    NCERT — Microeconomics vs Macroeconomics, p. 3Open in new tab

    02Emergence of Macroeconomics

    Macroeconomics didn't always exist as a separate subject — it was born out of a single catastrophic real-world event.

    Keynes and the Great Depression — a guaranteed fact-recall

    Try this first

    Before 1936, most economists believed every worker willing to work would find employment. What real-world event proved this assumption wrong?

    1

    The dominant "classical tradition" assumed markets would always clear — full employment was the normal state.

    2

    The Great Depression (starting 1929) shattered that: in the USA, unemployment rose from 3% to 25% between 1929 and 1933, while aggregate output fell by about 33%.

    3

    This showed unemployment could be long-lasting, not a temporary blip — something classical theory couldn't explain.

    4

    British economist John Maynard Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1936, examining the economy in its entirety — and macroeconomics as a separate subject was born.

    NCERT Definition §1.1

    "Macroeconomics, as a separate branch of economics, emerged after the British economist John Maynard Keynes published his celebrated book The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1936."

    The Great Depression, in numbers

    USA, 1929 to 1933: unemployment rate rose from 3% to 25%. Aggregate output fell by about 33%. Demand for goods was low, factories lay idle, workers lost jobs — and the effects spread well beyond Europe and North America.

    The classical tradition, before Keynes

    The dominant pre-Keynesian view held that all workers ready to work would find employment, and all factories would run at full capacity — markets were assumed to self-correct towards full employment automatically.

    Memory Trick

    1929 crash → 1936 book → new subject. The Great Depression supplied the real-world puzzle; Keynes's General Theory supplied the theory that could explain it.

    Why CUET asks this —The exact book title, year (1936), and the Great Depression statistics are precise, checkable facts — a near-guaranteed one-liner MCQ.
    NCERT — Emergence of Macroeconomics, p. 5Open in new tab

    03The Capitalist Economy

    This entire textbook studies one specific kind of economy — and knowing its exact defining features is worth real marks.

    The 3-criteria definition is a favourite fact-recall

    Try this first

    A peasant family farms land collectively owned by their tribe, consuming most of what they grow themselves. Does this count as a "capitalist" production unit for this book's analysis?

    1

    No — there's no private ownership of the land (tribal ownership), and production isn't mainly for sale in the market (much is self-consumed).

    2

    Wage labour is barely used either — most work is done by family members themselves, not hired workers paid a wage.

    3

    A true capitalist economy needs: private ownership of production, output sold in the market, and labour hired for a wage.

    4

    NCERT is explicit that this book's analysis doesn't apply to such non-capitalist arrangements, even though many developing countries have a significant capitalist sector alongside them.

    NCERT Definition — Capitalist Economy §1.2

    "A capitalist economy can be defined as an economy in which most of the economic activities have the following characteristics (a) there is private ownership of means of production (b) production takes place for selling the output in the market (c) there is sale and purchase of labour services at a price which is called the wage rate."

    The Firm and its three factors of production

    An entrepreneur hires wage labour, capital, and land, undertakes production, and sells output (goods and services) in the market to earn revenue. Part of revenue pays rent (to land), part pays interest (to capital), part pays wages (to labour) — the rest is the entrepreneur's profit.

    Factor of ProductionPayment it earns
    Land (natural resources)Rent
    CapitalInterest
    LabourWages
    Entrepreneurship (residual)Profit

    Investment expenditure

    Profits are often used by producers to buy new machinery or build new factories — expenses that raise productive capacity. NCERT calls these investment expenditure.

    Memory Trick

    Three tests for "capitalist": Private ownership + Market sale + Wage labour. Miss any one of the three, and it's not a capitalist production unit by this book's definition.

    CUET Insight —Expect a scenario describing a production arrangement, asking whether it meets the capitalist economy's three defining criteria.
    NCERT — The Capitalist Economy, p. 6Open in new tab

    04The Four Sectors of the Economy

    Every macroeconomic model in this book is really just tracking money and goods moving between four groups of players.

    Sets up every later chapter's circular flow diagrams

    Try this first

    A worker earns a salary from a private firm, and separately pays income tax to the government. Which sectors is she connecting?

    1

    As a worker, she belongs to the household sector — households supply labour and earn wages/salaries in return.

    2

    Her employer is a firm — the sector that hires factors of production and produces output for sale.

    3

    Her tax payment flows to the government sector — which frames laws, provides public services, and also produces some output itself.

    4

    The fourth sector, the external sector, doesn't appear in this example at all — it only enters when trade or capital crosses national borders.

    NCERT's four sectors §1.2

    "Macroeconomics sees an economy as a combination of four sectors, namely households, firms, government and external sector."
    SectorRole
    HouseholdsIndividuals/groups who consume, save, pay taxes, and supply factors of production (labour, land, capital) to firms
    FirmsHire factors of production, produce output, sell it in the market to earn profit
    GovernmentFrames and enforces laws, delivers justice, undertakes production, imposes taxes, spends on infrastructure/schools/health
    External SectorThe rest of the world — connected via exports, imports, and capital flows

    Exports, Imports, and Capital Flows

    A country can sell goods abroad (exports) or buy goods from abroad (imports). Besides trade in goods, capital can also flow in from foreign countries, or flow out as the domestic country invests abroad.

    Where do households get their money?

    Households work in firms and earn wages, work in government and earn salaries, or own firms and earn profits — and the market in which firms sell their products couldn't function without demand coming from households. Households can also earn rent (leasing land) or interest (lending capital).

    Memory Trick

    H-F-G-E: Households, Firms, Government, External sector. The first three make up the domestic economy; the External sector is what turns a closed economy into an open one — the exact topic of this course's final chapter.

    CUET Insight —Expect a direct "name the four sectors" or "which sector does X belong to" question — this is foundational vocabulary every later chapter assumes you already know.
    NCERT — The Four Sectors of the Economy, p. 7Open in new tab

    01Balance of Payments — Current Account

    Every transaction India makes with the rest of the world in a year gets recorded somewhere — the Current Account tracks the trade and transfer side of that record.

    BOT vs Current Account is a classic mix-up

    Try this first

    India exports ₹150 crore of goods and imports ₹240 crore of goods this year. Is India's Balance of Trade in surplus or deficit?

    1

    Balance of Trade (BOT) = value of exports − value of imports = 150 − 240 = −₹90 crore.

    2

    Since imports exceed exports, this is a Trade Deficit.

    3

    BOT is only PART of the Current Account — the rest is Net Invisibles (services, transfers, and income flows), which could still push the overall Current Account into surplus or a smaller deficit.

    4

    Current Account Balance = Balance of Trade + Net Invisibles.

    NCERT Definition §6.1

    "The balance of payments (BoP) record the transactions in goods, services and assets between residents of a country with the rest of the world for a specified time period typically a year." "Current Account is the record of trade in goods and services and transfer payments."

    What's inside the Current Account

    Trade in goods (exports and imports of physical goods), trade in services (factor and non-factor income — shipping, banking, tourism, software), and transfer payments (gifts, remittances, grants received "for free," without providing anything in return).

    TermMeaning
    Balance of Trade (BOT) / Trade BalanceValue of exports − value of imports of goods only
    Net InvisiblesValue of exports − value of imports of services, transfers, and income flows
    Current Account BalanceBOT + Net Invisibles

    Current Account status

    Receipts > Payments → Surplus  |  Receipts = Payments → Balanced  |  Receipts < Payments → Deficit

    A surplus current account means the nation is a lender to other countries; a deficit means it's a borrower from the rest of the world.

    Memory Trick

    BOT = goods only. Current Account = goods + services + transfers. Never treat "trade deficit" and "current account deficit" as the same number — BOT is just one ingredient.

    CUET Insight —Expect a numerical asking you to compute BOT or the Current Account Balance from given export/import/invisibles figures, or a "distinguish BOT from Current Account" conceptual question.
    NCERT — Balance of Payments — Current Account, p. 86Open in new tab

    02Capital Account & Balance of Payments Equilibrium

    If a country spends more abroad than it earns, that gap has to be financed somehow — the Capital Account is where that financing shows up.

    Autonomous vs Accommodating is a favourite conceptual pair

    Try this first

    India runs a Current Account deficit this year. What must be true of its Capital Account for the overall Balance of Payments to stay in equilibrium?

    1

    Just like a person who spends more than their income must borrow or sell assets, a country with a current account deficit must finance it by borrowing abroad or selling assets.

    2

    This means the Capital Account must show a surplus — a net capital inflow — to offset the current account deficit.

    3

    In equilibrium: Current Account + Capital Account ≡ 0.

    4

    If the two don't naturally balance, the central bank can step in and sell (or buy) foreign exchange reserves to make up the difference — an official reserve transaction.

    NCERT Definition — Capital Account §6.1.2

    "Capital Account records all international transactions of assets... Purchase of assets is a debit item on the capital account... sale of assets... is a credit item."
    ItemExamples (NCERT Fig. 6.2)
    Capital Account inflows/itemsForeign Direct Investment (FDI), Foreign Institutional Investment (FII), external borrowings and assistance

    The core BoP identity

    Current Account + Capital Account ≡ 0

    This holds when the current account deficit is financed entirely by international lending, with no reserve movements needed.

    Autonomous vs Accommodating Transactions

    Autonomous transactions ("above the line") happen for reasons unrelated to the BoP gap — e.g. to earn profit. Accommodating transactions ("below the line") exist specifically to bridge whatever gap the autonomous transactions leave — official reserve transactions are the classic accommodating item.

    Errors and Omissions

    Since it's difficult to record every international transaction with perfect accuracy, BoP accounts include a third element — Errors and Omissions — alongside the current and capital accounts.

    Memory Trick

    A deficit in one account needs a surplus in the other — they must sum to zero. Official reserve transactions are the "shock absorber" when they don't naturally balance.

    CUET Insight —Expect a question distinguishing autonomous from accommodating transactions, or asking what a current account deficit implies about the capital account.
    NCERT — Capital Account & Balance of Payments Equilibrium, p. 88Open in new tab

    03The Foreign Exchange Market

    Before an Indian tourist can spend a single pound in London, someone has to sell her those pounds — that's the market this topic is about.

    Demand/Supply direction is the exam's favourite trap

    Try this first

    An Indian resident wants to visit London on vacation. Does she create demand for pounds, or supply of pounds, in the foreign exchange market?

    1

    She needs pounds to pay for her stay — she's a buyer of foreign currency, so she creates demand for foreign exchange (pounds).

    2

    People demand foreign exchange to buy foreign goods/services, send gifts abroad, or buy foreign financial assets.

    3

    The opposite flow — foreigners buying Indian exports, sending gifts to India, or buying Indian assets — creates supply of foreign exchange into India.

    4

    The Foreign Exchange Rate is simply the price of one currency in terms of another — e.g. Rs 50 per dollar.

    NCERT Definition — Foreign Exchange Rate §6.2.1

    "Foreign Exchange Rate (also called Forex Rate) is the price of one currency in terms of another. It links the currencies of different countries and enables comparison of international costs and prices."
    SideDriven byEffect of a rise in exchange rate (price of $ in ₹)
    Demand for forexBuying foreign goods, sending gifts abroad, buying foreign assetsImports become costlier → demand for forex falls
    Supply of forexExports, gifts/transfers received, foreigners buying domestic assetsForeigners find domestic goods cheaper → exports rise → supply of forex may rise

    Who trades in this market?

    Commercial banks, foreign exchange brokers, other authorised dealers, and monetary authorities. The market itself is world-wide — trading centres stay in close, continuous contact even though participants may be based in different countries.

    Memory Trick

    Buying from abroad = demand for forex. Selling abroad = supply of forex. Whichever direction the payment flows, foreign exchange flows the opposite way.

    CUET Insight —Expect a scenario (tourism, exports, foreign investment) asking whether it creates demand for or supply of foreign exchange.
    NCERT — The Foreign Exchange Market, p. 91Open in new tab

    04Flexible Exchange Rate — Depreciation & Appreciation

    Left alone, the exchange rate settles wherever demand for foreign currency exactly matches its supply — and that resting point can move.

    Depreciation vs Appreciation — the exam's #1 confusion pair

    Try this first

    Indians start travelling abroad more, raising demand for foreign currency. If the exchange rate rises from Rs 50/$ to Rs 70/$, has the rupee appreciated or depreciated?

    1

    The exchange rate rising means you now need more rupees to buy one dollar (Rs 70 instead of Rs 50).

    2

    The value of the rupee, in terms of dollars, has fallen — this is called Depreciation of the domestic currency.

    3

    If instead the exchange rate had FALLEN (fewer rupees needed per dollar), that would be Appreciation of the rupee.

    4

    Under a Flexible (Floating) Exchange Rate system, this is all determined purely by market demand and supply — the central bank does not intervene.

    NCERT Definition — Flexible Exchange Rate §6.2.2

    "This exchange rate is determined by the market forces of demand and supply. It is also known as Floating Exchange Rate... In a completely flexible system, the Central banks do not intervene in the foreign exchange market."
    TermMeaning
    DepreciationExchange rate (₹ per $) RISES → rupee is worth LESS in dollar terms
    AppreciationExchange rate (₹ per $) FALLS → rupee is worth MORE in dollar terms

    Other forces that move a flexible exchange rate

    Speculation — if investors expect a currency to appreciate, buying it now to profit later can make that expectation self-fulfilling. Interest rate differentials — higher interest rates at home attract foreign investors, appreciating the domestic currency. Income — higher domestic income raises import demand, tending to depreciate the currency.

    Memory Trick

    Rate UP = currency DOWN (depreciation). Rate DOWN = currency UP (appreciation). The exchange rate and the currency's value always move in opposite directions.

    Why CUET asks this —Depreciation/appreciation direction is deceptively easy to flip under exam pressure — a near-guaranteed direct or scenario-based MCQ.
    NCERT — Flexible Exchange Rate — Depreciation & Appreciation, p. 92Open in new tab

    05Fixed Exchange Rate & Managed Floating

    Instead of letting the market decide, a government can simply announce a rate and defend it — but defending it isn't free.

    Devaluation vs Revaluation pairs with Depreciation vs Appreciation

    Try this first

    India's government wants to encourage exports, so it deliberately fixes the exchange rate at Rs 70/$ instead of the market rate of Rs 50/$. What must the RBI now do?

    1

    At Rs 70/$ (a weaker rupee than the market wants), the supply of dollars will exceed demand for dollars.

    2

    The RBI must step in and buy up the excess dollars with rupees, to absorb the surplus and hold the rate at 70.

    3

    This deliberate government action of raising the fixed exchange rate (making the domestic currency cheaper) is called Devaluation.

    4

    The opposite move — the government lowering the fixed rate — is called Revaluation. As this intervention continues, the RBI keeps accumulating more foreign exchange reserves.

    NCERT Definition — Fixed Exchange Rate §6.2.2

    "In this exchange rate system, the Government fixes the exchange rate at a particular level." A rise in the fixed rate (cheaper domestic currency) is Devaluation; a fall (costlier domestic currency) is Revaluation.
    TermSystemMeaning
    Depreciation / AppreciationFlexible exchange rateMarket-driven change in currency value
    Devaluation / RevaluationFixed exchange rateDeliberate government action to change the fixed rate

    Merits & Demerits

    Fixed rate: needs credibility that the government can maintain it — inadequate reserves can trigger a speculative attack forcing devaluation. Flexible rate: gives the government more freedom, doesn't require large reserves, automatically absorbs BoP surpluses/deficits, and lets a country run independent monetary policy.

    Managed Floating

    A mix of both — also called dirty floating. The exchange rate mostly floats with market forces, but the central bank intervenes at times to moderate excessive movements. Official reserve transactions are therefore NOT zero, unlike a fully flexible system.

    Memory Trick

    Depreciation/Appreciation = the market did it. Devaluation/Revaluation = the government did it. Same direction of change, different system, different word.

    CUET Insight —A favourite pairing question: match "depreciation/appreciation" to flexible rates, and "devaluation/revaluation" to fixed rates.
    NCERT — Fixed Exchange Rate & Managed Floating, p. 94Open in new tab

    06Nominal vs Real Exchange Rate & Purchasing Power Parity

    The rupee-dollar rate you see quoted isn't the whole story — it doesn't say whether goods are actually cheaper or costlier once you account for prices on both sides.

    The PPP numerical is a recurring exercise-style question

    Try this first

    A shirt costs $8 in the US and ₹400 in India. At what rupee-dollar exchange rate would the two prices be exactly equivalent?

    1

    We need the exchange rate at which $8 is worth exactly ₹400.

    2

    Rate = 400 ÷ 8 = Rs 50 per dollar.

    3

    At any rate higher than 50 (say Rs 60), the shirt would cost more in the US (Rs 480) than in India (Rs 400) — all buyers would just buy from India, correcting the rate back down.

    4

    This is the logic of Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) — in the long run, exchange rates adjust so identical goods cost the same regardless of which country's currency you measure them in.

    Nominal vs Real Exchange Rate

    Nominal Exchange Rate: the number of units of domestic currency needed to buy one unit of foreign currency — the rate you see quoted. Real Exchange Rate: the relative price of foreign goods in terms of domestic goods — what actually matters for deciding whether to buy domestic or imported goods.

    Real Exchange Rate

    Real Exchange Rate (R) = Nominal Exchange Rate (e) × (Foreign Price Level ÷ Domestic Price Level)

    If R rises, foreign goods have become relatively more expensive than domestic goods — domestic buyers shift toward domestic goods, and imports tend to fall.

    NCERT's own exercise (worked)

    It takes 1.25 yen to buy one rupee (nominal exchange rate, yen per rupee). Price level in Japan = 3, price level in India = 1.2. Real exchange rate (price of Japanese goods in terms of Indian goods) = 1.25 × (3 ÷ 1.2) ≈ 3.125 — one unit of a representative Japanese good costs about 3.1 units of the equivalent Indian good.

    Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) — long-run theory

    As long as there are no trade barriers (tariffs, quotas), exchange rates should eventually adjust so the same product costs the same, whether measured in rupees, dollars, or yen (aside from transport costs). If domestic prices rise faster than foreign prices, the domestic currency must depreciate to keep goods comparably priced.

    Memory Trick

    Nominal = the number on the board. Real = what it actually buys, once prices are accounted for. PPP is just "real exchange rate should equal 1 in the long run, once markets arbitrage away any gap."

    CUET Insight —Expect a numerical exactly like NCERT's own yen/rupee exercise — compute the real exchange rate given the nominal rate and both countries' price levels.
    NCERT — Nominal vs Real Exchange Rate & Purchasing Power Parity, p. 93Open in new tab

    07Open Economy Income Determination

    Opening the economy to trade doesn't just add exports and imports to the identity — it also shrinks the multiplier itself.

    The open-economy multiplier is always smaller — a favourite "explain why"

    Try this first

    MPC = 0.8 and marginal propensity to import (m) = 0.3. Is the open economy multiplier bigger or smaller than the closed economy multiplier (1÷(1−c)=5)?

    1

    Open economy multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − c + m) = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8 + 0.3) = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.

    2

    2 is much smaller than the closed-economy multiplier of 5.

    3

    Why? Part of every round's re-spent income now leaks abroad as imports (m), on top of the leakage into savings — a bigger total leakage means a smaller multiplier.

    4

    So if autonomous demand rises by 100, a closed economy's output rises by 500, but the same economy, opened up, would only rise by 200.

    National Income Identity, open economy

    Y = C + I + G + X − M  ≡  C + I + G + NX

    NX = Net Exports = X − M. Positive NX = trade surplus; negative NX = trade deficit.

    Import function & Marginal Propensity to Import

    M = M̄ + mY

    m = marginal propensity to import — the fraction of an extra rupee of income spent on imports (0 < m < 1), directly analogous to MPC.

    The Open Economy Multiplier

    Open Economy Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − c + m)

    Since m > 0, this is always smaller than the closed-economy multiplier, 1 ÷ (1 − c).

    NCERT Example 6.2

    c = 0.8, m = 0.3. Closed economy multiplier = 1÷0.2 = 5. Open economy multiplier = 1÷(1−0.8+0.3) = 1÷0.5 = 2. A ₹100 rise in autonomous demand raises output by ₹500 in a closed economy, but only ₹200 once the economy is opened up.

    Effect of a rise in exports vs a rise in imports

    A rise in exports (X) is an increase in demand for domestic output — it raises equilibrium income, just like a rise in G or I. A rise in autonomous import demand (M̄) instead causes equilibrium income to fall, since it's a leakage away from domestic output.

    Memory Trick

    Openness = an extra leak in the bucket. The open economy multiplier formula is just the closed economy one with an extra "+m" in the denominator — more leakage, smaller multiplier, always.

    CUET Insight —Given c and m, expect a "calculate the open economy multiplier" numerical, or an "explain why it's smaller than the closed economy multiplier" conceptual question.
    NCERT — Open Economy Income Determination, p. 97Open in new tab

    01Central Problems of an Economy

    Every economy has the same scarce resources problem as a single family — just at a much bigger scale, and NCERT boils it down to three questions.

    The WHAT / HOW / FOR WHOM framework — asked almost every year

    Try this first

    An economy can produce corn and cotton. Using all its resources on corn alone gives 4 units of corn; using all its resources on cotton alone gives 10 units of cotton. It currently produces 2 units of corn and 7 units of cotton — using all its resources. Is this point on, above, or below the Production Possibility Frontier?

    1

    The PPF shows the maximum combinations obtainable when all resources are fully and efficiently utilised.

    2

    Since the economy is using all its resources to produce this combination, (2 corn, 7 cotton) must lie exactly on the PPF — not below it.

    3

    A point below the PPF (e.g. 1 corn, 5 cotton) would mean resources are underemployed or wasted — achievable, but not efficient.

    4

    A point above the PPF (e.g. 3 corn, 9 cotton) is simply unattainable with the economy's current resources and technology.

    NCERT Definition — The Three Central Problems §1.2

    "Every economy faces the problem of allocating the scarce resources to the production of different possible goods and services and of distributing the produced goods and services among the individuals within the economy. The allocation of scarce resources and the distribution of the final goods and services are the central problems of any economy."
    QuestionWhat it actually asks
    What is produced, and in what quantities?Food vs clothing vs housing? Consumption goods vs investment goods (machines)?
    How are these goods produced?More labour or more machines? Which available technology?
    For whom are these goods produced?Who gets how much? Is a minimum consumption level guaranteed for everyone?

    NCERT's own worked example — the Corn–Cotton Production Possibility Schedule

    PossibilityCornCotton
    A010
    B19
    C27
    D34
    E40

    All resources fully used in each case. The curve joining A–E on a Cotton (y-axis) vs Corn (x-axis) graph is the Production Possibility Frontier — any point on or below it is achievable; any point strictly below represents underemployed or wastefully used resources.

    Opportunity Cost

    Moving along the PPF from A to B, cotton falls from 10 to 9 (a loss of 1) to gain 1 unit of corn. Moving from D to E, cotton falls from 4 to 0 (a loss of 4) for the same 1-unit gain in corn. The cost of an extra unit of one good, measured in terms of the other good given up, is its opportunity cost — and NCERT notes this is also called the economic cost.

    Memory Trick

    WHAT–HOW–FOR WHOM. Every scenario question about an economy's central problem is testing whether you can slot it into one of these three buckets — allocation (what/how) or distribution (for whom).

    Why CUET asks this —PPF numbers-table questions (reading off opportunity cost, identifying a point as attainable/on-frontier/unattainable) are a recurring CUET numerical-reasoning format.
    NCERT — Central Problems of an Economy, p. 2Open in new tab

    02Organisation of Economic Activities

    The same three central problems can be solved two structurally opposite ways — by a planning authority, or by millions of individuals responding to price signals.

    Centrally Planned vs Market Economy — a classic compare-and-contrast MCQ

    Try this first

    Demand for a good rises sharply. In a market economy, what typically happens to its price, and how does that price change end up increasing the good's supply — with no government instruction to any producer?

    1

    Higher demand means buyers are willing to pay more, so the good's price rises.

    2

    The price rise signals to producers that society wants more of this good than is currently being produced.

    3

    Producers, chasing higher profit, respond by increasing production — entirely through self-interest, not central instruction.

    4

    This is exactly what NCERT means by prices achieving "coordination" in a market system — millions of independent decisions align through price signals alone.

    NCERT Definition — A Market §1.3.2

    "A market is a set of arrangements where economic agents can freely exchange their endowments or products with each other." NCERT stresses this is different from the everyday sense of "marketplace" — buyers and sellers need not physically meet; a phone or internet exchange still counts.
    BasisCentrally Planned EconomyMarket Economy
    Who decides what/how/for whomGovernment / central authorityFree interaction of individuals pursuing their own objectives
    Coordination mechanismCentral planning and directivesPrices, mutually agreed by buyers and sellers
    Real-world closest example (NCERT)China, for the major part of the 20th centuryUnited States of America — minimal government role

    Mixed Economy

    "In reality, all economies are mixed economies where some important decisions are taken by the government and the economic activities are by and large conducted through the market." Countries differ only in how much role government plays — India's government role has "been reduced considerably in the last couple of decades" since Independence, per NCERT's own note.

    Memory Trick

    Planned = plan, Market = price. If a scenario mentions a government directive or fixed target, it's centrally planned; if it mentions price movements driving a response, it's market coordination.

    CUET Insight —Watch for questions naming a specific country (USA, China, India) and asking which economic organisation it exemplifies — these are the exact NCERT-cited examples.
    NCERT — Organisation of Economic Activities, p. 4Open in new tab

    03Positive and Normative Economics

    One asks "what actually happens?" — the other asks "what should happen?" — and CUET loves testing whether you can tell the two apart in a single sentence.

    A near-guaranteed "classify this statement" MCQ

    Try this first

    Statement: "A rise in the minimum support price for wheat increases farmers' income." Is this a positive or a normative statement?

    1

    Ask: does the statement describe a factual, testable cause-and-effect, or does it pass judgement on what's desirable?

    2

    "Raising MSP increases farmers' income" is a claim about how the mechanism functions — it can, in principle, be checked against data.

    3

    That makes it a positive statement — it studies how a mechanism functions, not whether it's good or bad.

    4

    Had the statement instead been "the government should raise MSP to help farmers," that value judgement would make it normative.

    NCERT Definition §1.4

    "In positive economic analysis, we study how the different mechanisms function, and in normative economics, we try to understand whether these mechanisms are desirable or not."
    BasisPositive EconomicsNormative Economics
    NatureDescriptive — how it functionsPrescriptive — whether it's desirable
    Testable?Yes, in principle, against factsNo — depends on value judgements
    Typical wording"is," "will," "causes""should," "ought to," "must"

    NCERT's own caution — the line isn't razor-sharp

    "This distinction between positive and normative economic analysis is not a very sharp one. The positive and the normative issues involved in the study of the central economic problems are very closely related to each other and a proper understanding of one is not possible in isolation to the other."

    Memory Trick

    Positive = "what IS," Normative = "what SHOULD BE." Any word like "should," "ought," or "must" is your normative giveaway.

    CUET Insight —Expect one-line statements to classify — don't just look for "should"; a statement predicting an effect ("if X, then Y") is positive even without that word.
    NCERT — Positive and Normative Economics, p. 6Open in new tab

    04Microeconomics and Macroeconomics

    This entire book studies just one of economics' two traditional branches — knowing exactly where the dividing line falls sets up everything that follows.

    The chapter's closing distinction — and this book's own scope statement

    Try this first

    "The unemployment rate in the country rose to 7.8% this quarter." Is this a microeconomic or macroeconomic statement?

    1

    Ask: is this about one individual market/agent, or about the economy's aggregate performance?

    2

    "The unemployment rate in the country" is an aggregate measure — it doesn't refer to any single firm's or worker's decision.

    3

    Aggregate measures like total output, employment, and the price level are exactly what macroeconomics studies.

    4

    So this is macroeconomic — had the statement been about one firm's hiring decision, it would be microeconomic instead.

    NCERT Definition §1.5

    "In microeconomics, we study the behaviour of individual economic agents in the markets for different goods and services and try to figure out how prices and quantities of goods and services are determined... In macroeconomics... we try to get an understanding of the economy as a whole by focusing our attention on aggregate measures such as total output, employment and aggregate price level."
    BasisMicroeconomicsMacroeconomics
    ScopeIndividual markets, agents, prices, quantitiesThe economy as a whole — aggregates
    Sample questionsHow is the price of one commodity determined?What is total output? Is unemployment rising? Why do prices rise overall?

    This book's own scope

    NCERT states its "Plan of the Book" plainly: "This book is meant to introduce you to the basic ideas in microeconomics... we will focus on the behaviour of the individual consumers and producers of a single commodity and try to analyse how the price and the quantity is determined in the market for a single commodity." That single-commodity focus is exactly what Chapters 2–5 of this course build, step by step.

    Memory Trick

    Micro = one market's price and quantity. Macro = the whole economy's aggregates. If a number is "total," "aggregate," or "the economy's," it's macro; if it's about one good or one agent, it's micro.

    Why CUET asks this —This exact distinction is tested from both the Microeconomics and Macroeconomics books' own opening chapters — expect it to reappear, sometimes word-for-word, across both halves of the syllabus.
    NCERT — Microeconomics and Macroeconomics, p. 6Open in new tab

    01Cardinal Utility Analysis

    The oldest way to explain why demand curves slope down — assume satisfaction can literally be counted in numbers, then watch each extra unit deliver less of it.

    TU/MU numerical tables are a guaranteed calculation question

    Try this first

    Consuming 4 bananas gives a consumer 24 units of total utility. Consuming 5 bananas gives 24 units of total utility too. What is the marginal utility of the 5th banana, and what does that tell you?

    1

    Marginal utility of the nth unit = TUn − TUn−1.

    2

    MU5 = TU5 − TU4 = 24 − 24 = 0.

    3

    MU turning zero exactly where TU stops rising is not a coincidence — TU is the running sum of all MUs, so TU can only be unchanged when the newest MU added is zero.

    4

    Beyond this point, if TU were to fall, MU would turn negative — the consumer is now so full that one more unit actively reduces satisfaction.

    NCERT Definitions §2.1.1

    "Total Utility of a fixed quantity of a commodity (TU) is the total satisfaction derived from consuming the given amount of some commodity x." "Marginal Utility (MU) is the change in total utility due to consumption of one additional unit of a commodity."

    The TU–MU Formulas

    MUn = TUn − TUn−1
    TUn = MU1 + MU2 + … + MUn

    NCERT's own Table 2.1 — worked TU/MU schedule

    UnitsTotal UtilityMarginal Utility
    11212
    2186
    3224
    4242
    5240
    622−2

    MU keeps falling (12→6→4→2→0→−2) even as TU rises then falls — exactly the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility in action.

    Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility → the demand curve

    "Marginal utility from consuming each additional unit of a commodity declines as its consumption increases, while keeping consumption of other commodities constant." Since the consumer won't pay as much for a unit worth less to her, each additional unit is bought only at a lower price — this is cardinal analysis's explanation for why demand curves slope downward. At ₹40/unit, if demand was 5 units, the 6th unit — worth less than the 5th — will only be bought if price drops below ₹40.

    Memory Trick

    TU is the running total; MU is today's addition. MU = 0 exactly where TU peaks; MU turns negative exactly where TU starts falling.

    Why CUET asks this —Fill-in-the-table MU/TU questions and "identify diminishing MU" scenarios are recurring CUET numerical items.
    NCERT — Cardinal Utility Analysis, p. 9Open in new tab

    02Ordinal Utility & Indifference Curves

    Instead of counting satisfaction in numbers, this approach just asks the consumer to rank bundles — "I like this combination as much as that one" is all it needs.

    IC properties + MRS are THE most-tested concept in this chapter

    Try this first

    Going from combination A to B, a consumer gives up 3 mangoes to gain 1 banana. Going from B to C, she gives up only 2 mangoes for 1 more banana. What law does this illustrate, and why does it happen?

    1

    The mangoes sacrificed per extra banana is the Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS) — here it falls from 3:1 to 2:1.

    2

    A falling MRS as bananas increase is the Law of Diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution.

    3

    Why it happens: as bananas pile up, MU from each extra banana falls; as mangoes get scarcer, MU from mangoes rises — so the consumer needs less and less mango-compensation per extra banana.

    4

    This diminishing MRS is exactly what makes an indifference curve convex to the origin — its most common, textbook shape.

    NCERT Definitions §2.1.2

    "A curve joining all points representing bundles among which the consumer is indifferent is called an indifference curve." "MRS is simply the rate at which the consumer will substitute bananas for mangoes, so that her total utility remains constant."

    NCERT's own Table 2.2 — diminishing MRS

    CombinationBananasMangoesMRS
    A115—
    B2123:1
    C3102:1
    D491:1

    Perfect Substitutes — the exception

    For goods like five-rupee coins and five-rupee notes, MRS does not diminish — it stays constant (e.g. 1:1 throughout NCERT's Table 2.3). Their indifference curve is a straight line, not convex.

    #Property of an Indifference CurveWhy
    1Slopes downward, left to rightMore of one good must be offset by less of the other to keep utility constant
    2Higher IC = greater utilityPositive MU means more of a good always raises satisfaction (monotonic preferences)
    3Two ICs never intersectIntersection implies contradictory utility rankings — a logical impossibility

    Monotonic Preferences & the Indifference Map

    Preferences are monotonic if, between two bundles, the one with more of at least one good and no less of the other is always preferred. A consumer's full set of indifference curves is her indifference map — curves further from the origin represent higher satisfaction.

    Memory Trick

    Convex IC = diminishing MRS = normal goods. Straight-line IC = constant MRS = perfect substitutes.

    CUET Insight —Expect a "why can't two indifference curves intersect" reasoning question, or an MRS calculation from a bundle table.
    NCERT — Ordinal Utility & Indifference Curves, p. 11Open in new tab

    03Budget Set & Budget Line

    Preferences alone don't decide what a consumer buys — she also needs to be able to afford it. The budget line draws the exact boundary of what's affordable.

    Slope, intercepts, and shift direction are a formula-heavy favourite

    Try this first

    A consumer has ₹20. Both bananas and mangoes cost ₹5 each and are sold only in whole units. Can she afford the bundle (3, 3) — 3 bananas and 3 mangoes?

    1

    Cost of (3,3) = 5(3) + 5(3) = ₹15 + ₹15 = ₹30.

    2

    Her income is only ₹20, and ₹30 > ₹20.

    3

    So (3,3) violates the budget constraint p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ ≤ M and is not in her budget set.

    4

    NCERT's own example confirms this directly — (3,3) and (4,5) are explicitly named as bundles this exact consumer cannot afford.

    NCERT Definitions §2.2.1

    "The set of bundles available to the consumer is called the budget set... the collection of all bundles that the consumer can buy with her income at the prevailing market prices." The line p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ = M, consisting of bundles costing exactly M, "is called the budget line."

    The Core Formulas

    Budget constraint: p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ ≤ M
    Budget line: p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ = M
    Horizontal intercept = M/p₁   (all income on good 1)
    Vertical intercept = M/p₂   (all income on good 2)
    Slope of budget line = −p₁/p₂

    Why the slope is the price ratio

    The absolute value of the slope, p₁/p₂, is the rate at which the market lets the consumer substitute good 1 for good 2 — give up p₁/p₂ units of good 2 to buy one more unit of good 1, while spending exactly the same total.

    ChangeEffect on Budget Line
    Income rises (M' > M), prices constantParallel outward shift (both intercepts increase, slope unchanged)
    Income falls (M' < M), prices constantParallel inward shift (both intercepts decrease, slope unchanged)
    Price of good 1 rises, M & p₂ constantLine pivots inward around the vertical intercept — steeper, horizontal intercept falls
    Price of good 1 falls, M & p₂ constantLine pivots outward around the vertical intercept — flatter, horizontal intercept rises

    Memory Trick

    Income change → parallel shift (slope same). Price change → pivot (slope changes). Whichever good's price didn't change keeps its own intercept fixed — the line pivots around that axis.

    Why CUET asks this —"Write the budget line equation and find intercepts/slope" from given prices and income is one of NCERT's own exercise formats, reused almost verbatim in CUET papers.
    NCERT — Budget Set & Budget Line, p. 15Open in new tab

    04Consumer's Equilibrium (Optimal Choice)

    Two curves, one tangency point — this is where "what the consumer wants" (indifference curves) meets "what she can afford" (the budget line).

    The MRS = Price Ratio condition is asked almost every single year

    Try this first

    At a consumer's current bundle, her MRS of bananas for mangoes is 2, but both goods have the same price (so the price ratio is 1). Is she at her optimum? If not, what should she do?

    1

    MRS = 2 means she's willing to give up 2 mangoes for 1 extra banana.

    2

    Price ratio = 1 means the market only requires her to give up 1 mango for 1 extra banana.

    3

    Since MRS > price ratio, buying an extra banana costs her less (in mangoes) than she's willing to pay — she gains by buying more bananas.

    4

    She is not at equilibrium; she should keep substituting bananas for mangoes until MRS falls to equal the price ratio (=1).

    NCERT's Equilibrium Condition §2.3

    "The optimum bundle of the consumer is located at the point where the budget line is tangent to one of the indifference curves." At that point, "the absolute value of the slope of the indifference curve (MRS) and that of the budget line (price ratio) are same."

    The Equilibrium Condition

    MRS = Price Ratio = p₁/p₂

    Equivalently: the consumer is on the highest attainable indifference curve given her budget set.

    CaseWhat it meansConsumer's response
    MRS > price ratioWilling to give up more of good 2 than the market requiresBuy more of good 1 (move along IC toward equilibrium)
    MRS < price ratioNot willing to give up as much as the market requiresBuy less of good 1, more of good 2
    MRS = price ratioExactly balancedConsumer is at equilibrium — no incentive to move

    Two conditions, restated together

    A rational, monotonic-preference consumer's optimum bundle must (1) lie exactly on the budget line — not below it (unspent income could buy more, which monotonic preferences always prefer) — and (2) be the point of tangency with the highest reachable indifference curve, since any other point on the budget line sits on a lower IC and is therefore inferior.

    Memory Trick

    Tangency = equilibrium. Where the IC just touches (not crosses) the budget line, the "rate I want to trade" (MRS) exactly equals the "rate the market lets me trade" (price ratio).

    Why CUET asks this —Diagram-based MCQs showing a tangency point, or "MRS vs price ratio, which direction will the consumer move" reasoning questions, are a recurring format.
    NCERT — Consumer's Equilibrium, p. 19Open in new tab

    05Price Effect & Derivation of the Demand Curve

    Drop the price of one good, keep everything else fixed, and trace where the new equilibrium lands — do this repeatedly and you've just drawn the demand curve.

    Connects indifference-curve theory directly to the demand curve you already know

    Try this first

    The price of bananas drops, with mango price and income unchanged. What happens to the budget line, and why does this typically increase the consumer's optimal quantity of bananas?

    1

    A lower price of bananas flattens the budget line and pushes its horizontal intercept (M/p₁) further out — more bananas are now affordable at every level of mango consumption.

    2

    The consumer's new tangency point (new equilibrium) generally lands on a higher indifference curve.

    3

    At this new equilibrium, she typically consumes more bananas than before.

    4

    Plotting each (price, quantity-of-bananas) pair from these successive equilibria — as price drops further and further — traces out the demand curve for bananas, which slopes downward.

    NCERT Definition — Demand Function §2.4.1

    "The consumer's demand function for a good gives the amount of the good that the consumer chooses at different levels of its price when the other things remain unchanged." Symbolically, X = f(P).

    Two reasons a price drop raises demand — Substitution + Income effects

    Substitution effect: as bananas get relatively cheaper, the consumer substitutes bananas for mangoes to reach the same satisfaction level more cheaply — raising banana demand. Income effect: a lower price also raises real purchasing power, which (for a normal good) further raises demand. Both effects push banana demand up when bananas get cheaper — reinforcing the negative slope of the demand curve.

    Linear Demand Function

    d(p) = a − bp,   for 0 ≤ p ≤ a/b
    d(p) = 0,   for p > a/b

    a = vertical (price) intercept; −b = slope; demand falls by b units for every unit rise in price.

    Law of Demand §2.4.2

    "Other things being equal, there is a negative relation between demand for a commodity and its price."

    Memory Trick

    Every point on the demand curve is really a tangency point in disguise — one equilibrium bundle per price, replotted onto a Price–Quantity graph.

    CUET Insight —Be ready to identify which of substitution/income effect is being described in a given scenario — this distinction becomes the entire subject of the next two topics.
    NCERT — Price Effect & Derivation of Demand Curve, p. 21Open in new tab

    06Income Effect, Normal & Inferior Goods

    Instead of asking "what if price changes," this topic asks "what if the consumer just got richer" — and the answer isn't always "buy more."

    The Giffen good trap — a classic distractor in MCQs

    Try this first

    A student's income rises, and she starts buying fewer coarse cereals — switching to better quality rice instead. What kind of good are coarse cereals for her, and would this always be true regardless of her income level?

    1

    Demand for coarse cereals fell when income rose — moving in the opposite direction of income.

    2

    A good whose demand moves opposite to income is an inferior good.

    3

    NCERT explicitly names low-quality food items like coarse cereals as inferior-good examples.

    4

    But this isn't fixed forever: at very low income, coarse cereals can behave as a normal good (demand rises with income) — only past some income threshold does she switch away to better cereals, making it inferior. The same good can be normal at one income range and inferior at another.

    NCERT Definitions §2.4.3

    "For most goods, the quantity that a consumer chooses, increases as the consumer's income increases... Such goods are called normal goods." "There are some goods the demands for which move in the opposite direction of the income of the consumer. Such goods are called inferior goods."
    Good typeDemand vs IncomeEffect on Demand Curve when income rises
    Normal goodMoves in the same direction as incomeShifts rightward
    Inferior goodMoves in the opposite direction to incomeShifts leftward

    The Giffen Good — when income effect overpowers substitution effect

    Normally, substitution and income effects both push demand the same way when price falls. But for some inferior goods, a price drop raises real income enough that the consumer actually buys less of it (switching to a preferred substitute instead) — if this income effect is stronger than the substitution effect, demand moves in the same direction as price. Such a good is called a Giffen good.

    Memory Trick

    Normal = income and demand move together. Inferior = they move apart. Giffen = an inferior good so extreme that even price and demand move together.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a scenario-based classification question (normal vs inferior), and watch for Giffen good as a distractor option even when the scenario just describes an ordinary inferior good.
    NCERT — Income Effect, Normal & Inferior Goods, p. 24Open in new tab

    07Substitution Effect, Substitutes & Complements

    Two goods can be linked to each other in exactly opposite ways — bought together, or bought instead of each other — and CUET wants you to tell which is which instantly.

    Tea-sugar-coffee is NCERT's own running example — expect it verbatim

    Try this first

    The price of coffee rises sharply. What is likely to happen to the demand for tea, and what does this tell you about the relationship between tea and coffee?

    1

    As coffee gets pricier, consumers look for a cheaper alternative that serves a similar purpose.

    2

    Tea fills that role, so consumption of tea is likely to go up.

    3

    Demand for tea moved in the same direction as the price of coffee — the defining test for substitutes.

    4

    Had tea and coffee instead been used together (like tea and sugar), a price rise in one would have reduced demand for the other — the complements test.

    NCERT's Own Examples §2.4.4

    "Goods which are consumed together are called complementary goods" — e.g. tea and sugar, shoes and socks, pen and ink. "The demand for a good usually moves in the direction of the price of its substitutes" — e.g. tea and coffee.
    BasisSubstitutesComplements
    Consumption patternUsed instead of each otherUsed together
    Demand moves with the OTHER good's priceSame directionOpposite direction
    NCERT examplesTea and coffeeTea and sugar; shoes and socks; pen and ink

    Effect on the demand curve

    An increase in the price of a substitute good shifts a good's demand curve rightward. An increase in the price of a complementary good shifts it leftward.

    Memory Trick

    Substitutes move together (price up → other's demand up). Complements move apart (price up → other's demand down).

    CUET Insight —A one-line scenario naming a price change in one good, asking the effect on a related good's demand, is the standard format here.
    NCERT — Substitutes & Complements, p. 25Open in new tab

    08Market Demand & Shifts vs Movements

    One individual's demand curve is only half the story — add up every consumer in the market, and separately, learn to tell "moving along a curve" apart from "the whole curve relocating."

    "Movement vs Shift" is one of the single most-repeated CUET distinctions

    Try this first

    Two consumers have demand functions d₁(p) = 10 − p and d₂(p) = 15 − p. What is the market demand at any price p ≤ 10?

    1

    Market demand at a given price = sum of every individual consumer's demand at that same price — this is called horizontal summation.

    2

    Add the two demand functions directly: (10 − p) + (15 − p) = 25 − 2p.

    3

    This holds only for p ≤ 10, since consumer 1's demand drops to 0 beyond that price.

    4

    For 10 < p ≤ 15, only consumer 2 is still buying, so market demand is just 15 − p; beyond p = 15, market demand is 0 — exactly NCERT's own worked example.

    NCERT Definition §2.5

    "The market demand for a good at a particular price is the total demand of all consumers taken together." Graphically, the market demand curve is derived "by adding up the individual demand curves horizontally... called horizontal summation."
    BasisMovement Along the Demand CurveShift of the Demand Curve
    Caused byA change in the good's own priceA change in anything else — income, related goods' prices, tastes
    What happensSame curve, different point on itAn entirely new curve, parallel-shifted
    Rightward/leftward driversN/A — it's the same curveRight: income↑ (normal good), substitute price↑, favourable taste shift. Left: the opposite of each.

    NCERT's own seasonal example

    The demand curve for ice-creams shifts rightward in summer (preferences favour it more). A health scare about cold drinks shifts that demand curve leftward (preferences turn unfavourable) — both are taste-driven shifts, with the good's own price unchanged throughout.

    Memory Trick

    Its OWN price changing = movement ALONG. Anything else changing = the curve SHIFTS.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a numerical market-demand-summation question exactly like NCERT's own worked example, plus a classification question ("is this a shift or a movement") from a one-line scenario.
    NCERT — Market Demand & Shifts vs Movements, p. 26Open in new tab

    09Price Elasticity of Demand

    Knowing demand falls when price rises isn't enough — CUET wants you to measure exactly HOW MUCH it falls, as a clean percentage-based number.

    The single most numerically-tested formula in this entire chapter

    Try this first

    An individual buys 15 bananas at ₹5 each. When the price rises to ₹7, she buys only 12. Calculate the price elasticity of demand.

    1

    % change in quantity = (12 − 15)/15 × 100 = −20%.

    2

    % change in price = (7 − 5)/5 × 100 = +40%.

    3

    eD = −20% ÷ 40% = −0.5 — by convention we quote the absolute value, so eD = 0.5.

    4

    Since 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic — bananas aren't very responsive to this price change. This is NCERT's own Example 2.2, worked exactly this way.

    NCERT Definition §2.6

    "Price elasticity of demand for a good is defined as the percentage change in demand for the good divided by the percentage change in its price."

    The Elasticity Formula

    eD = (%Δ Quantity Demanded) ÷ (%Δ Price) = (ΔQ/Q ÷ ΔP/P)

    eD is technically negative (demand falls as price rises), but by convention we always quote its absolute value.

    Value of eDClassificationTypical good
    eD < 1InelasticEssentials / necessities (e.g. food)
    eD > 1ElasticLuxuries
    eD = 1Unitary elastic—
    eD = 0 (vertical demand curve)Perfectly inelasticQuantity fixed regardless of price
    eD = ∞ (horizontal demand curve)Perfectly elasticPrice fixed regardless of quantity

    Elasticity varies along a straight-line demand curve

    For a linear demand curve q = a − bp: elasticity is 0 at p = 0 (where the curve meets the quantity axis), ∞ at q = 0 (where it meets the price axis), and exactly 1 at the curve's midpoint (p = a/2b). At any point above the midpoint (higher price), elasticity > 1; below the midpoint, elasticity < 1.

    Memory Trick

    Vertical demand curve = perfectly inelastic (0). Horizontal = perfectly elastic (∞). Straight-line's own midpoint = exactly 1.

    Why CUET asks this —Direct numerical elasticity calculations from a price-quantity pair (exactly like the try-first box above) appear almost every year.
    NCERT — Price Elasticity of Demand, p. 27Open in new tab

    10Elasticity, Expenditure & its Determinants

    Elasticity isn't just an abstract number — it directly decides whether a price hike makes a seller richer or poorer, and CUET tests that link constantly.

    Elasticity-expenditure direction rule — a guaranteed reasoning MCQ

    Try this first

    A seller raises the price of a good by 10%, and as a result, demand for it falls by 12%. Does the seller's total revenue (expenditure by buyers) rise or fall — and is this good elastic or inelastic?

    1

    %Δ quantity (12%) > %Δ price (10%), so eD = 12/10 = 1.2 > 1 — the good is price elastic.

    2

    Expenditure = Price × Quantity. Price rose only 10% but quantity fell a bigger 12%.

    3

    The bigger percentage fall in quantity dominates, so total expenditure falls.

    4

    General rule confirmed: when a good is elastic, price and expenditure move in opposite directions — exactly NCERT's own Table 2.5, row 2.

    NCERT's Rule §2.6.3

    "The expenditure on the good would change in the opposite direction as the price change if and only if... the good is price-elastic... would change in the same direction as the price change if and only if... the good is price inelastic... would remain unchanged if and only if... unit-elastic."
    ElasticityPrice rises →Price falls →
    Elastic (eD > 1)Expenditure fallsExpenditure rises
    Inelastic (eD < 1)Expenditure risesExpenditure falls
    Unitary elastic (eD = 1)Expenditure unchangedExpenditure unchanged

    What determines whether a good is elastic or inelastic — NCERT's two factors

    Nature of the good: necessities (like food) tend to be inelastic; luxuries tend to be elastic. Availability of close substitutes: if close substitutes exist (e.g. one variety of pulses for another), demand is more elastic — consumers can easily switch away from a price rise. Without close substitutes, demand tends to be inelastic.

    Rectangular Hyperbola — the unit-elastic demand curve

    A demand curve of the form pq = e (a constant) is a rectangular hyperbola — expenditure is exactly the same (= e) at every single point on it, since |eD| = 1 throughout.

    Memory Trick

    Elastic = expenditure runs opposite to price. Inelastic = expenditure runs with price. Unitary = expenditure doesn't move at all.

    Why CUET asks this —"Price rises/falls by X%, quantity changes by Y% — what happens to expenditure and what is the elasticity" is a direct, frequent NCERT-exercise-style question (see Q22–27 of this chapter's own exercises).
    NCERT — Elasticity, Expenditure & its Determinants, p. 31Open in new tab

    01Production Function & Short Run vs Long Run

    Every firm's production boils down to one question: what's the MAXIMUM output obtainable from a given set of inputs — and how much freedom does the firm have to change those inputs?

    The isoquant concept mirrors indifference curves from Chapter 2

    Try this first

    A firm's production table shows that 4 units of labour + 1 unit of capital, 2 labour + 2 capital, and 1 labour + 4 capital all produce exactly 10 units of output. What is the curve joining these three input combinations called?

    1

    All three combinations yield the same maximum output level (10 units) using different input mixes.

    2

    A curve joining all input combinations that yield the same output level is called an isoquant.

    3

    This is structurally identical to an indifference curve from Chapter 2 — except it ranks input combinations by output, not bundles by utility.

    4

    Since more of one input lets the firm use less of the other for the same output, isoquants — like indifference curves — are negatively sloped.

    NCERT Definition — Production Function §3.1

    "The production function of a firm is a relationship between inputs used and output produced by the firm. For various quantities of inputs used, it gives the maximum quantity of output that can be produced."

    The Two-Factor Production Function

    q = f(L, K)

    where L = labour, K = capital, q = maximum output obtainable from that combination. Defined for a given technology — better technology creates an entirely new production function.

    NCERT's own Table 3.1 (excerpt) — reading off an isoquant

    Labour \ Capital124
    11310
    231024
    4102450

    Reading the diagonal: (4L,1K), (2L,2K), and (1L,4K) all yield exactly 10 units — three points on the same q=10 isoquant.

    BasisShort RunLong Run
    Fixed factorAt least one factor is fixedNo fixed factor — all can be varied
    Variable factorOnly the non-fixed factor can changeBoth/all factors can change simultaneously
    Defined byWhether inputs can be varied — NOT a fixed time length like "days" or "months"Same criterion, opposite answer

    Memory Trick

    Isoquant = "equal quantity" of output. Indifference curve = "equal quantity" of utility. Same shape, same logic, different axis meaning.

    CUET Insight —Watch for a trick question implying short run/long run is about calendar time — NCERT explicitly says it is NOT defined by days/months/years, only by whether all inputs can vary.
    NCERT — Production Function & Short/Long Run, p. 37Open in new tab

    02Total, Average and Marginal Product

    Vary just one input, freeze the rest — and three related numbers (TP, AP, MP) tell you everything about how that one input contributes to output.

    A guaranteed fill-in-the-table calculation question

    Try this first

    With capital fixed, 1 unit of labour produces 10 units of output; 2 units of labour produce 24 units. What is the Marginal Product of the 2nd unit of labour, and the Average Product at 2 units of labour?

    1

    MPL = TP at 2 units − TP at 1 unit = 24 − 10 = 14.

    2

    APL at 2 units = TP ÷ L = 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

    3

    Notice MP (14) is greater than AP (12) here — exactly NCERT's Table 3.2 numbers.

    4

    Whenever MP > AP, the AP must still be rising — pulling the average up.

    NCERT Definitions §3.3

    "Total Product (TP)... this relationship between the variable input and output, keeping all other inputs constant." "Average product is defined as the output per unit of variable input." "Marginal product of an input is defined as the change in output per unit of change in the input when all other inputs are held constant."

    The Formulas

    APL = TPL / L
    MPL = ΔTPL / ΔL = (TP at L units) − (TP at L−1 units)

    Marginal product is undefined at zero input level (no preceding unit to subtract). For any level, the sum of all marginal products up to that level equals total product.

    NCERT's own Table 3.2 (capital fixed at 4 units)

    LabourTPMPLAPL
    1101010
    2241412
    3401613.33
    4501012.5
    556611.2
    65719.5

    Memory Trick

    AP is the average of all MPs up to that point. Just like a batting average: a new innings above your current average pulls the average UP; below it pulls the average DOWN.

    Why CUET asks this —Given a partial TP/MP/AP table, filling in the missing values (exactly like NCERT's Table 3.2) is one of the most common numerical formats in this chapter.
    NCERT — Total, Average and Marginal Product, p. 39Open in new tab

    03Law of Diminishing Marginal Product & Law of Variable Proportions

    Add more and more workers to a fixed plot of land, and at some point each new worker starts adding less than the one before — this is one of microeconomics' most famous "laws."

    The land-gets-"crowded" reasoning is NCERT's own explanation, often asked directly

    Try this first

    A farmer has a fixed 4 hectares of land. Hiring the 4th worker onto this land starts adding LESS extra output than the 3rd worker did. Why does this happen, in NCERT's own reasoning?

    1

    With few workers, each has "too much land" — adding a worker makes the labour-to-land factor proportion more suitable, so MP initially rises.

    2

    By the 4th worker, the land starts getting "crowded" — each worker now has insufficient land to work efficiently.

    3

    So the extra output added by each additional worker becomes proportionally less — MP starts falling.

    4

    This rise-then-fall pattern of MP, driven purely by changing factor proportions (since land is fixed), is the Law of Variable Proportions — also called the Law of Diminishing Marginal Product.

    NCERT Definition §3.4

    "Law of variable proportions say that the marginal product of a factor input initially rises with its employment level. But after reaching a certain level of employment, it starts falling."

    Factor Proportions — the WHY behind the law

    "Factor proportions represent the ratio in which the two inputs are combined to produce output." As one factor is held fixed and the other keeps rising, factor proportions keep changing — first becoming more suitable (MP rises), then too crowded with the variable input (MP falls).

    The Marginal Product Formula, restated

    MPL = (TP at L units) − (TP at L−1 unit)

    Worked example from NCERT: TP goes from 10 (at L=1) to 24 (at L=2) → MP of the 2nd unit of labour = 24 − 10 = 14.

    Memory Trick

    Rises first (factor proportions improve), then falls (input gets "crowded"). This is why every MP curve is an inverse-U, never a straight line.

    CUET Insight —Expect a scenario (like the farmer/land example) asking you to identify WHY marginal product is falling — the answer is always "the fixed factor is getting crowded relative to the variable factor."
    NCERT — Law of Diminishing Marginal Product, p. 40Open in new tab

    04Shapes of the TP, AP and MP Curves

    Three curves, one consistent geometric rule: wherever MP crosses AP, it always crosses from above — never the other way round.

    "MP cuts AP at its maximum, from above" — a guaranteed diagram-reasoning MCQ

    Try this first

    At a given level of labour employment, MP is greater than AP. Is AP rising, falling, or at its maximum at this point?

    1

    AP is the running average of all MPs so far — just like a batting average.

    2

    If the newest MP (this unit's contribution) is above the current average, it must pull the average up.

    3

    So MP > AP means AP must be rising.

    4

    By the same logic, AP is at its maximum exactly where MP = AP — the point where MP crosses AP from above.

    NCERT's Shape Rules §3.5

    "The MP curve therefore, looks like an inverse 'U'-shaped curve." "As long as the AP increases, it must be the case that MP is greater than AP... when AP falls, MP has to be less than AP. It follows that MP curve cuts AP curve from above at its maximum."
    CurveShapeWhy
    Total Product (TP)Rises throughout (in the relevant range), rate of rise changesMore of the variable input, all else constant, raises output
    Marginal Product (MP)Inverse-U shapedRises then falls per the Law of Variable Proportions
    Average Product (AP)Inverse-U shaped, but peaks after MP and falls more gentlyAP is the running average — reacts more slowly than MP itself

    The single geometric rule to remember

    MP > AP ⟹ AP rising. MP < AP ⟹ AP falling. MP = AP ⟹ AP at its maximum. This is exactly why the MP curve always cuts the AP curve from above, at AP's peak — never from below.

    Memory Trick

    Above the average pulls it up; below the average pulls it down; equal to it means it's flat (at the peak). Applies to MP–AP here, and later to MC–AC in costs.

    Why CUET asks this —Diagram-based questions showing MP and AP curves crossing, asking to identify the point/shape/direction, are extremely common — and the exact same MP–AP logic reappears for MC–AC in the Costs topics ahead.
    NCERT — Shapes of TP, AP and MP Curves, p. 41Open in new tab

    05Returns to Scale

    The Law of Variable Proportions asks "what if I add more of ONE input?" Returns to Scale asks the long-run question instead: "what if I scale up EVERY input together?"

    The doubling-inputs test (CRS/IRS/DRS) is a guaranteed numerical question

    Try this first

    A firm doubles both its labour and capital. As a result, its output increases from 100 units to 250 units. Does this production function exhibit CRS, IRS, or DRS?

    1

    Inputs were scaled up by a factor of 2 (doubled).

    2

    If output had also exactly doubled (to 200), that would be Constant Returns to Scale.

    3

    Output actually rose to 250 — more than double the original 100.

    4

    Output increased by a larger proportion than inputs — this is Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS).

    NCERT Definitions §3.6

    "When a proportional increase in all inputs results in an increase in output by the same proportion, the production function is said to display Constant returns to scale (CRS)." Increasing Returns to Scale: output rises by a larger proportion. Decreasing Returns to Scale: output rises by a smaller proportion.

    The Mathematical Test

    For q = f(x₁, x₂), scale both inputs by t (t > 1):
