    The government sells a small portion of equity in a Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) to the public, while retaining majority ownership and control. Is this privatisation or disinvestment?

    1

    Privatisation, per NCERT, means "shedding of the ownership or management" of a government enterprise — a change in who CONTROLS it.

    2

    Here, the government still holds majority ownership and management control — nothing has actually shifted.

    3

    Selling off PART of the equity of a PSE to the public, specifically, is called disinvestment.

    4

    So this scenario is disinvestment, not (necessarily) privatisation — the two terms are related but not identical.

    NCERT Definitions §3.4

    "Privatisation... implies shedding of the ownership or management of a government owned enterprise." "Privatisation of the public sector enterprises by selling off part of the equity of PSEs to the public is known as disinvestment."
    MechanismWhat happens
    Withdrawal of government ownership/managementOne route to privatisation
    Outright sale of PSEAnother route to privatisation
    DisinvestmentSelling off PART of a PSE's equity to the public

    Navratnas, Maharatnas, Miniratnas

    Rather than privatise every PSE, the government identified select ones and granted them greater financial, managerial and operational autonomy — improving efficiency and competitiveness in the liberalised global environment, without full ownership change. Examples: Indian Oil Corporation (Maharatna).

    Disinvestment target vs actual (NCERT examples)Amount
    1991-92 target₹2,500 crore
    1991-92 actual₹3,040 crore more than target
    2022-23 mobilised≈₹46,000 crore

    Critics' concerns about disinvestment

    PSE assets are often undervalued and sold cheaply to private buyers — a real loss to the government. Proceeds are frequently used to plug government revenue shortfalls rather than reinvested into PSE development or social infrastructure.

    Memory Trick

    Privatisation = ownership/control actually changes hands. Disinvestment = selling PART of the equity — control may not change at all.

    Why CUET asks this —"Distinguish between Strategic and Minority sale" is NCERT's own exact exercise wording — anchor your answer to the privatisation-vs-disinvestment distinction above (does ownership/control actually change, or just a portion of equity).
    NCERT — Privatisation & Disinvestment, p. 44Open in new tab

    05Globalisation — Outsourcing & the WTO

    Globalisation isn't just "more trade" — NCERT frames it as creating a borderless world where events far away directly affect people at home, and outsourcing is its clearest everyday example.

    WTO's founding year and its predecessor (GATT) are guaranteed fact-recall

    Try this first

    A US company hires an Indian firm to handle its customer service calls (a "BPO"/call centre) instead of running this department in-house in America. What NCERT term describes this, and why has it intensified recently?

    1

    Hiring an external source — often in another country — for a service previously provided in-house is called outsourcing.

    2

    NCERT names voice-based business processes (BPO/call centres), record keeping, accountancy, banking, even teaching as outsourced services.

    3

    This intensified because of fast communication modes — specifically the growth of Information Technology (IT).

    4

    India's skilled, English-speaking, relatively cheap manpower made it a top global outsourcing destination in the post-reform period.

    NCERT Definitions §3.5

    "Globalisation... is generally understood to mean integration of the economy of the country with the world economy... turning the world into one whole or creating a borderless world." "The WTO was founded in 1995 as the successor organisation to the General Agreement on Trade and Tariff (GATT). GATT was established in 1948 with 23 countries."
    TermDetail
    GATTEstablished 1948, 23 founding countries
    WTOFounded 1995, successor to GATT
    WTO's purposeEstablish a rule-based trade regime; ensure optimum use of world resources; cover trade in goods AND services

    A genuine two-sided debate on WTO membership

    Critics argue major trade volume occurs among developed nations anyway, and developing countries are "forced to open their markets" while denied equal access to developed markets — e.g. developed countries still restrict textile imports from India/China even after India removed its own quota restrictions.

    Real Indian companies "going global" (NCERT's own examples)

    ONGC Videsh operates in 16 countries; Tata Steel operates in 26 countries, sells in 50; HCL Technologies has offices in 31 countries with ~15,000 staff abroad — globalisation working in both directions, not just inbound.

    Memory Trick

    GATT (1948) → WTO (1995). Outsourcing is globalisation's most visible everyday face — and India's IT growth is exactly why it became the world's outsourcing hub.

    Why CUET asks this —"What advantages make India a favourite outsourcing destination?" and "why is WTO membership necessary?" are both NCERT's own verbatim exercise questions.
    NCERT — Globalisation — Outsourcing & the WTO, p. 45Open in new tab

    06Indian Economy During Reforms — GDP Growth by Sector

    Three decades of reform produced one clear, consistent pattern in the growth data — and it's not the sector most people would guess.

    "GDP growth is mainly driven by the service sector" is this topic's single most-quoted line

    Try this first

    Post-1991, India's overall GDP growth rate rose sharply — but which single sector's growth does NCERT say is mainly DRIVING this rise?

    1

    Agriculture's growth rate declined during the reform period.

    2

    Industry's growth fluctuated — no consistent trend.

    3

    The service sector is the one sector that consistently "gone up" and stayed higher than overall GDP growth (2007-22).

    4

    NCERT's direct conclusion: "GDP growth is mainly driven by growth in the service sector."

    NCERT's Own Words §3.6

    "The growth of GDP increased from 5.6 per cent during 1980-91 to 9.4 per cent during 2021-22. During the reform period, the growth of agriculture has declined. While the industrial sector reported fluctuation, the growth of the service sector has gone up."

    NCERT's own Table 3.1 — Growth of GDP and Major Sectors (%)

    Sector1980-912002-072021-22
    Agriculture3.62.34.8*
    Industry7.19.412.7*
    Services6.77.89.2*
    Total5.67.89.4

    *2021-22 figures are Gross Value Added (GVA), not GDP directly.

    Two other clear post-reform gains

    Foreign investment (FDI + FII) rose from ~US$100 million (1990-91) to ~US$23 billion (2022-23). Foreign exchange reserves rose from ~US$6 billion (1990-91) to ~US$646 billion (2023-24) — India is now among the largest forex reserve holders globally. India also became a successful exporter of auto parts, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, IT software, and textiles.

    Memory Trick

    Agriculture down, Industry fluctuates, Services drives GDP up. That's the reform-era growth pattern in one line.

    Why CUET asks this —"What are the major factors responsible for the high growth of the service sector?" is NCERT's own exact exercise question — expect it directly, along with reading Table 3.1's sector figures.
    NCERT — Indian Economy During Reforms — GDP Growth, p. 48Open in new tab

    07Critiques of the Reform Process

    The service sector boomed — but NCERT is explicit that agriculture and industry, the sectors that employ the vast majority of Indians, were left behind.

    "Growth without adequate employment generation" is the chapter's central, recurring criticism

    Try this first

    Post-1991, reduced government investment in irrigation, roads, and research combined with partial removal of fertiliser subsidy. Which specific group of farmers does NCERT say was hit hardest by these changes, and why?

    1

    Reduced fertiliser subsidy raised the cost of production for all farmers.

    2

    Small and marginal farmers have the least ability to absorb rising input costs.

    3

    Meanwhile, falling import duties and lifted quantitative restrictions exposed these same farmers to increased international competition.

    4

    NCERT's own case study (Mahadeva, a groundnut farmer in drought-prone Anantapur) illustrates exactly this — rising costs plus cheap imported edible oil flooding local markets, leaving him unable to recover his own cost of cultivation.

    NCERT's Own Words §3.6

    "Though the GDP growth rate has increased in the reform period, scholars point out that the reform-led growth has not generated sufficient employment opportunities in the country." "Reforms have not been able to benefit agriculture, where the growth rate has been decelerating."
    SectorCriticism
    EmploymentReform-led GDP growth has not generated sufficient employment
    AgricultureFalling public investment (irrigation, roads, R&D); reduced fertiliser subsidy; import competition; shift toward cash crops for export over food grains
    IndustrySlowdown from cheaper imports + inadequate infrastructure investment
    Fiscal policyTax reductions haven't raised tax revenue; reduced scope for social/welfare expenditure

    The deeper structural critique

    Some studies argue the 1991 crisis itself stemmed from "deep-rooted inequalities in Indian society," and that the reform package — advised externally — actually worsened these inequalities: income gains concentrated in high-income groups and in select service areas (telecom, IT, finance, real estate) rather than agriculture and industry, which employ the vast majority of Indians.

    The Siricilla Tragedy (Box 3.3)

    Power sector reforms removed subsidised electricity in several states, sharply raising tariffs. Since powerloom weavers' wages were linked to cloth production (which fell with power cuts), this triggered a livelihood crisis — 50 powerloom workers in Siricilla, Andhra Pradesh, died by suicide as a direct consequence.

    Memory Trick

    High growth ≠ inclusive growth. GDP rose, but the sectors employing most Indians (agriculture, industry) and the goal of equity were the reform era's clearest casualties.

    Why CUET asks this —"Discuss economic reforms in India in the light of social justice and welfare" is NCERT's own final exercise question — a strong answer must cite BOTH the genuine GDP/forex gains and this topic's specific employment/agriculture/inequality critiques.
    NCERT — Critiques of the Reform Process, p. 50Open in new tab

    01What is Human Capital?

    Just as land becomes a factory through investment, people become "human capital" through investment — and NCERT draws out exactly where the two forms of capital agree and where they sharply diverge.

    The Physical vs Human Capital comparison table (Box 4.1) is a guaranteed compare-and-contrast MCQ

    Try this first

    A bus can be owned by someone who never drives it themselves — but a bus driver's skill is useless unless the driver is physically present when the bus runs. What key difference between physical and human capital does this illustrate?

    1

    Physical capital (the bus) is separable from its owner — ownership and use can belong to different people.

    2

    Human capital (the driver's skill) is inseparable from its owner — only the SERVICES of human capital can be sold, never the capital itself.

    3

    This is why the human capital's owner must always be physically present wherever that capital is put to use.

    4

    This inseparability is one of several structural differences between physical and human capital that NCERT draws out in Box 4.1.

    NCERT's Framing §4.2

    "Just as a country can turn physical resources like land into physical capital like factories, similarly, it can also turn human resources like nurses, farmers, teachers, students into human capital like engineers and doctors... we need good human capital to produce other human capital."
    Basis (Box 4.1)Physical CapitalHuman Capital
    Separability from ownerSeparable — can be sold/used by othersInseparable — only its services can be sold
    Mobility across countriesCompletely mobile (barring trade restrictions)Not perfectly mobile — restricted by nationality/culture
    DepreciationWears out with use; obsolete with new technologyDepreciates with ageing; reducible via continued education/health investment
    Nature of benefitsOnly private benefit (to the payer)Both private AND external/social benefit
    Formation processPurely economic/technical, conscious decisionPartly social process, partly conscious decision (often decided by parents/society for children)

    Why investment in education parallels investment in capital goods

    NCERT draws a direct parallel: "Spending on education by individuals is similar to spending on capital goods by companies with the objective of increasing future profits" — individuals invest in education expecting higher future income, just as firms invest in machinery expecting higher future output.

    Memory Trick

    Physical capital: separable, mobile, private-benefit-only. Human capital: inseparable, restricted mobility, social benefit too. Same "capital" logic, opposite properties on almost every dimension.

    Why CUET asks this —Box 4.1's full comparison table is one of the richest, most-mined content blocks in this chapter — expect at least one MCQ built directly from it every year.
    NCERT — What is Human Capital?, p. 60Open in new tab

    02Sources of Human Capital Formation

    Education is the most obvious source of human capital — but NCERT names four more, each justified by the same simple test: does the investment's future return exceed its cost?

    The 5 sources (Education, Health, On-the-job training, Migration, Information) are a guaranteed list-recall question

    Try this first

    An engineer migrates from India to another country because the salary offered there is much higher, despite the real costs of relocating (transport, higher cost of living, psychic costs of adjusting to a new culture). Why does NCERT count this migration as a source of human capital formation?

    1

    Migration involves real, upfront costs: transport, cost of living, and "psychic costs" of a new socio-cultural setup.

    2

    But the engineer moves anyway because the enhanced earnings in the new location outweigh these migration costs.

    3

    Since expenditure on migration yields a future return (higher income) exceeding its cost, it counts as an investment.

    4

    This is exactly the same investment logic NCERT applies to education, health, training, and information-seeking.

    NCERT's Own Words §4.3

    "Investment in education is considered as one of the main sources of human capital. There are several other sources as well. Investments in health, on-the-job training, migration and information are the other sources of human capital formation."
    SourceWhy it counts as human capital investment
    EducationIncreases future income-earning capacity, like a firm's capital goods investment
    HealthPrevents productivity loss from illness — includes preventive, curative, and social medicine + clean water/sanitation
    On-the-job trainingFirms recover the training cost via enhanced worker productivity over a committed period
    MigrationEnhanced earnings at the new location outweigh transport/living/psychic costs
    InformationNeeded to make good investment decisions about jobs, education, and health markets

    Two forms of on-the-job training

    (1) Training within the firm itself, under a skilled worker's supervision; (2) sending workers off-campus for training. Either way, firms require workers to stay employed for a specific period afterward, so the firm can recover its training investment through the worker's enhanced productivity.

    Memory Trick

    E-H-T-M-I: Education, Health, Training, Migration, Information. All five pass the same test — future benefit exceeds present cost.

    Why CUET asks this —"What are the two major sources of human capital?" and "discuss health infrastructure / migration as a source of human capital" are NCERT's own verbatim exercise questions.
    NCERT — Sources of Human Capital Formation, p. 61Open in new tab

    03Human Capital vs Human Development

    These two terms sound almost identical — but they rest on opposite philosophies about WHY education and health actually matter.

    "Means to an end" vs "ends in themselves" is the exact phrase CUET tests

    Try this first

    A government funds basic literacy programs for elderly citizens who will never re-enter the workforce or contribute to measured labour productivity. Does the human capital view or the human development view justify this spending?

    1

    The human capital view treats education as valuable only if it raises output/productivity — this spending would look "unproductive" by that standard.

    2

    The human development view instead treats literacy as valuable in itself — as a capability that lets a person make choices they value, regardless of any productivity payoff.

    3

    Since human beings are "ends in themselves" under this view, the spending is justified purely by its contribution to well-being.

    4

    This is exactly the distinction NCERT draws: human capital = means to an end (productivity); human development = end in itself (well-being).

    NCERT's Own Words §4.4

    "Human capital treats human beings as a means to an end; the end being the increase in productivity... In the human development perspective, human beings are ends in themselves... every individual has a right to be literate and lead a healthy life."
    BasisHuman CapitalHuman Development
    Education/health treated asA means to raise labour productivityIntegral to human well-being — ends in themselves
    Investment justified byWhether it raises outputRight to be literate/healthy, regardless of productivity effect
    Which is broader?Narrower — productivity-focusedBroader — encompasses all valued choices, not just income

    The empirical link is genuinely uncertain

    NCERT is honest that "empirical evidence to prove that increase in human capital causes economic growth is rather nebulous" — partly due to measurement problems (years of schooling ≠ quality of education). Analysis shows human capital measures have converged across countries faster than per capita real income has — and causality may run in both directions (income → human capital, and human capital → income).

    Memory Trick

    Human Capital = means to an end (productivity). Human Development = end in itself (well-being). Human Development is the broader of the two terms.

    Why CUET asks this —"Bring out the differences between human capital and human development" and "how is human development a broader term" are NCERT's own exact exercise questions — expect them directly.
    NCERT — Human Capital vs Human Development, p. 66Open in new tab

    04State of Human Capital Formation in India

    Education and health markets have a peculiar problem — mistakes are costly and hard to reverse — and that's exactly why NCERT says government intervention becomes essential.

    The 2 reasons for government intervention in education/health are a guaranteed reasoning question

    Try this first

    A parent enrolls their child in a low-quality private school, not realising the school lacks proper facilities until years later. Why does NCERT say this specific kind of mistake justifies government regulation of education providers?

    1

    By the time poor quality becomes obvious, "substantial amount of damage would have been done" — the harm isn't easily reversible.

    2

    Parents/consumers also lack complete information about a provider's true quality and costs upfront.

    3

    This information gap lets private providers gain monopoly power and potentially exploit consumers.

    4

    Government's role is to ensure private providers meet stipulated standards and charge fair prices — regulating exactly the gap that market forces alone can't fix.

    NCERT's Own Words §4.5

    "Expenditures on education and health make substantial long-term impact and they cannot be easily reversed; hence, government intervention is essential... individual consumers of these services do not have complete information about the quality of services and their costs."
    SectorKey facilitating institutions (India)
    EducationNCERT, UGC (University Grants Commission), AICTE (All India Council of Technical Education)
    HealthNational Medical Commission, ICMR (Indian Council for Medical Research)

    NCERT's own Table 4.1 — Development Indicators (1951 → 2018-22)

    Indicator19512018-22
    Real Per Capita Income (₹)7,65194,054
    Infant Mortality Rate14628
    Life Expectancy at Birth (years)37.268.6
    Literacy Rate (%)16.6778

    Education expenditure — the real growth numbers

    Between 1952–2020, education expenditure as % of total government expenditure rose from 7.92% to 16.54%; as % of GDP, from 0.64% to 4.47% — a genuine but irregular increase, still below the widely-cited 6%-of-GDP target.

    Memory Trick

    Irreversible harm + incomplete consumer information = government must intervene. These are the exact two reasons NCERT gives for regulating education/health markets.

    Why CUET asks this —"Argue in favour of the need for different forms of government intervention in education and health sectors" is NCERT's own exact exercise question.
    NCERT — State of Human Capital Formation in India, p. 67Open in new tab

    05Education Sector — Government Expenditure

    Expert commissions have long said India should spend about 6% of GDP on education — and decades later, actual spending is still falling short of that target.

    The "6% of GDP" recommendation is one of the single most-quoted numbers in this chapter

    Try this first

    India's per capita public expenditure on elementary education in 2020-21 was ₹96,968 in Sikkim but only ₹10,710 in Bihar. What does this gap directly cause, according to NCERT?

    1

    Different states spend vastly different amounts per elementary student.

    2

    Since education spending directly shapes the quality of schooling available.

    3

    This spending gap "leads to differences in educational opportunities and attainments across states" — exactly NCERT's own conclusion.

    4

    So regional inequality in human capital formation is partly a direct product of unequal state-level spending, not just unequal need.

    NCERT's Own Words §4.6

    "The Education Commission (1964–66) had recommended that at least 6 per cent of GDP be spent on education... Compared to this desired level... the current level of a little over 4 per cent has been quite inadequate."
    MeasureWhat it indicates
    Education expenditure as % of total govt. expenditureImportance of education in the government's own priorities
    Education expenditure as % of GDPHow much of society's total income is committed to education

    Key policy milestones

    Tapas Majumdar Committee (1999): estimated ~₹1.37 lakh crore needed over 1998-99 to 2006-07 to bring all children aged 6-14 under school education. Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009: made free education a fundamental right for ages 6-14. Education cess: a 2% levy on all Union taxes, earmarked for elementary education spending.

    Elementary vs Tertiary education spending — a subtlety

    Elementary education takes the largest SHARE of total education spending, while tertiary (college/university) gets the least share overall — yet expenditure PER STUDENT in tertiary education is actually higher than in elementary. NCERT is explicit this does NOT mean funds should shift from tertiary to elementary — expanding schools needs more teachers, who themselves are trained at the tertiary level, so both need increased funding together.

    Memory Trick

    Target: 6% of GDP. Reality: just over 4%. The gap between recommendation and reality is this topic's single most-tested fact.

    Why CUET asks this —"Why do we observe regional differences in educational attainment in India?" is NCERT's own verbatim exercise question — the Sikkim/Bihar per-student spending gap is the exact evidence to cite.
    NCERT — Education Sector — Government Expenditure, p. 68Open in new tab

    06Educational Achievement & Attainment in India

    Three specific indicators are how NCERT measures a country's educational progress — and India's numbers on all three have risen substantially, even if gaps remain.

    Naming the 3 indicators of educational achievement is a guaranteed fact-recall

    Try this first

    Between 1990 and 2017-18, India's female adult literacy rate rose from 37.9% to 66%, while male adult literacy rose from 61.9% to 82%. Has the gender gap in literacy widened or narrowed over this period?

    1

    1990 gap: 61.9 − 37.9 = 24 percentage points.

    2

    2017-18 gap: 82 − 66 = 16 percentage points.

    3

    The gap narrowed from 24 to 16 points.

    4

    NCERT calls this a positive development in gender equity — even though it stresses the need to keep promoting women's education, since the gap hasn't closed entirely.

    NCERT's Own Words §4.6

    "Educational achievements in a country are indicated in terms of adult literacy level, primary education completion rate and youth literacy rate."

    NCERT's own Table 4.2 — Educational Attainment (1990 → 2017-18)

    Indicator1990 (M/F)2017-18 (M/F)
    Adult literacy rate (15+)61.9 / 37.982 / 66
    Primary completion rate78 / 6193 / 96
    Youth literacy rate (15-24)76.6 / 54.293 / 90

    Note: by 2017-18, female primary completion rate (96%) actually exceeds the male rate (93%) — a genuine reversal from 1990.

    The three indicators, defined

    Adult literacy rate: % of people aged 15+ who can read/write. Primary completion rate: % of the relevant age group completing primary education. Youth literacy rate: % of people aged 15-24 who are literate — a forward-looking indicator, since today's youth are tomorrow's adult workforce.

    Memory Trick

    3 indicators: Adult literacy, Primary completion, Youth literacy. All three show genuine progress AND a narrowing (not yet closed) gender gap.

    Why CUET asks this —"What are the indicators of educational achievement in a country?" and "interpret the data in Table 4.2" are NCERT's own exact exercise/activity questions.
    NCERT — Educational Achievement & Attainment, p. 70Open in new tab

    07Future Prospects — Gaps That Remain

    Rising literacy rates hide an uncomfortable truth: India's absolute number of illiterate people is still roughly the size of the entire country's population at independence — and there's a genuine paradox around educated unemployment too.

    The "educated unemployment paradox" is this chapter's most thought-provoking, most-asked reasoning question

    Try this first

    NSSO data showed rural young female graduates had a NEAR 30% unemployment rate, versus only 3-6% among primary-level educated rural/urban youth. Doesn't more education normally mean better job prospects — so why are highly-educated youth actually MORE likely to be unemployed here?

    1

    Primary-level educated workers typically take up any available low-skill work — few options, so few stay "unemployed" by definition.

    2

    Graduates, especially rural women, hold out for jobs that MATCH their qualifications and expectations — jobs that are scarce.

    3

    Higher education institutions may also fail to impart genuinely "employable skills," leaving graduates credentialed but not job-ready.

    4

    NCERT's own recommendation follows directly: increase higher-education allocation AND improve institutional standards so graduates gain real employable skills.

    NCERT's Own Words §4.7

    "Though literacy rates for both — adults as well as youth — have increased, still the absolute number of illiterates in India is as much as India's population was at the time of independence." "When compared to less educated, a large proportion of educated persons are unemployed."
    Group (graduate+, NSSO 2011-12)Unemployment Rate
    Rural young male graduates19%
    Urban young male graduates16%
    Rural young female graduates~30% (most severely affected)
    Primary-level educated youth (rural/urban)Only 3-6%

    1950's unmet constitutional promise

    The Constitution's Directive Principles (1950) called for free, compulsory education for all children up to age 14, to be achieved within 10 years. NCERT notes plainly: "Had we achieved this, we would have cent per cent literacy by now" — it wasn't achieved on that timeline.

    Gender equity — genuine progress, not yet complete

    Male-female literacy gaps have narrowed, a real positive. But NCERT stresses continued need to promote women's education — citing its favourable knock-on effects on fertility rate and on children's own health and care.

    Memory Trick

    The Indian education "pyramid" is steep — fewer and fewer people reach higher education, and paradoxically, THOSE who reach it face higher unemployment than the less-educated — a mismatch between credentials and employable skills, not a failure of education itself.

    Why CUET asks this —A scenario or data question asking WHY educated youth unemployment exceeds less-educated unemployment tests exactly this paradox — the credentials-vs-employable-skills gap is the answer CUET wants.
    NCERT — Future Prospects — Gaps That Remain, p. 71Open in new tab

    01What is Rural Development?

    Mahatma Gandhi said India's real progress meant developing its villages, not just its cities — and the numbers still back him up today.

    The 5 focus areas of rural development are a guaranteed list-recall question

    Try this first

    More than two-thirds of India's population depends on agriculture, yet one-fourth of rural India still lives in abject poverty. Why does NCERT say this makes rural development central to India's overall progress?

    1

    The overwhelming majority of Indians still depend on agriculture for their livelihood.

    2

    This sector is "yet to become productive enough to provide for them" — meaning most Indians' economic well-being is tied to a still-underperforming sector.

    3

    A quarter of rural India remains in abject poverty despite this dependence.

    4

    So national progress cannot be "real" while the sector most Indians rely on remains underdeveloped — exactly Gandhi's point, restated in modern terms.

    NCERT's Own Words §5.1-5.2

    "Mahatma Gandhi once said that the real progress of India did not mean simply the growth and expansion of industrial urban centres but mainly the development of the villages." "Rural development is a comprehensive term. It essentially focuses on action for the development of areas that are lagging behind."
    Focus Area of Rural DevelopmentIncludes
    Human resourcesLiteracy (especially female literacy), education, skill development, health, sanitation
    Land reformsOwnership and land-use reform
    Productive resourcesDevelopment of each locality's own productive resources
    InfrastructureElectricity, irrigation, credit, marketing, transport, village roads, agricultural research & extension
    Poverty alleviationSpecial measures for weaker sections; access to productive employment

    A recurring warning sign: agricultural stagnation continued post-1991

    Agriculture's growth rate decelerated to about 3% per year during 1991-2012 (lower than earlier years) — and by 2023-24, agricultural GVA growth was only about 2%. Scholars link this to declining public investment since 1991, inadequate infrastructure, and lack of alternate (non-agricultural) employment.

    Memory Trick

    5 focus areas: Human resources, Land reforms, Productive resources, Infrastructure, Poverty alleviation. Rural development isn't just about farms — it's genuinely comprehensive.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a direct "list the key areas requiring fresh initiative for rural development" question — NCERT's own bulleted list is the exact answer key.
    NCERT — What is Rural Development?, p. 76Open in new tab

    02Rural Credit

    Before independence, moneylenders trapped small farmers in cycles of debt through manipulated accounts — India's rural banking system was built specifically to break that trap.

    NABARD's founding year (1982) and its role are guaranteed fact-recall

    Try this first

    Self-Help Groups (SHGs) emerged specifically to fill a gap in the FORMAL rural credit system, even though banks, cooperatives, and RRBs already existed. What specific gap did SHGs address that formal institutions couldn't?

    1

    Formal credit institutions typically require collateral before lending.

    2

    A vast proportion of poor rural households have no collateral to offer — automatically excluding them from the formal credit network.

    3

    SHGs instead pool small member contributions (promoting thrift) and lend from this pooled fund to needy members, repayable in small instalments.

    4

    This "micro-credit" approach reached the very households collateral requirements had shut out — by May 2019, nearly 6 crore women had joined 54 lakh women's SHGs.

    NCERT's Own Words §5.3

    "National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) was set up in 1982 as an apex body to coordinate the activities of all institutions involved in the rural financing system." "Self-Help Groups... have emerged to fill the gap in the formal credit system."
    Institution/PolicyRole
    Multi-agency networkCommercial banks, Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), cooperatives, land development banks
    NABARD (1982)Apex body coordinating all rural financing institutions
    Self-Help Groups (SHGs)Micro-credit via pooled member savings — no collateral required
    Jan-Dhan YojanaUniversal bank account access + accidental insurance + overdraft facility, no minimum balance required

    Kudumbashree — "The Poor Women's Bank" (Box 5.1)

    A Kerala women-oriented poverty-reduction programme (from 1995) built around a thrift and credit society — mobilised ₹1 crore in thrift savings and became acclaimed as one of Asia's largest informal banking networks by participation and savings.

    1969 — the pivot to social banking

    Before this, moneylenders and traders exploited small/marginal farmers with high interest rates and manipulated accounts, keeping them trapped in debt. After 1969, India adopted social banking and a multi-agency approach to meet rural credit needs — a deliberate policy response to that exploitation.

    A critical appraisal — not an unqualified success

    Banking expansion genuinely helped post-Green-Revolution farmers and ended famines. But agricultural loan default rates remain chronically high, and most formal institutions (besides commercial banks) never developed a strong culture of deposit mobilisation and effective loan recovery.

    Memory Trick

    1969 = social banking begins. 1982 = NABARD, the apex coordinator. SHGs = the no-collateral fix for those formal credit still couldn't reach.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect NABARD's founding year and role, plus a "why did SHGs emerge" reasoning question tied directly to the collateral-exclusion problem.
    NCERT — Rural Credit, p. 77Open in new tab

    03Agricultural Marketing System

    Before reform, farmers selling their produce faced rigged scales and price manipulation — the government's response was four specific, distinct policy tools.

    The 4 government marketing measures are a guaranteed list-recall question

    Try this first

    A farmer without market price information sells produce to a trader at a very low price, unaware of the fair market rate. Which of the government's four marketing interventions most directly addresses this specific problem?

    1

    The core problem here is lack of price transparency in an unregulated private market.

    2

    The government's first measure — regulation of markets — was specifically designed to create "orderly and transparent marketing conditions."

    3

    Regulated market yards (mandis) let farmers see prevailing prices openly, rather than being at a trader's mercy.

    4

    Even so, NCERT notes about 27,000 more rural periodic markets still need development as regulated market places — the job isn't finished.

    NCERT's Own Words §5.4

    "Prior to independence, farmers, while selling their produce to traders, suffered from faulty weighing and manipulation of accounts... Let us discuss four such measures that were initiated to improve the marketing aspect."
    #Government MeasurePurpose
    1Regulation of marketsOrderly, transparent marketing conditions
    2Physical infrastructureRoads, railways, warehouses, godowns, cold storage, processing units
    3Cooperative marketingFair prices for farmers (e.g. milk cooperatives in Gujarat)
    4Policy instrumentsMinimum Support Price (MSP), buffer stocks (FCI), PDS distribution

    A genuine, still-unresolved gap

    Despite all four measures, private trade (moneylenders, rural political elites, big merchants, rich farmers) still predominates agricultural markets. More than 10% of farm produce is wasted today due to inadequate storage — a problem infrastructure measures were meant to solve but haven't fully.

    Emerging Alternate Marketing Channels

    Direct-to-consumer channels increase farmer incomes: Apni Mandi (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan), Hadaspar Mandi (Pune), Rythu Bazars (Andhra Pradesh, Telangana), Uzhavar Sandies (Tamil Nadu). Also, e-NAM (2016) — a Pan-India online portal connecting mandis and Regional Market Yards.

    Memory Trick

    4 measures: Regulate, Build infrastructure, Cooperativise, Use policy tools (MSP/buffer/PDS). Each targets a different specific market failure — transparency, storage, fair pricing, income protection.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a direct "name the four government measures to improve agricultural marketing" question, and possibly a scenario matching a farmer's problem to the right measure.
    NCERT — Agricultural Marketing System, p. 80Open in new tab

    04Diversification into Productive Activities

    Farming alone leaves rural workers idle for half the year and exposed to crop failure — diversifying into livestock, fisheries, and horticulture spreads that risk.

    The Kharif/Rabi seasonal-employment gap is the "why diversify" reasoning question CUET asks

    Try this first

    In areas with inadequate irrigation, agricultural workers find plenty of employment during the Kharif season but struggle to find gainful work during the Rabi season. Why does this specifically justify diversification into non-farm and allied activities?

    1

    Agricultural employment is heavily concentrated in the Kharif season.

    2

    Without adequate irrigation, Rabi-season farming isn't viable, leaving workers without work for part of the year.

    3

    Diversifying into livestock, fisheries, or non-farm activities provides supplementary, gainful employment exactly in these otherwise-idle periods.

    4

    This also reduces the risk of depending exclusively on one seasonal, weather-dependent income source.

    NCERT's Own Words §5.5

    "Diversification includes two aspects — one relates to change in cropping pattern and the other relates to a shift of workforce from agriculture to other allied activities (livestock, poultry, fisheries etc.) and non-agriculture sector."
    Allied ActivityKey Fact
    Animal husbandry / LivestockProvides alternate livelihood to 70+ million small/marginal farmers and landless labourers; poultry = 61% of livestock distribution
    Dairy (Operation Flood)Milk production rose ~12x between 1951-2021; Gujarat is the milk cooperative success story
    FisheriesInland sources = 75% of fish production value; contributes ~1.5% of GDP; women = 60% of export-marketing workforce
    Horticulture~1/3 of agricultural output value; ~6% of GDP; India is 2nd largest fruit/vegetable producer globally

    Non-farm economy — dynamic vs subsistence segments

    Some non-farm segments have "dynamic linkages that permit healthy growth" — agro-processing, food processing, leather, tourism. Others are stuck at "subsistence, low productivity" — traditional home-based industries like pottery, crafts, and handlooms, which have potential but lack infrastructure and support.

    TANWA — Tamil Nadu Women in Agriculture (Box 5.2)

    A late-1980s project training women in modern agricultural techniques and organic farming — trained women went on to make/sell vermicompost, run micro-credit "mini banks" within Farm Women's Groups, and start small household enterprises (mushroom cultivation, soap-making, doll-making).

    Memory Trick

    Diversification = two things: change WHAT you grow (cropping pattern) + change WHERE the workforce works (into allied/non-farm activities). Both reduce dependence on one risky, seasonal source.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a direct question distinguishing the two aspects of diversification, plus fact-recall on livestock/fisheries/horticulture's specific GDP/output contribution figures.
    NCERT — Diversification into Productive Activities, p. 82Open in new tab

    05Sustainable Development & Organic Farming

    Chemical fertilisers boosted output but quietly poisoned water, soil, and food supply — organic farming is NCERT's proposed eco-friendly alternative, with real trade-offs on both sides.

    Balancing organic farming's benefits AND limitations is a guaranteed two-sided essay question

    Try this first

    Organic farming requires MORE labour input than conventional chemical farming. Why does NCERT frame this as an ADVANTAGE for India specifically, rather than a drawback?

    1

    More labour input per unit of output would raise costs in a labour-scarce economy.

    2

    But India has an abundant, comparatively cheap rural labour force.

    3

    Organic farming's labour-intensity therefore creates more rural employment rather than raising costs prohibitively.

    4

    NCERT explicitly concludes: "India will find organic farming an attractive proposition" for exactly this reason.

    NCERT's Own Words §5.6

    "Organic agriculture is a whole system of farming that restores, maintains and enhances the ecological balance." "Organic agriculture offers a means to substitute costlier agricultural inputs... with locally produced organic inputs that are cheaper."
    Benefits of Organic FarmingLimitations of Organic Farming
    Cheaper local inputs replace costly chemical onesYields are lower than conventional farming, especially in initial years
    Rising export demand and higher prices (10-100% more, per Box 5.4)Requires farmer awareness/willingness to adopt new methods
    Higher nutritional value than chemically-farmed foodProduce may have more blemishes, shorter shelf life
    More labour-intensive → more rural employment (an advantage in India's context)Limited choice for off-season crops
    Pesticide-free, environmentally sustainableInadequate infrastructure and marketing challenges

    Organically Produced Cotton in Maharashtra (Box 5.5)

    When first proposed in 1995 by an NGO (Prakruti), a cotton research institute director dismissed it ("Do you want India to go naked?"). Today, 130 farmers grow cotton organically on 1,200 hectares, certified by a German accredited agency (AGRECO) — proof the sceptics were wrong, at least at small scale. About 78% of Indian farmers are marginal (owning <0.8 hectare), for whom organic farming can be more profitable long-term.

    Chapter's closing theme — environment and rural development are no longer separate subjects

    NCERT's conclusion states plainly: "we cannot look at the environment and rural development as two distinct subjects" — sustainable, eco-friendly technologies must be invented or procured to fit different rural circumstances, tying this chapter directly into the next one (Environment and Sustainable Development).

    Memory Trick

    Organic farming: cheaper inputs + higher nutrition + more jobs, BUT lower initial yields + shorter shelf life. A genuine trade-off, not a one-sided win — always present both sides.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a "discuss the benefits and limitations of organic farming in India" essay-style question — a strong answer must cite BOTH sides, exactly as NCERT presents them.
    NCERT — Sustainable Development & Organic Farming, p. 86Open in new tab

    01Workers, Employment & Related Concepts

    NCERT's definition of "worker" is far broader than most people assume — and getting this definition right is the foundation for everything else in this chapter.

    "Who counts as a worker" is a guaranteed trick-scenario MCQ

    Try this first

    A self-employed pavement vegetable vendor and a farmer temporarily absent from work due to illness — are both of these people "workers," according to NCERT's definition?

    1

    NCERT defines workers as anyone "engaged in economic activities, in whatever capacity — high or low."

    2

    Self-employed people (like the vendor) are explicitly included — being paid by an employer is NOT a requirement.

    3

    Workers temporarily absent due to illness, injury, bad weather, festivals, or social/religious functions are still counted as workers.

    4

    So YES to both — this definition is deliberately broader than the everyday sense of "having a job."

    NCERT's Own Words §6.2

    "Those activities which contribute to the gross national product are called economic activities. All those who are engaged in economic activities, in whatever capacity — high or low, are workers."
    ConceptDefinition
    Economic activityAn activity that contributes to the Gross National Product
    WorkerAnyone engaged in economic activities, in any capacity — including self-employed and temporarily absent workers
    GDPTotal money value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year
    GNPGDP plus/minus net earnings from foreign transactions (exports minus imports)

    A genuine, unresolved debate — unpaid women's work

    NCERT explicitly raises this tension: women doing unpaid household work, farm labour, cooking, or fetching water/fuelwood are NOT categorised as workers under the current definition, even though economists argue they should be. India's workforce was ~545 million in 2022-23; about 77% men, 23% women — a gap partly explained by this narrow definition excluding unpaid domestic/farm work.

    Why studying "workers" matters beyond just counting jobs

    It reveals the quality and nature of employment, helps plan human resources, shows each sector's contribution to national income, and helps address social issues like exploitation of marginalised groups and child labour.

    Memory Trick

    Paid OR self-employed, present OR temporarily absent — both count as "worker." The definition is about contributing to economic activity, not receiving a wage specifically.

    Why CUET asks this —"Who is a worker?" is NCERT's own exact first exercise question — expect scenario-based MCQs testing whether unusual cases (self-employed, temporarily absent) count.
    NCERT — Workers, Employment & Related Concepts, p. 93Open in new tab

    02Worker-Population Ratio & Participation Patterns

    One simple ratio tells you how much of a population is actually engaged in producing the country's goods and services — and India's numbers reveal a stark, persistent gender gap.

    The Worker-Population Ratio formula and Table 6.1's gender gap are guaranteed exam content

    Try this first

    Per Table 6.1 (2023-24), for every 100 urban women, only about 21 are engaged in economic activity, versus about 35 out of every 100 rural women. Why does NCERT say urban women participate LESS than rural women?

    1

    Where men earn high incomes, families often discourage women from taking up jobs — more common in urban settings.

    2

    Much of rural women's work (farm labour) is directly counted as economic activity, while similar urban household work often isn't.

    3

    This narrow definition of "work" under-recognises women's actual economic contribution, especially in cities.

    4

    NCERT flags this as underestimation, not necessarily true lower participation — the numbers reflect definitional limits, not just genuine choice.

    NCERT's Own Words §6.3

    "Worker-population ratio is an indicator which is used for analysing the employment situation in the country... divide the total number of workers in India by the population in India and multiply it by 100."

    The Formula

    Worker-Population Ratio = (Total Workers ÷ Total Population) × 100

    NCERT's own Table 6.1 — Worker-Population Ratio, 2023-24

    SexTotalRuralUrban
    Men56.456.356.4
    Women30.734.820.7
    Total43.745.638.9

    Why rural participation exceeds urban overall

    Rural people have fewer resources for extended education and often can't afford to stay out of the workforce — economic necessity forces earlier/broader participation. Urban people, by contrast, often stay in education longer and can be more selective about matching jobs to their qualifications.

    Memory Trick

    WPR = Workers ÷ Population × 100. Men's ratio stays flat (~56) across rural/urban; women's ratio swings sharply (35 rural vs 21 urban) — the real story is in the gender gap, not the rural-urban gap.

    Why CUET asks this —"Define worker-population ratio" is NCERT's own exact exercise question, and Table 6.1's numbers are a direct numerical-recall target.
    NCERT — Worker-Population Ratio & Participation, p. 95Open in new tab

    03Self-Employed vs Hired Workers

    Two workers can do completely different jobs but share the same "employment status" — and that status, not the job itself, is what reveals the real quality of someone's work.

    The 3-way employment-status classification is a guaranteed scenario-matching question

    Try this first

    A construction worker is casually engaged on different building sites, paid only for the days worked. A civil engineer works permanently for the same construction company, earning a fixed monthly salary. What employment status does each hold?

    1

    The construction worker is casually engaged on others' worksites, paid per task/day — this is a casual wage labourer.

    2

    The civil engineer is engaged by one enterprise and paid wages regularly — this is a regular salaried employee.

    3

    Neither owns/operates their own enterprise, so neither is self-employed (unlike, say, a cement shop owner).

    4

    This 3-way classification — self-employed, regular salaried, casual wage labourer — is exactly how NCERT categorises employment status.

    NCERT's Own Words §6.4

    "Workers who own and operate an enterprise to earn their livelihood are known as self-employed." "When a worker is engaged by someone or an enterprise and paid his or her wages on a regular basis, they are known as regular salaried employees."
    StatusDefinitionShare of India's workforce
    Self-employedOwns/operates their own enterprise~58%
    Casual wage labourersCasually engaged on others' farms/sites, paid per task~20%
    Regular salaried employeesEngaged regularly by one employer, paid wages on a fixed basis~22%

    Rural vs Urban distribution — a genuine structural difference

    Self-employment dominates in rural areas (where landowning farmers cultivate independently). Both self-employment AND regular salaried work are significant in urban areas, since urban enterprises need workers on a regular ongoing basis, not casually.

    Casual wage labourers — the most vulnerable category

    Economists specifically flag casual wage labourers as the most vulnerable of the three categories — no ownership stake (unlike self-employed), no regular income security (unlike salaried employees), and typically no social security protections at all.

    Memory Trick

    Own it = self-employed. Regular one employer = salaried. Casual, task-by-task = casual wage labourer. The status test is about the relationship to the enterprise, not the job's prestige.

    Why CUET asks this —NCERT's own "mark (a)/(b)/(c)" exercise (classifying a saloon owner, a cashier, a handloom weaver, etc.) is the exact scenario-matching format CUET reuses.
    NCERT — Self-Employed vs Hired Workers, p. 97Open in new tab

    04Growth and Changing Structure of Employment

    India's GDP has grown steadily for decades — but employment hasn't kept pace, producing a phenomenon economists gave a deliberately unsettling name.

    "Jobless growth" and "casualisation of the workforce" are this chapter's two most-tested named phenomena

    Try this first

    Between 1950 and 2010, India's GDP consistently grew faster than employment, with employment growth never exceeding about 2% per year. What term do economists use for an economy producing more goods and services WITHOUT generating proportional new jobs?

    1

    GDP kept rising — the economy was genuinely producing more output.

    2

    But employment growth stayed capped at roughly 2% per year, well below GDP growth.

    3

    The gap between GDP growth and employment growth kept widening, especially from the late 1990s.

    4

    Scholars call this "jobless growth" — producing more without generating proportionally more employment.

    NCERT's Own Words §6.6

    "During this period, employment grew at the rate of not more than 2 per cent... This means that in the Indian economy, without generating employment, we have been able to produce more goods and services. Scholars refer to this phenomenon as jobless growth."

    The sectoral shift, 1972-73 → 2023-24 (Table 6.3)

    Sector1972-732023-24
    Primary74.3%46.1%
    Secondary10.9%24.1%
    Services14.8%29.8%

    Casualisation of the workforce — a second named trend

    Over 1972-2024, workers have shifted from self-employment and regular salaried work TOWARD casual wage work — economists call this casualisation of the workforce, and it makes workers more vulnerable (no job security, no benefits). Self-employment, however, still remains the largest single category throughout.

    Memory Trick

    Jobless growth = output rises, jobs don't keep pace. Casualisation = the jobs that DO exist shift toward less secure casual work. Two related but distinct problems.

    Why CUET asks this —"What will happen if there is no additional employment generated even though we produce more goods and services?" is NCERT's own exact exercise question — the answer is "jobless growth," by name.
    NCERT — Growth and Changing Structure of Employment, p. 100Open in new tab

    05Informalisation of the Indian Workforce

    Planners hoped formal-sector jobs would keep expanding as India developed — instead, nearly 9 in every 10 Indian workers ended up in the informal sector.

    The formal/informal sector definition (the "10 workers" threshold) is a guaranteed fact-recall

    Try this first

    In 2019-20, India had about 535 million workers total, but only about 59 million were in the formal sector. What percentage of India's workforce was in the informal sector that year?

    1

    Formal sector share = 59 ÷ 535 × 100 ≈ 11%.

    2

    Informal sector share = 100% − 11% = 89%.

    3

    This means nearly 9 out of every 10 Indian workers were in the informal sector in 2019-20.

    4

    This is the exact opposite of what development planning originally envisaged — that formal-sector jobs would steadily expand as the economy grew.

    NCERT's Own Words §6.7

    "All the public sector establishments and those private sector establishments which employ 10 hired workers or more are called formal sector establishments... All other enterprises and workers working in those enterprises form the informal sector."
    SectorDefinitionKey traits
    Formal (organised)Public sector + private establishments with 10+ hired workersSocial security benefits, more regulated, higher earnings
    Informal (unorganised)All other enterprises/workers, including farmers, self-employed without hired staff, casual non-farm labourersNo regular income protection, no government regulation, outdated technology, no formal accounts

    Informalisation in Ahmedabad (Box 6.2) — a real case study

    Ahmedabad's textile mills once gave 150,000 workers secure jobs, living wages, health/old-age social security, and strong trade union representation. When mills closed in the 1980s-90s (over a drawn-out decade), over 80,000 permanent + 50,000 non-permanent workers were pushed into the informal sector — triggering economic recession, communal riots, alcoholism, suicides, and child labour as families fell from the middle class into poverty.

    Formal sector — genuinely male-dominated

    Women make up only about one-sixth of the formal sector workforce, versus a considerably larger share in the informal sector — reinforcing that formalisation hasn't reached women workers equally.

    Memory Trick

    10+ hired workers (or public sector) = formal. Everyone else = informal. ~89% of India's workforce falls in the informal category — the opposite of what planners expected.

    Why CUET asks this —The exact formal-sector definition (10+ hired workers) and the ~89% informal-sector share are precise, checkable facts — expect both tested directly, plus a classification scenario (NCERT's own tick-mark exercise).
    NCERT — Informalisation of the Indian Workforce, p. 103Open in new tab

    06Unemployment — Types & Measurement

    Unemployment in India rarely looks like "no job at all" for long — it usually hides in plain sight, disguised as too many people doing one job, or work that vanishes with the seasons.

    Disguised vs Seasonal vs Open unemployment is a guaranteed compare-and-contrast MCQ

    Try this first

    A farmer's 4-acre farm genuinely needs only 2 workers plus himself, but he employs 5 workers including his wife and children. Everyone appears "employed" — so why does NCERT still call this a form of unemployment?

    1

    All 5+ people are technically "working" on the farm — nobody is idle by the everyday definition.

    2

    But the farm's actual labour requirement is only 2 workers plus the farmer himself.

    3

    The "extra" workers add essentially zero marginal output — their labour is redundant, just hidden within family/farm employment.

    4

    This is disguised unemployment — unemployment that doesn't show up as joblessness because it's absorbed invisibly into family farm labour.

    NCERT's Own Words §6.8

    "Economists call unemployment prevailing in Indian farms as disguised unemployment... One study conducted in the late 1950s showed about one-third of agriculture workers in India as disguisedly unemployed."
    TypeDefinition
    Open unemploymentActively seeking work but unable to find any — the everyday sense of "unemployed"
    Disguised unemploymentMore workers than actually needed for a task, hidden within family/farm labour, adding zero marginal output
    Seasonal unemploymentNo work available during certain months due to agriculture's seasonal nature (e.g. the rainy season)

    National Statistical Office's (NSO) definition of unemployment

    A situation where people, lacking work, are not working but are actively seeking work — through employment exchanges, intermediaries, friends/relatives, or direct applications — or express willingness/availability for work under prevailing conditions. Economists use a stricter operational rule: unable to get even one hour of work in half a day.

    Four sources of Indian unemployment data

    Census of India; National Statistical Office's Employment/Unemployment Situation reports; Periodic Labour Force Survey (annual); Directorate General of Employment and Training's Employment Exchange registration data. Each gives different estimates but together reveal the real variety of unemployment types.

    Why long-term "complete" unemployment is rare in India

    NCERT notes that desperate economic circumstances prevent most Indians from staying completely unemployed for long — instead, they're forced to accept unpleasant, dangerous, or unhealthy jobs that others would refuse, rather than remain jobless.

    Memory Trick

    Open = visibly jobless. Disguised = "employed" but redundant (farms). Seasonal = jobless only in the off-season. All three genuinely coexist in India, not mutually exclusive across the whole economy.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a scenario question (e.g. the 4-acre farm example) asking you to identify WHICH type of unemployment is being described — disguised unemployment is the one most students confuse with "being employed."
    NCERT — Unemployment — Types & Measurement, p. 106Open in new tab

    07Government Initiatives for Employment Generation

    Government job creation doesn't only mean hiring people directly — a steel company's own hiring can ripple outward and create jobs at private firms that never touched a government payroll.

    Direct vs Indirect employment generation is a guaranteed compare-and-contrast MCQ

    Try this first

    A government-owned steel company increases its output and hires more workers. A private company that buys steel from this government company also increases its own output and hiring as a result. Which of these two hiring increases is "direct" and which is "indirect" government employment generation?

    1

    The government steel company's own new hires are direct employment generation — the government enterprise itself is doing the hiring.

    2

    The private company's new hires happen only because it received cheaper/more steel input — the government never employed these workers itself.

    3

    This ripple-effect hiring at a separate private company is indirect employment generation.

    4

    Both trace back to the same government initiative, but only one involves the government as the direct employer.

    NCERT's Own Words §6.9

    "When the output of goods and services from government enterprises increases, then private enterprises which receive raw materials from government enterprises will also raise their output and hence increase the number of employment opportunities in the economy... This is the indirect generation of employment opportunities."
    CategoryMechanism
    DirectGovernment directly employs people — administration, government-run industries, hotels, transport companies
    IndirectGovernment enterprise output growth raises private-sector demand/output, creating jobs the government never directly funds

    MGNREGA — Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005

    Promises 100 days of guaranteed wage employment per year to any rural household volunteering for unskilled manual work — one of the government's flagship direct employment-generation measures for rural India.

    Employment generation programmes — broader than just "jobs"

    These programmes bundle employment with services in primary health, primary education, rural drinking water, nutrition, income/employment-generating assets, community asset development, housing/sanitation construction, rural roads, and wasteland/degraded land development — poverty alleviation through combined employment + welfare delivery.

    The chapter's closing tension

    NCERT's conclusion notes new jobs increasingly concentrate in the service sector, outsourcing is becoming common (even sending work to other countries), and the home is increasingly becoming the workplace — but none of this has favoured the individual worker, since employment has become more informal with limited social security. Rapid GDP growth without matching employment growth is exactly why government employment-generation initiatives remain necessary.

    Memory Trick

    Direct = government is the employer. Indirect = government's OWN output growth creates jobs elsewhere. MGNREGA (2005, 100 days) is the flagship direct example to remember by name.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a scenario distinguishing direct from indirect employment generation (the steel-company ripple-effect example is NCERT's own), plus a direct MGNREGA fact-recall (2005, 100 days).
    NCERT — Government Initiatives for Employment Generation, p. 108Open in new tab

    01Environment — Definition & Functions

    The environment does far more than just "exist around us" — NCERT names four distinct jobs it performs, and a crisis begins the moment any one of them is overloaded.

    The 4 functions of environment + renewable vs non-renewable classification are guaranteed exam content

    Try this first

    Classify the following as renewable or non-renewable: trees, fish, petroleum, coal, iron-ore, water.

    1

    Renewable = can be used without becoming depleted, given a continuous supply: trees, fish, water.

    2

    Non-renewable = gets exhausted with extraction and use: petroleum, coal, iron-ore.

    3

    Note: even "renewable" resources like trees/fish can behave like non-renewables if extracted faster than they regenerate.

    4

    This exact exercise — classify these six resources — is NCERT's own Chapter 7 exercise question.

    NCERT's Own Words §7.2

    "Environment is defined as the total planetary inheritance and the totality of all resources. It includes all the biotic and abiotic factors that influence each other." The environment performs "four vital functions."
    FunctionWhat it means
    1. Supplies resourcesBoth renewable (trees, fish) and non-renewable (fossil fuel)
    2. Assimilates wasteAbsorbs and processes waste generated by human activity
    3. Sustains lifeProvides genetic and biodiversity
    4. Provides aesthetic servicesScenery and similar non-material value
    BasisBiotic elementsAbiotic elements
    DefinitionLiving elementsNon-living elements
    ExamplesBirds, animals, plants, forests, fisheriesAir, water, land, rocks, sunlight

    The concept that decides everything else in this chapter — Carrying Capacity

    The environment performs its functions "without any interruption as long as the demand on these functions is within its carrying capacity" — meaning resource extraction stays below the rate of regeneration, and waste stays within the environment's absorptive capacity. Cross this line, and function 3 (life sustenance) fails — triggering an environmental crisis.

    Memory Trick

    4 functions: Supply resources, Assimilate waste, Sustain life, Provide aesthetics. Carrying capacity = the invisible line that, once crossed, turns normal use into a crisis.

    Why CUET asks this —"What is meant by environment?" and the renewable/non-renewable classification exercise are NCERT's own exact opening questions.
    NCERT — Environment — Definition & Functions, p. 116Open in new tab

    02Environmental Degradation & Its Causes

    Environmental problems aren't new to this century by accident — NCERT explains precisely why they only became critical after population growth and industrialisation reversed an age-old balance.

    Global warming and ozone depletion mechanisms are guaranteed fact-recall from Boxes 7.1-7.2

    Try this first

    Before industrialisation and rapid population growth, environmental problems were far less severe. What exactly reversed to change this?

    1

    Originally, demand for environmental resources/services was well BELOW their supply — resource extraction stayed below the rate of regeneration.

    2

    Population explosion + industrial revolution pushed demand for both production and consumption resources sharply upward.

    3

    Demand now exceeds the rate of regeneration, and waste exceeds the environment's absorptive capacity.

    4

    NCERT calls this "a reversal of supply-demand relationship for environmental quality" — the root cause of today's environmental crisis.

    NCERT's Own Words §7.2

    "We are now faced with increased demand for environmental resources and services but their supply is limited due to overuse and misuse. Hence the environmental issues of waste generation and pollution have become critical today."
    Global IssueMechanismKey fact
    Global warming (Box 7.1)Greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane) from fossil fuels & deforestation trap heatCO₂ up 31%, methane up 149% since 1750; temp risen 0.6°C in past century; Kyoto Protocol (1997)
    Ozone depletion (Box 7.2)CFCs (ACs, fridges, aerosols) and halons (fire extinguishers) destroy stratospheric ozone~5% ozone reduction detected 1979-1990; Montreal Protocol banned CFCs

    The real cost of degradation, in India specifically

    70% of India's water is polluted, driving up respiratory and water-borne disease incidence and government health spending. NCERT frames this directly: "the opportunity costs of negative environmental impacts are high."

    Memory Trick

    Global warming = too much heat-trapping gas. Ozone depletion = too much CFC destroying the shield. Different gases, different mechanisms, both driven by industrialisation.

    Why CUET asks this —"What happens when the rate of resource extraction exceeds that of regeneration?" is NCERT's own exact exercise question — the supply-demand reversal is the precise answer expected.
    NCERT — Environmental Degradation & Its Causes, p. 118Open in new tab

    03State of India's Environment

    India's environmental threat is genuinely two-faced — poverty-driven degradation on one side, affluence-driven pollution on the other — and NCERT names five specific priority issues.

    The "dichotomy" of poverty vs affluence-driven degradation is a guaranteed reasoning question

    Try this first

    India faces environmental threats from BOTH poverty AND affluence simultaneously. Give one example of each kind of threat.

    1

    Poverty-induced degradation: poor rural households relying on wood/dung/biomass fuel, causing deforestation and reduced green cover.

    2

    Affluence-driven pollution: rapidly growing industrial sector and rising vehicle ownership (from 3 lakh vehicles in 1951 to 35 crore in 2022) causing urban air pollution.

    3

    Both threats operate simultaneously in India — it's not one OR the other.

    4

    NCERT explicitly calls this "a dichotomy — threat of poverty-induced environmental degradation and, at the same time, threat of pollution from affluence."

    NCERT's 5 Priority Environmental Issues §7.3

    "(i) land degradation (ii) biodiversity loss (iii) air pollution with special reference to vehicular pollution in urban cities (iv) management of fresh water and (v) solid waste management."

    Key numbers on India's environmental stress

    FactFigure
    Per capita forest land (actual vs required)0.06 hectare vs 0.47 hectare needed
    Soil erosion rate5.3 billion tonnes/year
    India's share of world population / livestock, on how much land~17% humans, ~20% livestock, on just 2.5% of world's land
    Motor vehicles, 1951 → 20223 lakh → 35 crore
    Two-wheelers + cars share of registered vehicles~85%
    CPCB-identified significantly polluting industry categories17 categories (large/medium scale)

    The Appiko Movement (Box 7.3)

    On 8 September 1983, 160 villagers in Sirsi district, Karnataka hugged trees ("Appiko" = to hug) to stop commercial felling in Salkani forest — saving 12,000 trees. Modelled on the Himalayan Chipko Movement, it spread to neighbouring districts within months.

    Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), 1974 (Box 7.4)

    Set up to address water and air pollution — monitors water quality across 125 rivers (plus tributaries, wells, lakes), sets emission/effluent standards, and conducts industry inspections. State-level boards followed.

    Memory Trick

    Two threats, same country: poverty degrades, affluence pollutes. 5 priority issues: Land, Biodiversity, Air (vehicles), Fresh water, Solid waste.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a direct "name India's five priority environmental issues" question, plus fact-recall on the specific numbers (vehicle growth, forest land deficit, CPCB's founding year).
