    04Sustainable Development — The Concept

    One famous UN definition boils an entire philosophy of development down to two words: "needs" and "future generations" — and NCERT wants you to notice exactly why those two words matter most.

    The Brundtland definition, quoted verbatim, is one of this chapter's most-tested exact quotes

    Try this first

    The Brundtland Commission's definition of sustainable development is "development that meets the need of the present generation without compromising the ability of the future generation to meet their own needs." Why does NCERT specifically flag the words 'need' and 'future generations' as the definition's catch-phrases?

    1

    "Need" ties sustainable development to the distribution of resources — meeting basic needs for everyone, not just growth for its own sake.

    2

    "Future generations" builds in an explicit obligation that today's development can't be paid for by tomorrow's people.

    3

    Together, these two ideas turn "meeting needs" into a moral issue about redistribution, not just an economic growth target.

    4

    This is why NCERT explicitly calls meeting everyone's needs "a moral issue," not merely a technical or economic one.

    The Brundtland Commission's Definition (UNCED) §7.4

    "Development that meets the need of the present generation without compromising the ability of the future generation to meet their own needs."
    Thinker/BodyTheir framing of sustainable development
    Brundtland Commission / UNCEDPresent needs met without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs
    Edward BarbierRaising the material standard of living of the poor at the grassroots — measured via income, education, health, sanitation, water
    Herman Daly (5 conditions)Population within carrying capacity; input-efficient technology; renewable extraction ≤ regeneration rate; non-renewable depletion ≤ substitute-creation rate; correct pollution inefficiencies

    Herman Daly's "Plimsoll line" analogy

    The carrying capacity of the environment is compared to a ship's Plimsoll line — its load limit mark. Just as a ship sinks if loaded past this line, an economy that grows past the environment's carrying capacity deviates from sustainable development.

    SDGs — the 2030 global target

    In 2015, the UN formulated 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), intended to be achieved by 2030 — the current global framework operationalising sustainable development.

    Memory Trick

    "Need" + "future generations" = the two catch-phrases. Daly's Plimsoll line = carrying capacity as a hard load limit, not a soft guideline.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect the Brundtland definition quoted back verbatim as a fact-recall question, and possibly a "why are 'need' and 'future generations' significant" reasoning question.
    NCERT — Sustainable Development — The Concept, p. 124Open in new tab

    05Strategies for Sustainable Development

    From gobar gas plants to photovoltaic solar cells, India has real, working alternatives to its most polluting energy and farming habits — each with a specific niche where it works best.

    Matching each strategy to its specific benefit is a guaranteed scenario-matching question

    Try this first

    A remote mountain village has no access to the electricity grid, but a small perennial stream flows nearby. Which sustainable-energy strategy is best suited here, and why?

    1

    The village is remote (grid access is costly/impossible) but has a perennial water source.

    2

    A mini-hydel plant uses exactly such streams to power small local turbines.

    3

    It avoids large-scale transmission towers/cables and transmission loss, since power is generated and used locally.

    4

    It's also environment-friendly since it doesn't change the land-use pattern of the area — a perfect fit for this specific scenario.

    NCERT's Own Words §7.5

    Mini-hydel plants "are more or less environment-friendly as they do not change the land use pattern in areas where they are located; they generate enough power to meet local demands... [and] avoid transmission loss."
    StrategyBest suited for / key benefit
    LPG & Gobar gas (rural)Replaces wood/dung-cake burning — reduces deforestation, air pollution; slurry byproduct is organic fertiliser
    CNG (urban)Public transport fuel — sharply lowered Delhi's air pollution
    Wind powerHigh-wind areas; high initial cost but no adverse environmental impact
    Solar (photovoltaic)Remote areas without grid access; pollution-free; India leads the International Solar Alliance (ISA)
    Mini-hydel plantsMountainous regions with perennial streams; no land-use change, no transmission loss

    Traditional knowledge — a genuine, functioning resource

    India has ~15,000 medicinal plant species, with ~8,000 in regular use (Ayurveda, Unani, Tibetan, folk systems) — now resurging for chronic-condition treatment and herbal cosmetic products, as alternatives to heavy industrial/chemical processing.

    Biocomposting & Biopest control — reversing Green Revolution side-effects

    Biocomposting: using organic waste/cattle dung compost (accelerated by earthworms) instead of chemical fertiliser, reducing water/soil contamination. Biopest control: plant-based pesticides (neem-derived), mixed cropping, and natural predators (snakes, owls, peacocks, lizards) reduce reliance on chemical pesticides that had contaminated food, soil, and water since the Green Revolution.

    Memory Trick

    Each strategy has ONE ideal niche: LPG/gobar gas → rural households; CNG → urban transport; solar → remote/off-grid; mini-hydel → mountain streams; wind → high-wind zones.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a scenario question matching a specific rural/urban/remote situation to the correct energy strategy — each strategy in NCERT's list has one clearly-stated ideal use case.
    NCERT — Strategies for Sustainable Development, p. 125Open in new tab

    01Common Starting Points — India, China & Pakistan

    Three very different political systems today — a secular democracy, a militarist power structure, and a one-party command economy — all began their development journey at almost exactly the same historical moment.

    The independence years and first-plan years are guaranteed fact-recall

    Try this first

    India, China, and Pakistan all had similar growth rates and per capita incomes until roughly the 1980s, despite starting their planning processes within just a few years of each other. What does this tell you about how "similar starting point" and "similar political system" are two different things?

    1

    All three nations became independent/established within 2 years of each other (India & Pakistan 1947, China 1949) and began formal five year planning within a few years too.

    2

    Yet their political systems are radically different — India's secular liberal democracy, Pakistan's militarist power structure, China's one-party command economy.

    3

    Despite this political divergence, their economic starting conditions (growth, per capita income) stayed comparable until the 1980s.

    4

    This proves political structure and shared economic starting point are separate variables — the real divergence came later, from differing policy choices (the subject of the next two topics).

    NCERT's Own Words §8.1-8.2

    "Till the 1980s, all the three countries had similar growth rates and per capita incomes." India and Pakistan share "little similarity" in political structure with "the command economy of China that has only recently started moving towards a democratic system."
    CountryIndependence/FoundingFirst Five Year Plan
    India19471951-56
    Pakistan19471956 (now called Medium Term Development Plan)
    China (People's Republic)19491953

    A genuinely shared early strategy

    India and Pakistan both adopted a large public sector and raised public expenditure on social development — a real policy similarity in their early decades, despite their political differences.

    Why comparing neighbours matters — NCERT's own reasoning

    Developing countries face competition not just from developed nations but from each other, within a "relatively limited economic space." Regional/global groupings like SAARC, BRICS, G-20 reflect this same logic of neighbours needing to understand each other's strategies.

    Memory Trick

    1947/1947/1949 → 1951/1956/1953. Independence years and first-plan years, in that country order: India, Pakistan, China.

    Why CUET asks this —The exact independence and first-plan years for all three countries are precise, checkable facts and a near-guaranteed one-liner.

    02China's Development Strategy

    China's path ran through a famine that killed millions before it found the reforms that built today's manufacturing giant — and NCERT is explicit about both the failure and the fix.

    The Great Leap Forward's failure + 1978 reforms are the chapter's most-tested China facts

    Try this first

    China's 1978 reforms began in agriculture, dividing commune land into small plots allocated to individual households (for use, not ownership), who could keep income after paying taxes. Why did this specific reform matter so much for what came next?

    1

    Households now had a direct incentive to raise output, since they kept the income themselves (after tax).

    2

    This "brought prosperity to a vast number of poor people," per NCERT.

    3

    That prosperity created the conditions for the next phase — rapid growth of rural industries.

    4

    Success at this small, agricultural first step "built up a strong support base for more reforms" — China's reforms succeeded partly because each measure was tested small-scale before being scaled up nationally.

    NCERT's Own Words §8.2

    "The Great Leap Forward (GLF) campaign initiated in 1958... met with many problems. A severe drought caused havoc in China killing about 30 million people." "The present day fast industrial growth in China can be traced back to the reforms introduced in 1978."
    PhaseKey Events
    Pre-reform (1949 onward)All sectors/enterprises/land under government control; Great Leap Forward (1958) — mass industrialisation drive, 26,000 communes by 1958, failed with ~30 million deaths from drought/famine
    1966-76Cultural Proletarian Revolution — students/professionals sent to countryside
    1978 reforms, Phase 1Agriculture, foreign trade & investment — commune land divided into individual-use plots
    1978 reforms, Phase 2Industrial sector — private firms + township/village enterprises allowed; State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) faced competition; dual pricing; Special Economic Zones for foreign investment

    Dual pricing — a specific reform mechanism

    Farmers/industrial units had to buy/sell FIXED quantities at government-set prices, while anything beyond that quota was bought/sold at market prices. As production rose over time, the market-priced share of transactions grew — a gradual, not sudden, transition to market pricing.

    Why China had no external compulsion to reform (unlike India/Pakistan)

    Unlike India and Pakistan, China did NOT reform under World Bank/IMF pressure. New Chinese leadership was simply unhappy with slow growth under Maoist self-sufficiency — by 1978, per capita grain output was no higher than in the mid-1950s, despite land reforms and the GLF.

    Memory Trick

    1958 GLF = failure (30 million deaths). 1978 reforms = success (agriculture first, industry second, SEZs for foreign capital). China reformed by choice, not IMF/World Bank pressure.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect direct fact-recall on the GLF's failure (year, death toll) and the 1978 reform's two-phase sequencing (agriculture, then industry) — both are precise, frequently-tested facts.

    03Pakistan's Development Strategy

    Pakistan's strategy looked strikingly similar to India's for decades — until a very different post-reform trajectory revealed why "similar policy" doesn't guarantee "similar outcome."

    Pakistan's nationalisation-then-denationalisation reversal is a guaranteed sequencing question

    Try this first

    In the 1970s, Pakistan nationalised its capital goods industries. But by the late 1970s-80s, its policy thrust shifted to denationalisation and encouraging the private sector. Why does this policy REVERSAL matter for understanding Pakistan's development path?

    1

    Pakistan, like India, adopted a mixed economy model — but oscillated between more state control (1970s nationalisation) and less (late 1970s-80s denationalisation).

    2

    This reversal reflects genuine policy volatility, not a steady, consistent strategy.

    3

    During the denationalisation phase, Pakistan ALSO received financial support from western nations and remittances from Middle-East emigrants — external factors also shaped its growth, not policy alone.

    4

    This volatility, combined with reliance on external support and good/bad harvests rather than institutionalised technical change, is part of why scholars later found Pakistan's economic indicators worsened post-reform (1988).

    NCERT's Own Words §8.2

    "In the 1970s, nationalisation of capital goods industries took place. Pakistan then shifted its policy orientation in the late 1970s and 1980s when the major thrust areas were denationalisation and encouragement of private sector."
    PeriodPakistan's Policy Focus
    Late 1950s-1960sImport-substitution industrialisation — tariff protection + direct import controls
    Green Revolution eraMechanisation, public investment in infrastructure, rise in foodgrain production
    1970sNationalisation of capital goods industries
    Late 1970s-1980sDenationalisation, private sector encouragement; western financial support + Middle-East remittances
    1988Formal reforms initiated

    The verdict on Pakistan's reform outcome

    Scholars argue Pakistan's reform process led to worsening of economic indicators overall. Growth rate of GDP and its sectors have not improved compared to the 1980s. Poverty (by Pakistan's own official data) fell from over 40% (1960s) to 25% (1980s) — then began RISING again in recent decades.

    Why Pakistan's growth remained fragile — the key structural reason

    NCERT is explicit: agricultural growth and food supply depended on good harvests, not an institutionalised process of technical change. Good harvest → good economy; bad harvest → stagnation/negative trends. This weather-dependence, not deliberate policy, largely explains the slowdown.

    Memory Trick

    Nationalise (1970s) → Denationalise (late 1970s-80s) → Reform (1988). Pakistan's growth relied on good harvests, not institutionalised technical change — its key long-run vulnerability.

    Why CUET asks this —The nationalisation-then-denationalisation sequence and its exact decades are a guaranteed ordering/fact-recall question.
    NCERT — Pakistan's Development Strategy, p. 137Open in new tab

    04Demographic, GDP & Sectoral Comparison

    One in every six people on Earth is Indian or Chinese — and the hard numbers on population, growth, and sectoral output reveal exactly how differently these three neighbours turned that scale into development.

    China's GDP(PPP) figure and the sectoral GVA/workforce mismatch are guaranteed numerical questions

    Try this first

    In 2022, India's industry sector employed 26% of its workforce but contributed 28% to GVA, while agriculture employed 43% of the workforce but contributed only 18% to GVA. What does this mismatch reveal about the productivity of India's agricultural sector relative to industry?

    1

    Industry: 26% of workers produce 28% of output — output share slightly EXCEEDS workforce share.

    2

    Agriculture: 43% of workers produce only 18% of output — output share is far BELOW workforce share.

    3

    This means output-per-worker (productivity) is much lower in agriculture than in industry.

    4

    Nearly half of India's workforce remains stuck in the sector generating disproportionately little value — a structural inefficiency shared with (and even worse in) Pakistan.

    NCERT's Own Words §8.3-8.4

    "If we look at the global population, out of every six persons living in this world, one is an Indian and another a Chinese." "China has the second largest GDP (PPP) of $35 trillion in the world, whereas, India's GDP (PPP) is $15 trillion and Pakistan's GDP is $1.5 trillion."

    Table 8.1 — Demographic Indicators, 2021-23

    CountryPopulation (mn)Pop. GrowthDensitySex RatioUrbanisation
    India14280.8147393036%
    China1411−0.1015089865%
    Pakistan2401.9630094838%

    China's one-child policy (late 1970s) explains its low population growth — but also a skewed sex ratio, later prompting a shift to a two-child policy as the population began ageing.

    Table 8.3 — Sectoral Share, 2022 (% of GVA / % of Workforce)

    SectorIndia GVA/WorkforceChina GVA/WorkforcePakistan GVA/Workforce
    Agriculture18 / 438 / 2324 / 36
    Industry28 / 2638 / 3221 / 26

    China's growth engine vs India's

    China's growth has been driven by BOTH manufacturing and services; India's growth has been driven mainly by the service sector alone — India and Pakistan shifted workforce directly toward services, largely bypassing the industrial-employment stage China went through.

    Memory Trick

    China = manufacturing + services growth. India = services-only growth. Both India and Pakistan skipped the industrial-employment stage China went through — a structural difference, not just a numbers difference.

    Why CUET asks this —Expect a numerical question comparing sectoral GVA share vs workforce share (productivity mismatch), and China's specific GDP(PPP) figure as a fact-recall.

    05Human Development & Development Strategies — An Appraisal

    China leads India and Pakistan on almost every human development indicator — but NCERT insists the story isn't complete without asking what the HDI leaves out entirely.

    The "liberty indicators" critique of HDI is a distinctive, frequently-tested reasoning question

    Try this first

    China ranks well ahead of India and Pakistan on almost every Human Development Index component — income, health, education. Why does NCERT still caution against judging "which country has developed better" using HDI alone?

    1

    HDI measures income, health, and education — genuinely important, but not exhaustive measures of a good life.

    2

    NCERT argues we also need "liberty indicators" — measures of democratic participation, constitutional protection of rights, and independence of the judiciary/rule of law.

    3

    Only one such indicator (democratic participation) has even been added to HDI-related measures, and it isn't given extra weight; others aren't measured at all.

    4

    NCERT's own conclusion: without these, "the construction of a human development index may be said to be incomplete and its usefulness limited."

    NCERT's Own Words §8.5-8.6

    "We also need what may be called 'liberty indicators'... 'the extent of Constitutional protection given to rights of citizens' or 'the extent of constitutional protection of the Independence of the Judiciary and the Rule of Law' have not even been introduced so far."

    Table 8.5 — Human Development Indicators, 2017-2023

    IndicatorIndiaChinaPakistan
    HDI Value / Rank0.685 / 1300.797 / 780.544 / 168
    Life Expectancy72.078.067.6
    GNI per capita (PPP US$)9,04722,0295,501
    Infant Mortality (per 1000)25.54.851
    Maternal Mortality (per lakh births)10323154

    Why China's 1978 reforms succeeded — NCERT's own explanation

    Pre-existing infrastructure (education, health), land reforms, decentralised planning, and small enterprises all helped. Crucially, each reform was tested small-scale before nationwide rollout — allowing costs of failure to be assessed cheaply before scaling.

    The reform-year comparison — a direct 3-way contrast

    China (1978), Pakistan (1988), India (1991) — China reformed by internal choice (dissatisfaction with Maoist stagnation, not IMF/World Bank pressure), while India needed IMF/World Bank support to fix a genuine balance-of-payments crisis.

    Memory Trick

    China leads on HDI's own measures — but HDI itself is incomplete without "liberty indicators." Reform years, in order: China 1978 → Pakistan 1988 → India 1991.

    Why CUET asks this —"Why is the HDI construction said to be incomplete?" is a distinctive NCERT argument (not just fact-recall) — expect the liberty-indicators critique tested as a reasoning question, not a simple lookup.
